AGENTS:
CARTER & SON, BRIDGE ST. WARRINGTON.
SMALL HOLDERS IN FRANCE.

"While there are several points of close similarity between the French and the English poultry industry, the points of dissimilarity are still more striking. It is true that in both countries the bulk of those interested in the business are peasants and small farmers, but while in England poultry-keeping is still in its infancy in many respects, in France it has for many years past been regarded as of supreme import- ance among rural industries. In any country where the land is split up into a large number of small hold- ings one is certain to find poultry-keeping in a flourishing condition ; in a country. on the other hand, where large farms abound, the industry is almost sure to be neglected. Franca is eminently a land of small holdings, farms of more than forty acres being rare, while the average size does not exceed twenty to twenty-five acres. Tnousands of men and women in France to-day are supporting themselves and their families upon ten or fifteen acres, and while it is true that there is not much margin left after providing for the bare necessaries of life, yet a li‘ing is being secured. A large proportion of these men and women rely largely on their fowls, although, of course, they devote themselves to other important branches."—E T BrtowN, in "Farm and Home."

div.head: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
div.p: PRACTICAL POULTRY FARMING.
[BY REDCAP.]
DUCKS

Duck rearing is on of the most profitable branches of poultry farming. When bred for table they fetch good prices and if bred for egg production (providing you have the right strain) they show a good profit. Young ducklings need less attention than do young chickens, as a matter of fact they always determine to go on their own long before the broody hen has a desire to leave them. After the first three weeks they will almost brood themselves. Just a little attentien is required on cold nights, for like all other young life, they must be kept warm.

div.head: FEEDING.
div.p: FEEDING.

Quite the reverse should he observed in the feeding of ducklings to that of chickens. Whilst the food of chicks should be dry and crumbly, it should be moist -or even pasty for young ducklings. Egg food is required for the first two days only. Then for the next few day's, boiled rice and milk, or bread and milk should be given. The second week, continue to feed with rice and milk but mix with this, some oatmeal and animal food in a concentrated form. As they continue development you may put them on to biscuit meal and thirds with a little bran and maize meal added. A good many people imagine that unless ducks have free access to a pond they will not thrive. This is an erroneous idea, so long as you always have before them plenty of clean drinking water they will thrive.Of courae,one has to admit, that greater fertility is ensured when ducks have access to plenty of swimming water. ARTIFICIAL PONDS.

Plenty of duck breeders construct their own duck ponds. And where one has a good supply of water this is not a difficulty. A cavity in the earth should be made and then lined with rough concrete. The cavity need not he deep at all, simply deep enough for the ducks to dive overhead. h is always better if you can arrange for a constant flow of water through the artificial pond. Where this cannot be done, then it should be cleaned our twice a week. A drinking trough should always be handy and in the bottom of this, some good sharp sea sand and flint grit be placed.

div.head: BREEDS TO KEEP.
div.p: BREEDS TO KEEP.

Like poultry, the number of varieties of ducks con- tinue to increase. I was laughed at last week when I chanced to make mention of Buff Orpington Ducks. Nevertheles., they are numbered amongst the Duck family. Then we have Blue Orpington Ducks, White Indian Runner and Khaki Campbell Ducks amongst the newer varieties. For egg production the Indian Runner easily btands first. 'lbis is a grand breed of duck and by many they are farmed on an extensive scale for egg proctuction. I have no hesitation in recommending small holders to wake more use of the Indian Runner duck. They are su.all eaters and if they have access to a 'pond and meadow they cost very little to keep. A friend of mine who has kept them for a dozen years tells me that his greatest difficulty is in getting them home to feed. Yes ! they are rare foragers indeed. INT,iw unless properly trained ducks will lay away. The better plan is to keep them in the duck cote until they have laid, then turn them out to forage. They soon get used to this habit and are very little trouble.

div.head: ALL ROUND VARIETJES.
div.p: ALL ROUND VARIETJES.
Those whose space is limited, and whose desire is a good all-round bread, may select from the follow- ing : —Buff Orpington, Cayugas and Khaki Campbell.
BEST TABLE VARIETIES.

The Aylesbury Ducks are undoubtedly the best for table purposes. The Pekin and Rouen come next. For a quick growing cross you cannot go wrong if you inter-breed with these varieties. The Aylesbury- Pekin, and the Pekin-Rouen cross are amongst the very best for culinai y purposes. Amongst our small farmers duck-farming is a very neglected industry,and from a profit side of view, they would do well to culture them. They are less trouble to manage than poultry. They need less housing accommodation and are generally speaking more profitable than poultry.

div.head: QUERIES
div.p: QUERIES

I have more poultry queries to answer this week. I am glad that readers are making more use of the p,ultry column. But, by-the-way, those chicken hints for the competition are coming in slowly. Let me have them eariy if you please.

div.head: SAWDUST.
div.p: SAWDUST.

" ANXIOI:,, On" wants to know if I consider saw- dust a good thing to use in a scratching shed? —No, I do not, especi -lly when small seeds are given to the stock. They are apt to pick up a certain proportion and internal trouble is the tesult. Sawdust is a very 'useful in the sleeping quarters but not in the scratching shed. Straw litter and dead leaves are the best materials to use in the scratching shed. Get a neighbouring farmer or corn merchant to chop you half a bale of straw, st(a-e it in sacks and use it at your discretion. Chcpped straw is both cleaner and lasts longer than any other arateliad for the floor of a dry bcratching shed.

div.head: TIIE SIZE OF EGGS.
div.p: TIIE SIZE OF EGGS.

"SUBITRBIAN" wants to know if there is any means of increasing the size of eggs ? Be states that some breeds lay a lot of eggs, but they are small. One never knows, of con rse,what may happen in he future, but at the present time I do not know of any method of making a hen (which lays a small egg) lay a larger one—unless you give her a good talking to. I should recommend Suburbian " if he has some of these 'small egg machines' to get rid of them and obtain a better strain. That is, of course, if the eggs are for marketable purposes. What (ices it matter if they are small if you want them for home consumption, pro- viding you get plenty of them ? Ile further asks what breed of poultry lays the large,t egg? I should say the Black Spanish; next to these the Black Minorca and Blue Andalusian. The best way to get a strain of fowls laying large eggs is by selection in mating. You must never cross mate a racehorse with a cart horse if you want Derby winners.' Pedigree breed- ing in poultry farming is just as essential as in any other branch of farming. For instance, have yr,ll never heard of Messrs Garton's pedigree breed of farm seeds?
I.4IGG:i for Sitting.—Rosscomben Rhode island Reds, 12.4 3s. sitting.—E. HALSALL, High lane Farm, Bursm,ugh rd., near Ormskirk. _ _ .
EGGS for sitting.—Rhode Island Reds, S. C. de Grafts strain ; first pen, 3s 6d. ; second pen 2s. 6d. per sitting.—D. HARRISON, Mill lane,Rurscough,

div.head: REMINDERS FOR MARCH.
div.p: REMINDERS FOR MARCH.
Protect the chickens from cold winds. Sow mustard and cress in small boxes for the chicks. The weather i still very cold, give the laying stock an occasional feed of maize.
Sit every egg p_seible from the heavy breeds this month.
Don't forget to give the broody hen a good dusting with Keating's ' before setting her. Examine the young stock often ; if any vermin is found treat them likewise.
If you have got as many eggs from the breeding pen as you require for he present, givo the male hint a rest. Give him also a feor breakfasts of hot bread and milk. _ _
Recommend the poultry column to your friends and please don't forget the" Chicken Hints Competition."

div.head: !ALL UGILT3 r.ESERVED.3 A STUDY IN STRATEGY.
div.p: !ALL UGILT3 r.ESERVED.3 A STUDY IN STRATEGY.
131 FRANCES ARNOLD.

There was a sharp knock at the ball - door. George Marston knew by instinct that he was ; going to hear bad news. The very echo ' through the house had a dismal effect. He made a sudden jump from his chair, and up- set the breakfast things all over the table. Then he sat down again as quickly, and be- gan, with trembling hands, to sort the sugar -Jut of a mixture of jam and cold coffee. His wife got uD without making a remark, and left the room. She had the air of one who knew what the cause of his distress was all about, and did not see any reason to hurry. During her absence he listened to the beat- ings of his heart, waiting to learn the evil tidings. She came back after a while. There was an open telegram in her hand, and her face was flushed. Amy Marston looked with pleading eyes towards her husband. It was plain that she had some secret scheme on hand that gave her an anxious moment. Any- one would have seen she wished to get his approval in a quiet way; but the firm set of her jaw showed she would hardly try to move by tears. "Tell me, Amy, tell me, is there anything wrong? " George gasped. " I hope not," she quietly replied, going over behind his chair. " Come, out with it—let me know the worst ! " he cried, as he leant his clasped hands on the table. " Don't be afraid to shock me," he added, in an ambiguous way. She put her elbows on his shoulders, and stooping down till her face touched his, held the telegram in front of him. This is what he read " Letter just re- ceived coming evening mail meet me station mother." George now turned white with rage. He had not dreaded anything as bad as this. " Did you invite her here, or is she coming oa her own?" he demanded. _ _

"The question is a bit involved," his wife retorted, and not entirely free from slang." The evasion helped her to hide her agita- tion. "But to be plain about it," Amy con- tinued, more at her ease, "she and I have made it all up in secret, and I wrote and asked her to come—and you needn't be get- ting cross about it," she concluded, all in a breath, anticipating an outburst. This turned back the rising tide, or George's wrath, and increased its fury. It \\as the first time he had been angry with his wife. " Who's getting cross?" he inquired. He turned half-round, and, _ crossing his legs, . .

affected an easy manner. In the intense calm of his voice she caught the faint rumblings of the storm, and soon realised the risk as well as the folly of speaking her mind. All her at• tention was given to the spilt coffee, which had made little rivulets along the tablecloth, and began to drip on the carpet. If she wanted to annoy him she could not have hit on a better way. In a verbal conflict, nothin.g vexes a man more than to be put on his mettle with a taunt, and then yielded a doubt- ful victory. When George had waited in vain for a chance to argue the question, he was driven to confide in an imaginary sympathiser. He was quite certain that he was not losing his temper, he declared, in tremulous tones that mocked his words. Anyone who suggested he was getting cross did not know their man. Why, the very notion was absurd. People should have the goodness to lay the ghost they had raised. It was not very nice to make an insinuation and then back away from it. But he would not make reflections (an anyone ; others could do that. " I'm sure mamma would be extremely an- noyed to hear of all this fuss," Amy pouted. George was glad he had drawn her at last. But he felt at a loss how to use his advantage. He was goin,, to remark that Mrs. Haddon's rental anguish would give him a new zest in life. However, he heroically denied himself the relief and soothing effects of such an avowal.

"Why did you make so much mystery about it, any way?" he ventured to ask. - " Oh, I wanted to give you a surprise," she explained. Once again George did viol-mice to his feel- ings, almost to the extreme of suicide. You have succeeded admirably," be glied at length. This candid, if sarcastic, testi- mony to her efforts saved him from the agony, the tragedy of restraint. "Thou I had better wire mamma not to come?" she tearfully suggested. ".It does not follow at all, my dear." George tried to console her. There was a sud- den change in Isis manlier that she could not make out.

"Well, why were you so much put out, darling? " she timidly wanted to know, tread- ing again on dangerous ground. " Put out!" he echoed. " Who says I'm put out? I had very good reason to be put out if I was—but I'm not. Here I am, with- out a moment to prepare suitably for our first meeting. You should not spring a thing like that on a fellow; and, in any case, that tele- glam startled me." Even if George was excitable, he was still a man of resource, and generally managed to get his own way without having to fight for it. "Oh ! George darling! " his wife gushed, " I knew you would receive dear mamma kindly. I would never have written to her at all, only I knew you would be glad deep down in your heart." "Of course," he assured her; " but I'll have to hurry down direct to the station so as to save time, as we are frightfully rushed at the office."

"One would almost think you were serious, Amy dear," Mrs. Haddon interposed. "Well, supposing so?" was all poor Amy could say. "George should not admire any- one but me," she reflected. "Of course, it's only mamma; but even that. makes me wild, and its so unlike him to hint that—that " Here Amy discovered that the eggs required more boiling. When she returned it was quite plain that the fire had made her eyes very red. Really, George," she sobbed, as she kissed him in the hall, "I'm not such a fright as you seem to think." _ . _ _ .
- "But you know, dear, few girls could starld a comparison with mother," replied tho brute, as he retprned to speak to that estim- able lady. . .

mti o lel', he :suggested, "you ought to , come down to the office at five, and we'll stroll home together and see the shops. I'm sure you'll like the walk." "Most certainly, George," she beamed. People along the terrace wondered why the young man from Woodbine laughed so im- moderately along the way. There was also wonder within the cottage. Mrs. Haddon could not understand her daughter's sudden change of manner. "George is too delightful for anything," she .confided. "How people are so apt to be deceived," he added. The full significance of the words scarcely dawned on her. "I am glad you two get on together—much better than I had expected,'" Amy answered, with the slightest tone!' of bitterness in her tone. George would have listened with feel- ings of triumph and remorse. Whilst sitting alooe during the evening Amy felt herself neglected. "He has never once asked me down to meet him," she sighed. "In fact, he always detested that sort of thing; but I suppose he wants to show mamma round for my sake. It's almost seven o'clock and they're not home yet. Whatever can be keeping them? George is always home so punctually. Really, I shouldn't like this sort of thing to continue." "I thought mother would care for some tea, so we dropped into the Bohea," George ex- plained nail an hour afterwards. "Hope you weren't waiting for us, dear?" Of course she could not blame him. Dar- ling George was so unselfish. Still, it was not pleasant for her to sit so long alone while the dinner was getting spoilt. Any way, he had brought home her favourite bon-bons, about which she had specially re- minded him that morning. Really, my love, you must excuse me," he pleaded. "Mother was so delighted with Sweetem's chocolates that I had to go round for a couple of boxes. That took me out of the way, and in fact caused no little delay. Now you understand, dear. I know you detest Sweetem's, but mother declares they are the only chocolates worth buy- ing—and you know we must try to please her above everything now that she has honoured as. I've been telling her all the places I in- tend taking her. So sorry that baby will keep you at home." She was about to inform him firmly that baby would not keep her at home, when Mrs. Haddon entered. All the evening Amy re- mained in silence and the dumps, whilst George and Mrs. Haddon sang and played and talked together. She was altogether out in the cold, thinking over the first unhappy day in a whole year of married bliss. At another time the thought would have given her strength to suffer; but now the fact that George was unwittingly the cause of her misery only helped to render the tragedy more complete. "Although so glad to make it up," she was thinking, "and to give George and mamma a chance of knowing and appreciating each other, I nearly wish she hadn't come. What shall I do if this sort of thing continues the whole month, or maybe two? All his smiles are now too few for mamma, and every spare moment he devotes to her. I know it's only his goodness, but, after all, there's very little comfort in that. And I nearly think—is it right of me to dream of such a thing?—that she is actually trying to flirt with him. Really, there is not such a disparity in their ages. Let me see. George is thirty-four, whilst mamma is scarcely forty-three. Only just nine years; and George was fourteen when I was born. Oh, I hope it's not wrong of me—but, sitting here alone, I feel—yes, I feel—that she thinks George and she would have been better matched. And she is able to talk to hi so well too, while I can never do any- thing but love him!" "Discussing that subject, now," George was just saying to Mrs. Haddon, as if to con- firm her daughter's impressions, "I agree that very, very few women are entirely enter- taining before forty. At that age they have acquired a large experience of life, without losing any of its romance. This gives the sex a breadth and depth of view which is not only novel and surprising in itself, but refreshing to men tired with the trivialities of fashion and troubles of domestics." "It is that want of interest in the home circle ,that drives so many men to clubs and places after a year or two of married life," added Mrs. Haddon. "They really cannot help it, things grow so dull.' Then turning over some music, "I always loves this little trio. It's about the prettiest thing I know. Let us try ;it over. Oh, I forgot, Amy can't sing. What a pity, as it is a delightful com- position." George's heart melted for his little wife; but it would be ruinous to falter. "Oh, we'll try this duettino from 'Don Giovanni,'" he proposed. "Mozart is always tuneful." "'La ci clarem ' is certainly sweet," she admitted, affecting the part of Zerlina and humming over the music with the lightness of a peasant maiden. "But, George," interruptea Amy, who was beginning to resent the conduct of her mother, "you sing tenor, and Don Giovanni is supposed to be a baritone." "True, dear," George replied; "but mine is an accommodating quality of voice." And then they sang, "Hand Lin!sed in Hand We'll Wander ' until Amy almost fancied she could see George and her mother eloping, and leaving her forlorn for ever with a help- less babe to look after. George now believed that things were pro- gressing favourably. Nevertheless, all night long he cudgelled his brain to discover still more effective ways and means. The present system, while undoubtedly sound, was a bit tedious and exacting. It required too much attention to be lavished on his mother-in- law. Even the highest success could scarcely repay the trouble and mental strain. "I have planned out a regular little round of adventures for the remainder of the week," he announced next morning at break- fast. "This is Thursday, and I intend taking a half-day off. You had better be ready to go go out at 1.30, mother. I have ordered lunch for two at the hotel—l mean two persons and two o'clock," he explained. "There will be a band promenade at the tennis finals this afternoon, so time won't hang too heavily on our hands."' _ _

"The dear boy!" Amy Marston mused, as George hastened away to improve his toilet. "In spite of all he ever said, I knew—oh, yes, I knew it—that George would welcome mamma to our little home. Really though, I should have given him more time to arrange things. And I'm sure mamma will get over aui her silly prejudices as soon as she learns to know him as I do. Her letter was full of re- grets for all she said against our marriage. I must see what's the matter with baby—who is really otir little peacemaker." A few minutes afterwards George was hurrying down the street. Suddenly he jumped with the shock of a. new idea- " I have it he laughed, loudly enough to at- tract attention. A few, who could only see the mirth of madness in his antics, shook their heads in pity. During the day his col- leagues noticed a wild light in his eyes. He set out early for the station. When Mrs. Haddon stepped on to the platform, George seized the buxom lady in his arms and audibly kissed her. Men have been hailed as heroes, crowned as martyrs, for less; but George's scheme demanded the sacrifice. There was a charm about this hearty manner of greeting that appealed strongly to the widow, and left a good impression for the rest of the evening. George had grown desperate by the follow- ing morning. He had to admit to himself, in- deed, that Amy's mother—so far as he cared to observe—was not quite the Gorgon he had imagined her. At the same time, he had no desire to be on really friendly terms with her. If she wanted to make a fool of herself by re- ciprocating his pretended admiration and affection, he would be sorry to larevent her His whole plan—and he had added many finishing touches during the stillness of the night—was to get rid of her without delay. And, in any case, how did he know that she was not as deceitful as himself? These were the reflections of the ungallant young man as he came downstairs. "Doesn't mother's gown look charming?" he asked with rapture at breakfast. "Do you really think so?" Amy replied, raising her eyebrows. There was a little ,thrill of jealousy in her voice which filled George with hope. "My dear," he went on, "you should get something stylish like that—not those dowdy atrocities you wear. It's so bewitching!" "Really?" pouted Amy. "Well, of course," he softly admitted, "the tints are rather trying. Without a good com- plexion—such as mother's, for instance—the; would make one look perfectly hideous." "You shouldn't flatter mamma like that, Amy protested. " Unite unconscious. I- assure von.!' Georto repltecl, as tie helped his mother-in-law to more toast. "It does not sound so," Amy cuttingly re, marked.

"It never does," flattered Mrs. Haddon; and Amy sighed over her tea. She did not even think of asking him how he managd about that half-day—considering how busy they had been on the previous Tuesday. "To-morrow night the Italian Opera Com- pany are paying a flying visit to the Town Hall. I didn't mention that I had taken tickets? No. Well, there was a great run on the • booking-office, down at the stationer's —just two seats left in the reserved portion of the hall. In any case I knew Amy could not conveniently come. Then, on Saturday half-day again, I intend going np the river. The manager kindly offered me the use of his boat when I mentioned to him that you would

likesa row, mother. You remember the nice old gentleman we met yesterday evening?" "But you know, George, I can't stand the river," Amy protested. "Of course," George blandly admitted. " but as mother enjoys boating so much " The-matter-of-course way in which he threw out his hands almost threw Amy into tears. "Yes, indeed," assented Mrs. Haddon. "T think it is really delicious," and she smacked her rosy lips with the gusto of a Sybarite see- ing luxurious visions arise. "And I should so much like to hear the opera." Amy recovered herself, aroused by the aggravating selfishness of her mother.

"W-011. in that ease." Geor.,e zallanthr ro- plled," you and mother can go together—l'm really indifferent." This he regarded as master-stroke. It let Amy see that it was not for his own sake he had intended deserting her for the evehing.
The Examiner, Saturday, March 22, 1913.

• .Hut we could not go alone," both ladie:, psotested together.' "By Jupiter! here's a dilemma," thought George. It will be impossible for us to sit together," he explained. "It was with the greatest difficulty I secured oven two seats. .But I may be able to crush myself in some- where at the back. That won't mend matters much," he added, beneath his breath. "But, George," argued his wife, "wouldn't. it look strange for you and me to be seen in different parts of the house? People would be sure to talk."

"And I'm thinking," Mrs. Haddon ob- jected, "it wouldn't look altogether the thing for a stranger to be seep alone scrambling for a seat; or perhaps standing like • a wall- flower for three hours—a part that would be entirely new to me," she concluded, with crushing dignity, if not historical accuracy. "Perhaps, mamma," suggested the reflec- tive but unobservant Amy, "you wouldn't mind stopping at home. We poor, benighted wretches so seldom get an opportunity of seeing anything." Mrs. Haddon stared in amazement at her daughter. She could not have imagined any sane person making such a suggestion, except, indeed, such a one had lost all respect for herself and others. From her own daughter it was simply outrageous. The atmosphere was charged. George felt that the thunder- storm might burst at any moment. Looking excitedly at the clock, he prepared to leave. It was a good quarter of an hour before his usual time—a fact not observed by either of the ladies—but he feared his presence might avert the calamity he desired—might retard or prevent the disruptive shock which would rend the clouds ,asunder. "Arrange as best you can, my dears," George advised. His words were, in effect, a timely notification that he would decline to accept any responsibility in the matter. "I have to make a call on the way; and, mother, remember 1.30."

"That was a good morning's work," he heartlessly laughed, on his way to business. "I'm sure there will be wigs on the green before I return. Blowed if there wasn't a great—l don't know what—strategist, per- haps I should say, lost in me! Tom Smith, of the bank, offered me that third seat, but I didn't feel like trespassing on his kindness, ha! ha! Maybe, I should only have to be re- turning it at the last moment," he added, illogically. After a couple of hours, when the first flush of his brilliant triumph had faded away, George began to think how meanly he had be- haved all along. After all, Mrs. Haddon was Amy's mother, and would it not be something awful if there should be another falling out between them? And all for him! His own Amy, whom he would not see suffer for the riches of the world! And when he allowed himself to think over it dispassionately, he was convinced that the Widow was a charming woman, full of animation and spirit and social gifts and qualities in a splendid degree; a little selfish, perhaps, but that would be the effect of li)Oing alone. "I might not have discovered it so soon," he soliloquised, on the way home, "only for the desperate manner in which I have carried on. Really, 'twas my own selfishness that blinded me from the beginning. There are silly humorists who tilt at everything sacred and noble, and I always stupidly laughed when their raillery was directed against the grandest of our social institutions. Yes, that's what it is. The place would be lonery enough now without mother, as I used to mockingly call her. I must suggest to Amy how jolly it would be if she came and stopped with us altogether. And then that legacy she men- tioned last night is not a thing to be sneezed at. By Jupiter! it strike.; me forcibly—oh, my poor shin! When did they begin to leave those beastly dust-bins out on the middle of the path?—that I must hurry back to Tom Smith about that ticket." _ _ _

George arrived home a little late, but his spirits were very high. "I've secured three seats, all in a row," he sang. "I was prepared to pay a fancy price, but a friend down tovn can't go, so here we are. Glorious, isn't it? " He was answered by a gentle sobbing. "Why, what's the matter with the girl?" he asked, seeing Amy in distress. "Mamma's gone home," she faltered. "Well, I'm--" He paused, unable to find an expletive to express exactly his state of feeling and astonishment.
ETRE END.]

div.head: WARRINGTON ESPERANTO SOCIETY. Presentation to Mr. T. G. Cathro.
div.p: WARRINGTON ESPERANTO SOCIETY. Presentation to Mr. T. G. Cathro.

On Tuesday, a social reunion of the members of the Esperanto Club took place in their rooms, Bewsey- street, to make to Mr Cathro a presentation of hooks on the occasion of his leaving Warrington, owing to Many sympathetic speeches were made in which the parts that be bad played in the club's foundation rind since then ai secretary, were deservedly praised. The ?resident said that be telt ery keenly the loss as a personal one besides what it meant to the cause of Esperanto, but be assured Mr and Mrs Cathro that their memory and the memory of their excellent work would live atter them and he a spur to all the members carry on the work they all had so much at heart. Mr James Ham pson spoke regretfully of their departure as he had found, in the course of a friendship that bad been built on and cemented by Esporantisrn, that besides Esperanto and Esperantism be and Mr Cathro had many other sympathies in cornmcn. Miss SMITH, ;,vice-president, Miss D PARSONAGE, assistant secretary, and Mr E 0 ButtuEss expressed how sorry all the members were to lose Mr and Nlrs Cathro and wished them health and happiness through the whole course of their future lives. - .

Mr Camino, in reply, thlnked most sincerely the esteemed President and the others for their very kind speeches, and also for the very handsome gift which the Society had just presented to him, and in saying farewell expressed the keen regret which both his wife and he felt in parting from them all. He spoke furthcr of the many genuine and valu- able friendships formed with the members of the Society, and especially with their President, the influence of which had been a great gain to him. in saying "Adieu "he wished the society increased prosperity and a still greater number of members in the future. _ _
The ladies refreshment corn mittee,the Misses Smith, G and D Parsonage, E and J Corney, L3all, Gorman, Crolla, &c., gave 'very sat isfa'...tion by their kindly and untiring ministration.

div.head: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE
div.p: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE
TO ACIDITY.
SO SAYS EMINENT SPECIALIST.

So-called stomach troubles, such as indigestion, wind, stomach-ache and inability to retain food, instead of indicating that the stomach is out of order, are in nine cases out of ten simply evidence that fermentation is taking place in the food contents of the stomach, causing the formation of gas and acids. Wind distends the stomach, and causes that full, oppressive feeling sometimes known as heartburn, while the acid irritates and inflames the delicate lining of the stomach. The stomach, however, is not at fault. The trouble lies entirely in the fermenting food. Such fermentation is unnatuial, and acid formation is not only unnatural, but may involve the most serious consequences if not prevented. To pievent or stop fermentation of the food contents of the stomach and to neutralise the acid, and render it bland and harmless, half a teaspoonfal of bisurated magnesia, probably the best and most effeciive antacid known, should be taken in a quarter of a glass of hot or cold water immediately after eating, or whenever wind or acidity is felt. This stops the fermentation, and neutralises the acidity in a few moments. Fermentation, wind and acidity are dangerous and unnecessary. stop or prevent them by the use of a proper antacid, such as bisurated magnesia, which can be obtained from any chemist, and thus enable the stomach to do its work properly without being hindered by poisonous gas and danger- ous acids.-11.F.P.

div.head: FARMERS "FORCED" SALE. A RUNCORN LAWSUIT.
div.p: FARMERS "FORCED" SALE. A RUNCORN LAWSUIT.

Thomas Harrison, a Runcorn farmer, WEIR sued at Runcorn County Court on Tuesday, by Messrs Thomas Ashworth and Sons, patent manure manufacturers, of Frodsbaro, for £B. It was stated that Harrison purchased goods valued at £l7 from Messrs Ashworth in September. A sale at his farm was seen by nze plaintiffs to he advertised in February, and they instructed their solicitors to write him for the money due. He saw a representative of the firm next day, and offered ss. in the pound, stating that the sale was a forced one and would not realise £2OO, and that, he owed £5OO. The plaintiffs finally agreed to accept 10s. in the pound. It was now contended that the sale was not a forced one. Dr Arnett, of Messrs Evans, Lescher, and Webb, the Liverpool chemists, said his firm bought the farm at a very much higher price than £2OO. For the defence it was urged that the defendant had given a true account of his position at the time he saw Messrs Ashworth, and there was not then much prospect of the deal with Messrs Evans and Co. going through. Several witnesses called for plaintiff said in cross-examination that they had always found Harrison an honourable man. Tne bearing was adjourned.
GRAPPENHALL LIBERALS.

div.head: Mr. P_ EL Oliver and the Bankrupt Party
div.p: Mr. P_ EL Oliver and the Bankrupt Party
NO CONSTRUCTIVE POLICY.

The confusions and perplexities of the Tory Party at the present time were strikingly illustrated by Mr P M Oliver (the prospective Liberal candidate for the Koutsford Division) in a speech to a fair assembly of Liberals in the Methodist Chapel, Grappenball, cii Tuesday evening. Mr C Jackson Holmes, presided and an interesting speech Was also made by Coun- cillor Middleton of Oldham.

The Chairman referred to the recent annual roeet- ing of the Conservative party at which he noted Colonel Sykes did not attend. It was a long time since they had a visit from that gentlemen in the dis- trict. The chief speaker at that Conservatite meeting appeared to be Mr Lofthouse whose chief complaint seemed to be that the Government were clinging to office against the express wish of the people. He did not see how the speaker could come to that conclusion, because, if they took the majorities in the House of Commons, which had been so steady since the Government came into office, there did not seem to be anything to lead them to that conclusion, if, by any chance there was an atom of truth in that statement, they were not the first Government who had clung to office, for the Conseratives had stuck in power ae long as they could, and at the tail-end of their exist- ence they passed measures which suited their own particular Ii iends. No such charge could be made against the present Government, because all the Bills they had introduced were foreshadowed in the speeches of the Prime Minister and other members of the Liberal party, before they were returned to office. The Liberals in Grappenhail had put their house in order quite recently and in addition to having a strong committee, Mr Fox had undertaken the duties of honorary secretary. (Applause.) Nothing would be left undone in the way of registration and organisa- tion and they would be able to render every assistance to Mr Cliffs. (Applause). Mr Oliver, who was warmly received, said he did not know there had bean a Conservative meeting, such as the chairman had referred to. He also did no know the charges which might have been levelled a the Government at that meeting. From what th chairman had said the chief complaint was that th Liherals were clinging to office against the express wi of the electorate. It was quite true that during th ets' summer of last year, owing to a large amount of mis representation on one side and misconception on th other, the Liberal party lost a number of by-elections. In looking up the figures for the by-elections anon. October he tound that at Taunton they had tale highest Liberal poll on record iu that division. Then at Bolton they won a magnificent victory which finally smashed the food taxes. They had the highest Liberal poll on record at Flint, and at Londonderry they won a seat tor the' Government. At Chorley the Conservative majoritY was reduced by 569 votes. In each of those by: elections there was most substantial evidence Of Liberal life and strength in the constituencies. und lie thought their position was as strong now as it had beep since 1909 when Mr Lloyd George introduced biC Budget. He thought it was very appropriate, seeiog, that Sc. Patrick's Day had just gone by, that he shoulu say something in regard to Home Rule for Ireland. The Irish had their own patron Saint, their own, festival, their own National emblem, their own local, bodies, &c., and the Liberals believed it was right, and hoped before long, that Ireland would have Home Rule. (Applatse.) He noticed that the Grappenhall district had been flooded with Conservative pamphlets on the Home Rule question. One pamphlet alleged that the Catholic majority tyrannised over toe Protestant minority. That was utterly untrue. On the contrary. they found out, that in the counties whore the Catholics had a chance of being tyrannical, where there was & chance of Home Rile being Rome Rule, that the Catholics did not use their majority

div.head: Another Cup Victory. Kingston _Rovers _ Fail Again at
div.p: Another Cup Victory. Kingston _Rovers _ Fail Again at
Warrington.

History repeated itself on Saturday, when the Kingston Rovers of Hull failed for the fourth time to beat Warrington in a cup-tie. The . match was played at Wilderspool and attracted a capital crowd of fully 8,000, the receipts being £2lO. .Luckily, the day kept fine, and the ground was in capital oruer considering the quantity of rain which had Wien the previous day. Half a gale of wiud blew straight down the ground, and the borne side were lucky to have this at their backs in the first half. B3th teams were fully represented, end a couple of huudred supporters came with. the Hull team. Surman, Hudson and Braiu were omitted from the sixteen players selected by the Hull directors, and the team was the same as that which won at Brumley in Round I. Warrington made no changes, and the folio - leg were the players and officials : INrarrington: Jolly, back ; B Bradshaw, A Renwick, J Tranter and E Brooks, three-quarter backs; J Daintith and S Nicholas, half-backs; Li Thomas, A Naylor, J W Cheaters, A Skelhorn, 3 e'earnley and W 11 Cox for- wards. Hull Kingston Rovers : Carmichael, hack; Dilcock, Hicks, Hughes, and Hodgson, three-quarter backs; Dean and Sykes, half-backs; Mann, Moore, Sandhaw, Lewis. Trump and Husking, forwards. Referee, J W Whiteley, Wakefield. Touch judges, W T Chapman, Swinton aLd J A Blackburn, Leigh. Huskins started the game towards the pavilion end and notwithstanding the wind the visitors made a strong show in the home quarter, Hodson and Hughes both trying to force their way through. Renwick was penalised, and Carmichael tried to: goal, but the shot was almost impossible against the wind. Warrington eventually got to the other end after a mark by Fearnley and some speedy work by the forwards who prevented the Hull custodian Making any reply. Tranter tried to rush the defence and was temporarily laid out, while Jolley caused excitement with a quick shot at goal which went very near the mark. Warring- ton were in fine attacking position and a round of passes ended in Bradshaw making a great effort on the right wing which was only checked at the corner flag. Dean was very active for the Rovers, and aided by good scrummaging they got back to centre without disaster. Here Dean was penalised, and Renwick's kick changed the fortunes of the game. He punted to touch at the corner, and War- rington scored from the ensuing scrummage. Nicholas got the ball and passed to Breolo. The latter was tackled closed in, but gave the ball to Cox, who dived over at the corner in smart style amid hearty cheering. Thomas tried for goal, but failed. Twenty minutes had now gone, and the locals made great efforts to increase the score. The forwards were brilliant, sod kept the Rovers well within their own quarters. Daintith smartly got the ball away near centre and gave to Tranter. The latter made a fine dash and then threw wide to Brooks after bluffing Dean and Diloock with the " dummy" Brooks took the ball at top speed, and raced over with a brilliant try, which Renwick improved just as brilliantly. Skelhorne and Fearnley led the way again and Carmichael found it impossible to clear. The Warrington men were all over the Hull backs, and Nicholas snapping up the ball gave Brooks a lovely pass, and the burly wing again romped over in good position, Renwick adding another goal with a clever shot. The Rovers had to work hard to the interval to keep Warrington in check, aud when half-time came the score was : Warrington, 2 goals 3 tries (13 points); Hull K.R., nil. Warrington changed their tactics on resuming, and the close work of Nicholas,followed by arnert wheeling of the serums kept the Hull men from making immedi- ate headway. The first visit to the \Varriugtou end brought points, for Carmichael kicked a penalty goal, and maintained his record of scoring in every match this season. Less than five minutes had gone, and the visitors were jubilant. But Warrington were deter- mined and the defence of Jolley, Trainer and Renwick novel wavered under some dashing attacks led by Sandham and Mann. A smart movement between Nicholas, Daintith and Tranter was counterbalanced by Hicks and Dean setting the rear men going.. It was left to Brooks to check the visitors at i. e 25 flag. Warrington drove out the Rovers, but Tranter was ruled offside, and Carmichael was called up for the shot, and hei again succeeded from a long range. Tramp and Sandham were both pulled up when running strongly for the line. By stern work
The Exa iner, Saturday, March 22, 1913.

div.head: IMPS' BOAT RACE.
div.p: THE IMPS' BOAT RACE.

Warrington got well inside Hull quarters, and just when the home supporters were expecting something substantial to accrue a pass was snapped up by Hicks, who raced clear of the opposition, and Hull appeared certain to score. Tianter gave pursuit, and hauled down the intruder a yard from the line in sensational style. Warrington were hard pressed, and they awe decidedly lucky when Daintith brought off a smart tackle of Dean. Twice Warrington saved, but from a penalty granted near half- way Carmichael landed his third goal. The Warrington forwards again showed their mettle and rushed the game finely to the other end. Skelborn was hurt but the ball was sent across to the left, where Renwick tried to break through ad was heavily tackled by Carmichael. Warrington were again overplaying the Rovers, and Bradshaw made a dashing run on the right. Nieholas was very smart and broke clean through on one occasion only to fall a foot short of the line when the defence was beaten. Carmichael essayed to round several opponents. He was fl ored and being foroed to play the ball roused the ire of the home supporters for foul tactics, the referee administering a ottuti,as. Thomas was hurt, but was only absent a minute. Hull threatened danger, and twice got the ball working among the backs, but the tackling never wavered, and the home forwaras controlling the game Warrington had won well when the game was brought to a close. Result : -Warrington, two goals three tries (13 points); Hull Kingston Rovers, three goals (six points). WIDNES MISS CHANCES AT YORK. York continued their sequence of recent victories by beatiug idnes by ten points to four, before a crowd of about 5,000, the gate receipts being .Cl2B. A strong wind interfered with accurate play, and the game was more or less scrappy. Naylor enhanced his reputation as a goal-kicker, and gave the York men tee lead in the first quarter af an hour by landing the ball over the cross-bar from a difficult angle. Taylor had an oppor- tunity of equalising soon after, but failed. Redmond, O'Gara, and Reid showed some pretty passing for the visitors on several occasions, hut the home dsfence always rose to the position. The York forwards did not get possession as oi ten as their opponents, but Daniel made the most of his opportunities, and On one of thes, accasions he handed to Oliver, who passed on to Sellers, the latter crossing the line. The goal-kick by Naylor failed. Redmond responded by a capital ran, but was grassed near the corner flag, making amends, however, by kicking a goal. At half-time York were leading by 1 goal 1 try (5 points) to Widnes 1 goal (2 points).

In the second half the York halves got possesdion more frequently, but play was mostly uninteresting. Daniel was lucky in charging a kick by Reid, and he got over the line ne•tr the posts, Naylor further improving matters. After this the York attack slackened some- what, and Widnes were often in the home half. O'Gara and Redmond worked hard and put in excellent passing, but Reid was weak, and missed several opportunities of scoring. In the closing stages Widnes were awarded a penalty kick, and Redmond landed the points. Result: 'York 2 goals 2 tries (10 points), Widnes 2 goals points). Yearns :7'
York—Lee, back ; Cowmeadow, Lavelle, Oliver, end Sellers, three-quarter backs ; Dauiel and Bogein, half 13.icks ; Boylen, Naylor, ttaftrey, Lupton, Hoyle, and Nickson, forwards.

Widnes—Brassington, back ; Laws, Redmond,Taylor, and Reid, three-quarter backs; Noon and O'Gara, half backs ; G Aspey, S Aspey, Higgins, Lloyd, Corcoran, and Townsend, forwards. Referee, W McCutcheon, Oldham.

div.head: COMBINATION. WARRINGTON "A" v PENIBERTON.
div.p: THE COMBINATION. WARRINGTON "A" v PENIBERTON.

Played at Pemberton on Saturday. In the first half the home lot, with the br6w3ze in their favour, had muoh the best of matters. The first score came to Beardmore, who ran in a clever try. Wilcox next placed a penalty goal and at half-time the locals led by five points to nil. In the second stage Warrington forced mutters, whilst Pemberton offered a strong defence. Both sides scored a try, Warrington added a goal and the result was Pemberton one goal two tries (eight points) ; Waztington, one goal one try (five points).
FRIENDLY MATCH.
WARRINGTON SC,IOOLBOYS v BROUGHTON
SCHOOLBOYS.

Prior to the cup-tie game between Warrington and Hull Kingston Rovers on Saturday, a match was played between the boys selected from the Warrington elementary schools and the Broughton School Boys. With the wind in the first half the _home lads gave a bparkling display and soon ran up a splendid score, leading at half-time by 21 points to nil, Brady scoring two very fine tries. Broughton could not make much headway in the second half, for the defence of the Warrington custodian was exceptionally good. The scores recorded were two very fine tries, one by Brady, who, receiving the ball in his own quarters, ran splendidly, and crossed the line near the poste. There was no goal, and the home lads won by 29 points to nil.

Played at Runcorn on SAurday. Sankey %ere greatly handicapped by the absence of thea left wing, A Grainger and %V Booth. From the start, the visitors presaed and forced fruitless corners. Keeping up the pressure, El Ray tried a shot, but the high wind carried the ball wide. The forwards rushed down and were awarded a penalty tor hands, from which T Whitfield scored, giving G Streets no chatme. The visitors kept their oppon-nts penned in their own half, but the wind spoiled good play, awl half time arrived with the score: Great Sankey, one; Baltour-rued Old Boys' .0. In the second half Sankey had to fight the gale E Glover and B .1 Kelly were on the top form, and cleared with rare judgment, but they could not stop the borne men's repeated raids, D Hughes equalizing from a well-placed corner kick. Sankey milieu somewhat, but were unable to score. At the other end the locals forced another corn, from which R Clarke headel the winning goal. Result: Balfour-road Old Boys, 2; Great Sitakey, I.

div.p: ALTRINCHAM LADS V LATCHFORD.
On Stafford Park on Saturday a very plearant game ending with the snore sheet blank. BOWDON VALE V LATCHFORD

After fulfilling their game with Altrinchham Lads— Latchford journeyed on to the Vale, making one or two changes in the personnel of their tam. In the first half the Vale did the most of the pressing but their for- wards could not control the lively ball at all, half time arriving with the Ecore sheet blank. Upon, turning round matters were reversed, Latchford doing most of the aggressive work. Like the Vale forwards, the Latchford line totally failed to keep the ball under con- trol. div.head: HOCKEY.
div.p: HOCKEY.
LATCHFORD.

The First Eleven beat Sale "A " by 6-1. the team giving a sound display all round. The Sale Club have tportingly given fixtures (home and away) with their First Eleveu for next season. But for some stubborn defending by the visiting backs and goalkeeper last week the score would have reached big proportions. Southall the keeper hd a very unenviable tusk, shots being fairly rained at him at times, but he performed valiantly. Pearson (3) Travis (2) Minards (1) were the scorers and this inside trio were much too tricky for the visiting backs ; in fact the passing among the halves and forwards reached a high standard. Billing- ton at left full-back was in great form and no and Fletcher were the complete master of the Sale forward in the circle. Bradshaw was in good form at centre- half.

The Second Devon match at Bowdon was cancelled owing to the home club being very short-handed through illness and injuries. The First S4cond Eleven matches with Stockport to- day are cancelled by latter club owing to the shortage of players through holidays.

div.p: ANGLING.
WARRINGTON WORKINGMEN'S ANGLING ASSOCIATION. (N.A. CENTRE).

The reason there were no notes published last week was through an oversight. Notes were made out and forwarded to the" Examiner" Office but did not reach them. However, no great harm was done as notices were posted in the clubhouses warning members not to encroach on the close season.

div.head: THN GOWY.
div.p: THN GOWY.

The reports for the last- two week 3 in the open season were not up to expectations although several roach were brought Warrington way. They were not registered on the set board because those already weighed in did not give them a chance of appearing in the first three. The Gowy did not finish up as well as was expected, after the splendid roach that were taken during the beginning of the present month and the latter end of February, but taking into consideration the condition of the weather during the season since this year came in, it has fished better than for some years past. I think the oflioials of the Northern Anglers are well satisfied with their out- lay up to the present. Several officials tried the stream about a fortnight ago and returned without a fish. The reason for this is, either the fish were off feed or the anglers were not good enough for this water. As we have remarked several times, this is no stream for the novice, and if roach are caught vreekly, it is proof that they are there to be taken if the angler is skilful enough.

div.head: CANALS.
div.p: THE CANALS.

The reports from canaltr aWietter, but not a great deal, and fish that were taken were not put on the scgales. This goes to show that nothing great was caught. Chester has found little favour this winter among our locals. Hartford has had one or two members, and here the report was only moderate; a member of the Northern took a roach 11b. 40., but he was not a Warrington member.

The canal at Norton was visited before the close by several members. They said there was a slight improve- ment, but nothing doing with the heavy brigade. Several were taken of fair size with stone bait. Taking the winter fishing all round, this winter has fished very badly indeed. However, we will see what the rest during close season will do, and as there will be a list of specials published later for this water, there I think will be plenty of visitors during the warmer months.

SUNDAY AT THE COWL A fair muster visited here the Sunday before the close in anticipation of topping those already weighed in. In this they were disappointed, roach were taken by Messrs Green, Malpass, Britt sin, Graham, Potter and Stout, all ranging round the 11b. One member had five and this was about the best done. One or two of the roach were the smallest taken this turn, and were accounted for by anglers who were in the spot previously throwing ground bait in. The Gowy needs little feed- ing, if any during the water months, if specimen fish are sought for by the angler.

div.head: CLOSE SEASON.
div.p: THE CLOSE SEASON.

As regards close season the committee gave this matter fair consideration, but they decided to uphold the ruling from headquarters. We hope that the mem- bers who applied for the season to keep open until Easter Monday night, will realise that their case was given a fair hearing, but the committee decided to close as it would not be playing the game to go against the Northern Anglers Association i uling.

div.head: WOMAN'S FATAL FALL. SAD STORY OF -DRUNKENNESS.
div.p: WOMAN'S FATAL FALL. SAD STORY OF -DRUNKENNESS.

An inquest was conducted at the Warrington Coroner's Court on Monday, by Mr F A Jones, on the body of Martha Wood (64), tali(' of William Wood, general labour r. 3, liostock-street.—lt appears that on Saturday the deceased was found by her husband in a drunken condition on the kitchen floor. He lifted her into an arm chair and told her to go to sleep. She said she would go to bed. When about five steps up the stairs she fell backwards and her head struck the wall. Dr Martin was called in and pronounced life extinct, deceased's neck having been dislocated. The parties 'gad been married 44 years and for over 30 years deceased had been drinking excessively and had suffered- monetarily as a consequence.—A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

OCTOGENARIANS' FATAL ACCIDENT. Another inqui,y was made by the Deputy Coroner into the circumstanes surrounding the death of James Humphreys (83) inmate at the workhouse.—Osborne Moss (assistant workhouse master) said that on February 22nd he heard that the deceased bad been hurt as the result of a fall. He was removed to his bed suffering great pain. He complained that another inmate named Lawton bad pushed him down but made no allegation that it hart been done wilfully. He had sustained a fractured leg. He grew weaker and died on Thursday, death being due to broncntat pneunionie,. accelerated by the accident. He had been an inmate of the institution 10 years. George Lawton said that on the 22nd February deceased came up to him in the men's airing yard and complained of feeling cold. Witness replied "you might well, sleeping with your clothes on all night." Deceased said I wilt burst your face for you and struck at witness. Witness pushed deceased away and he fell on his back. He, witness, had no intention of hurting the deceased and they had always been on the best of terms ?—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

SIR .1 BRUNNER'S BABY BONUS SCHEME. Particulars were published on Tuesday of the result of Sir John's baby bonus scheme which is in force at Winnington, Northwich. In 1906 Sir John announced that he would give a bonus of £1 to the parents of every child which was horn .at Winnington and lived for twelve months. In cronjunction with the scheme instruction to mothers is given by a nurse. In all 160 births have been registered in the seven years, and 124 babies' parents have received the bonus. Only five children have died and five 'Ave removed from the district. The remaining 26 are still under twelve months old.

;hie —Warrington Chess Club. The Warrington Chess Club concluded one of the most succes-ful sessions in its history by a meeting at Prince's Cafe, on Thursday of last week. The Club's handsome trophy was presented by the Presi- dent, Mr J Newcombe, to Mr Frank Dunne. who had won 12 games, drawn 1 and lost 3. Mr J. R Wood was the runner up in the trophy competitinn. In the handicap competition Mr Wood succeeded in obtaining first place, Mr Newcombe being second. Caretakers' Federation. On Saturday evening the members cf the Warring- ton Branch of the National Federation of Caretakers presented a travelling case as a token of esteem to Mr R Cade (who is leaving for Canada). Mr Rhoden occupied the chair, and said they were sorry to lose such a good member of the branch. Mr Hewitt made the presentation, and said Mr Cade had always been willing to help the branch. Messrs. Hoeghton and Dykes wished Mr Cade every success in his new sphere. Mr Cade briefly responded. ARIOL-JoIINSTON, BAYARD. PALLADIUM and TALBOT CARS.—SoIe Agent, J. S. The CrOcifixion. A large congregation at the Wycliffe Congregational Church on Sunday evening enjoyed an impressive rendition by the choir of Stainers "Crucifixion." Mr W H Payton, Mus. Bac., was the organist, and the principal soloists were Mr J Ainsworth, Mr W Booth, and Mr H Hawthorn. Mrs J Hawthorne, Miss Hewitt and Mr W Booth and Mr B Hibhert rendered the quartette "God so loved the world" in a plensiug manner and the choruses were also expressively given. The Rev T T James delivered a short address —On Tuesday evening " The Crucifixion" was ren- dered by the choir of St John's, Earlestnwn, at St Luke's Church, Warrington. Mr J W Willett (tenor) and Mr E Walker (bass) were the soloists, Mr C H Dawson acting as conduCtor.

Ancient Order of Foresters. The interment of the late Bro W H Roylanee, who had been a member of Curt Jaaziel since 1899. took place at Warrington Cemetery on Sunday. All the Courts in Warrington and Grappenhall were represented by officers and members. The late brother was also secretary of the Bewsey Adult School and took a keen interest in the good work carried on there. This was evidenced by many members of the school joining in the procession to show their respect and sympathy He was also formerly a Sergeant in the local Territorial Force and was buried with military honours. The first portion of the burial service was held in St Paul's Church, the Rev W Bracecamp cfficiating. Numerous beautiful floral tributes were sent, which eloquently spoke of the deep sympathy and love felt by all with the bereaved family. DAISY VACUUM CLEANERS.42/-,63/-, 84/.—Try one on hire.—J. S. GARLAND. 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington. British Women's Temperance Association. There was a good attendance at the usual monthly meeting when Miss Bogstrom gave a very interesting address. Mrs Owen, Miss Bessie Dutton and Mrs Simpson also took part. Last week, Mrs Owen, Mrs Tanner, Mrs G Dale, Mrs Brimeloxv, Mrs Hough and Mrs Simpson attended the Lancoshire County Union Conference which was held at Bury. Mrs Simpson was again elected a member of the National Executive Committee. Miss Bertha Mason, of Lotdon, moved the following resolution which was carried unanimously :—" That this conference urges the Pr ime Minister to delay no longer the fulfilment of his pledge that he would place the 1908 Licensing Bill on the Statute Book as soon as the Parliament Act set the House of Commons free to carry out the legislation demanded by the people, and prays him to introduce the long promised temperance measure in the session of 1913.' National Health Insurance. As will be seen by our advertising columns, the existing Medical Tickets, now in the possession of all insured persons entitled to medical benefit under the Act, will remain in force until the 30th June, 1913.1 Insured persons are therefore advised to take every care of the tickets, as in case of loss there will be a difficulty in getting treatment from a doctor. There are still many insured persons in the Borough (we I understand, over 4,000) who have not yet chosen their' Panel doctor. These people are urged to do so with- out further delay, otherwise the Insurance Committee will, in due course, proceed to allocate them to a doctor on the Panel. Since the Panel was first formed we understand the following doctors have been included :—Dr Anderson, Dr Gandhi, Dr Hodgkinson, Dr Bower, and Dr Jago. It will seen from the advertisement that the surgery hours of the doctors are on week-da3s 9 to 9 30 a p m to 730 pm; Sundays and public holidays 9 a m to 10 a m. PREMIER MOTOR CYCLES.—SOIO Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Brides at., Warrington.—Advt. Presentation to a Teacher. On Wednesday a very pleasing ceremony took place in Our Lady's School. The children assembled at 6 30 p m in order to present Miss Byrne, one of the assistant mistresses, who is leaving, with souvenirs of her seven years' service at Our Lady's. The Rev J Tallon, corresponding manager, presided, and there were also present :—The Rev A J Wilson, the head teacher, members of the staff, Miss Richardson, and others. In a very happy and appropriate speech, Father Tenon expressed to Miss Byrne the regret which was felt at her departure and asked her to accept the good will and sincere wishes of all present for her future happiness and prosperity, Miss Byrne responding suitably and feelingly. A short musical programme followed, including violin solos by Miss Richardson, selections from "The Geisha" by the infants, and choruses "Mice in Council" and "I would that my love" by the school choir. The presents included a very handsome statue of Our Lady from Father Tallon and the managers, marble time piece from the head teacher and staff, and bronze ornaments from the children. PREMIER CYCLES. Excelsior Cycles, Lea Francis Cycles, £.l 10/-to .Cl 6 16/-.—Sole Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Latchford Without Parish Meeting. On Monday evening the annual parish meeting for Latchford Without was held in the Baptist Schoolroom Wash-lane. Mr H T Fairclough presided at the out- set but later Mr W C Litton occupied the chair. For the eight vacancies on the parish council the f .Ilowing nine gentlemen were nominated all being elected except Mr C Jackson Holmes :—Messrs R T Fairnlough, R Gordon, C Jackson Holmes, J Hudson, F A Jenkins, George Pilling, H L Taylor, William Throssell and William Roberts. Mr E Woods had not sought re-election, and this fact was very much regretted. Nothing of a definite character was arrived at in regard to the Sewerage Scheme, but it was evident that the feeling of the meeting was that, so far as their district was concerned, it was unnecessary, but as regarded Grappenhail something would have to be done. Mr Roberts said that if those in authority were satisfied that such a scheme was a necessity, they (the District Council) would have to accept it, for it was no good "kicking against the pricks." The condition of Grappenhalrwith respect tb this matter was deplor- able, and it was because of its condition that this scheme was forced upon them. Reference was made to the application to the Warrington Council for the use of the Corporation Fire Brigade when necessary.

Mr BONAR LAW'S TORY TRIALS Manchester speech was AND TROUBLES. another milestone on a

road which has been full of trouble and humiliation for the Tory leader. He has reached, by a devious route, precisely the ground on which Mr. BALFOUR stood when he declared that it was the duty of a leader to lead, and if the Party would not follow they must find another leader. Mr. BALFOUR resigned, for reasons of health; and Mr. BONAR LAW must be suffering from the March winds very severely. The Tory local organization in the Kendal Division chose a candidate who stood upon a Free Trade platform. After an interval of hesita- tion and uncertainty, the candidature was disavowed by Tory headquarters. Mr. BoNAR LAW was quite apologetic at Man- chester for so bold a decision. But the most indignant section of his Party is complaining not of the disavowal,but of Mr BONAR LAW'S dilatoriness in promulgating it. "The idea of a ' split ' " in the Tory party Lord DERBY told a Lancashire audience at the end of last week, (Lily existed in the minds of their opponents. The Tories were a thoroughly united party." But Mr. CHAPLIN was simultaneously proclaiming that "it was useless and idle to pretend there was peace when there was no peace, and useless also to speak of the complete unity of the party upon Taiiff Reform, which most certainly, in his opinion, did not exist." The Observer has been even more thorough in its shattering of the long dream of a "thoroughly united party." "In the name of unity," the Observer declares, "the whole normal cohesion of the Unionist forces was sedu- lously disintegrated. These methods shook to the foundation the faith of the party in its leaders and itself. The great shuffle on the food duties was so managed as to leave all men in doubt whether there remained any vital strength in the Imperial spirit and purpose which are the very life and soul of Unionist existence." Political cynicism could hardly go any further lengths than for a party which is so notoriously sceptical of its own leaders and its own sincerity to be keeping up the pretence that the electorate are pining for an opportunity to express their loss of confidence in the Government, and their eager desire to substitute a Government which, if the Tory organs:are trustworthy guidesiwould be con- structed on the model of the Kilkenny cats. Mr. BONAR LAW brought into his peroration

at Manchester the stock topic of an Opposition leader—the country's loss of confidence ill the Government. But the first need of the Opposition, according to the Tory Press, is to restore confidence in its own leaders and its own good faith. What is the use of press- ing upon the country a programme which those who are complaining most bitterl3r because the programme is not pressed with sufficient earnestness, in the same breath describe as " a great shuffle " ?
• Amalgamation is in GREATER the air, for the good WARRINGTON. people of Stockton_

Heath have abandoned their attitude of lofty superiority and are seriously considering the wisdom of joining the borough of Warrington. Hitherto the frame ot.mind of the "heathens," as voiced by their public men, might have been summed up in the question "Can any good thing come out cf Warrington?" and it would appear that the alarming increase in the County rate has been the chief factor in the striking change of front. However, the fact that Stockton Heath has until quite lately spurned the idea of joining forces with the municipality will not preclude the subject from receiving impartia consideration at the hands of the Corporation—indeed the Mayor, as shown in the interview published ifl another column, is very favourablY disposed towards the extension of the borough boundaries on the Cheshire side and he thinks a majority of the Council will be of a like opinion. Stockton Heath has been described by the ex-Chairman of the Parish Council as a " luscious plum" which War- rington was anxious to swallow, but there is quite another side to the question. The taking over of such an important and rapidly developing district and the bring- ing of it into line with the rest of the borough would undoubtedly involve serious responsibility in regard to sanitation, town planning, gas, water and trams. The inclu- i sion of such a large additional rateable value would not, fora considerable time at any rate, be any appreciable advantage to Warrington If the same course is followed as on the occasion of the last extension of the borough boundaries, any increase in the rates above the amount at present being paid by the ratepayers of Stockton Heath will be suspended for an agreed term of years. Warrington is therefore confronted with the prospect of running Stockton Heath at a loss for an indefinite period, but there is such a community of interest between the borough and the prosperous and attractive Cheshire suburb that amalgamation can hardly fail ultimately to be mutually beneficial.

From the Liberal point TIIE BY-ELECTIONS, of view the results of the by-elections in Houghton-le-Spring and Kendal were gratifying—the former because of the more than two to one majority against the Unionist, the latter because of the discom- fixture victory brings to the Opposition. Mr Tom Wing—who is so well known in War- rington—polled neaily 7,000 votes, Mr. House securing 4,165. The combined Pro- gressive vote was 11,095 compared with only 4,807 votes against the Government. In Kendal the usual party lines were disregarded Colonel Weston, the "back number," won bY the help of out-voters, who were brought up from neighbouring counties and from distant places—nearly 400 of them—and by Free 'irade votes. One section of the Tory party drove him into the position ofbeing a National Service or Conscriptionist candidate, but his views on this subject were not very fixed, although they became more certain as the poll drew near, and are quite definite now the election is over. The truth is (says the "London Chronicle ") that Colonel Weston can be claimed by any section of the Tory party—except thc food taxers. He was a popular candidate, but his party, which officially repudiated him, will not be very happy with him as a member.

The name conveys little CANBERRA. to an interested world at the moment. It bas all its associations to create, and it remains for the future to give it its place beside London, Berlin, Paris, New York,and Ottawa among the great centres of the world's great- est achievements. Canberra is the new capital of the Australian Commonwealth. The foundations of the mighty city have just been laid. All around are the begin- nings .of great engineering works, excava- tions for foundations, surveys for roads, railways, bridges, and electric and ' water power stations, enclosed by the wild and rocky heights of the outposts of the Australian Alps. Ere long this wilderness of preparation will be a city of palaces and offices, of happy homes and busy workshops.Th ere is something very inspiring in this thought of the beginnings of a new city which is to be the capital of a great continent only now getting into the stride of its development as one of the proudest posses- sions of the greatest Empire in the world. And there is something very appropriate about that simple, meaningless, unmusicAl name Canberra. Australia's great national heroes have still to appear. There is no name so far which could have been given to the new capital, as the of Washington was given to America s, centre of Government. Australia, again, is the last corner of the world in which one would look for the snobbishness which would have inspired the conferring upon the new capital of some of the fancy, high-sounding names which have been ' suggested from time to time by outsiders. In the simple name of the district in which the Federal city is to rise the Australians see a symbol of equality. There could be no more excellent reason for the choice of the name. May the city which it is to adorn ever find withinplente its walls. plenteousness within its palaces and peace
The Examiner, Saturday, March 22, 1913.

div.p: GOOD FRIDAY.
HOW IT WAS OBSERVED AT WARRINGTON.

The conditions yesterday oscillated between winter severity and spring-like mildness, but the spell of sunshine in the afternoon made outdoor recreations a pleasure. The only departure from tradition in the observance of the eay was the open- ing of the various picture palaces and, judging from the large audiences, the innova- tion was a popular one with a considerable section of the community. At the churches the anniversary was kept with the usual solemnity, one of the principal services at the Anglican and Roman Catholic churches being the three hours' devotional service from 12.0 to 3.0. At the Parish Church the addresses on the Seven Sayings from the Cross were given by the Rev. Lucius Cary, of the Society of St. John the Evangelist, Cowley, Oxford. His father is well remem- bered in Warrington as headmaster of the Boteler Grammar School 'before the late Rev E J Willcocks. In the evening the choir gave an impressive rendering of" The Way of the Cross" (Iliffe). At Wycliffe Congregational Church in the morning the Rev. T. T. James conducted a short service. As usual, foreign missionary services were held at Bold-street Wesleyan Church. In the afternoon the match Warrington v. Oldham was a great attraction to football enthusiasts, the crowd numbering 9,000.

div.head: MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY AT BOLD-STREET.
div.p: THE MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY AT BOLD-STREET.

The Foreign Missionary Anniversary services were held at Bold-street Wesleyan Church yesterday. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. J. C. Sowerbutts (late of India), who was also the deputation at the evening meeting, when Mr. W. Mood( presided. He was supported by the circuit min- isters and Messrs J,C. Holland and I. Barlow. The Rev. H. Williamson, 8.A., submitted the annual missionary report and stated that £307 14s. 6d. had been subscribed throughout the circuit, as against £293 13s. 4d. for the previous year. The general financial state- ment, however, was disappointing, as there was a serious debit balance. The total income from all sources was £190,061. Locally, there were several advances during the year, but probably the most notable was Latchford with an increase of £l9 10s. 7d. The contributions from Bold-street amounted to £3O 14s. 4d. as against £43 17s. 7d. for the previous year.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S FOOTBALL. Warrington Miss Chances.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S FOOTBALL. Warrington Miss Chances.

In one respect the Warrington club was fortunate yesterday. The early afternoon was brilliantly fine and a record crowd of fully 9,000 assembled for the popular return fixture with Oldham. Warrington played their full cup team, with the one change of Clare for Skelhorne, and Oldham were likewise fully represented, Lomas, who is under suspension, being the only absentee of note.

The home side won the toss and played with the sun at their backs, and a strong cross-wind which hampered both teams. Warrington early made head- way through Trauter vvho punted up the field and collared Cook near the line. Their stay here was brief owing to an infringement, and G- W Smith ran the ball back to centre. Here Renwick was awarded a penalty and with a long drop-kick he sent the WI sailing; just outside the posts. Oldham were getting posses- sion frequently, and Wharton and W Farnsworth were very active in getting the third line on the move, but the tackling of the hoinesters was not to be trifled with. Daintith retired with a temporary injury, and during his absence Oldham scored. Jolley failed to return a punt, and was charged over by the Oldham forwards. The ball went to Williams, who just scraped over at the corner. Warrington now rallied, and the forwards showing more dash forced play to the other end. Renwick got hold after a smart pass- ing move, and deceiving the opposition on the wing he threw inside to Fearnley, who scored smartly near the goal. Renwick missed the easy shot, and Jolley was no more fortunate with a penalty five minutes later. Warrington had the best of the game and Fearnley was held a yard from the line. Half-time, one, try each The story of the second half is soon told. Warring ton set about the task of winning in grim earnest, and forced Oldham to their own quarter. There was some keen tackling on both sides, but Nicholas, Daintith and Br(oks were all peppering away at the line and the defence seemed certain to fall. Renwick had a penalty kick right in front of the posts, and when he missed again, the Fates seemed to conclude that Warrington did not deserve points. The next minute a hurricane of wind and sleet broke over the ground and drove right into the forces of the Warrington men Thus handicapped they were gradually forced back. Oldham kept the advantage with long punting, and five minutes from the end Ferguson kicked a penalty goal which gave his side a fortunate victory. Final: Oldham, 1 goal, 1 try (5 pints); Warrington, 1 try (3 points).

div.head: GOOD FRIDAY PICTURES.
div.p: GOOD FRIDAY PICTURES.

A departure from the established order, as far se Good Friday observance in Warrington!was concerned, was the opening of all the picture palaces in the town yesterday evening. At a specially convened meeting of the Watch Committee on Monday the proprietors were granted permission to display appropriate pictures between the hours of 6 p.m. and 10 p.m. The decision was not arrived at without keen differences of opinion and a very close division. At the last ordinary meeting the committee refused an application made by Andrews' Picture Palace to open on Good Friday with a show cf sacred pictures. On Saturday last a deputation of cinema house managers waiting upon the Mayor made strong representations for the opening of the picture palaces on Good Friday. It was pointed out that entertainments were allowed on that day in other Lancashire towns, and an under- taking was given that no films to which objection could be taken would be shown, cowboy pictures, humorous sketches and like subjects being banned. His Worship called the special meeting which grante& the application.

TWENTY-FIVE YEARS RECTOR.
lv
fitoco Birtles. THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON (REV. CANON WILLIS.)

Yesterday the Rev. Canon F. W. Willis completed twenty-five years' work as Rector of Warrington. He came to Warrington from All Saints', Wellingborough, Northants, in 1888 and all who are familiar with Church life in the old parish will agree that, under his devoted and conscientious leadership, very considerable progress has been made. A convinced High Churchman, the Rector never hesitates to champion, both on the platform and in the Press, the .principles which he holds so dear, and he has frequently engaged in controversy on questions concerning the validity of Anglican orders and the continuity of the Church of England. During his oversight of the work of the Parish Church many important schemes, including the erection of Fairfield schools and the missions of St. George and St. Clement, had been carried out, the total amount subscribed for the various special undertakings being £20,000, exclusive of the value of sites which is estimated at £5,000. The Rector is beloved of his own parishioners and respected by workers of all religious denominations, and sincere good wishes will go forth to him on the cnninletion of a quarter of a century's labours in the town. ,
