Following on the open conference upon cooking held at the Town Hall last week under the auspices of the Mayor, the Ladies' Committee then app inted has since got to work. The plan of working is to avoid centralisation and to depend upon the co-opera- tion of the various mothers' meetings and similar organisations. In due course suggestions will be made in fuller detail and a little sub-committee is now producing a leaflet, which will contain a few simple cookery recipes and some practical advice On the wise choice of food. A PLEA FOR THE DOMESTIC SERVANTS. Sir,—Wilt you please publish these few lines, in defence of the hardworked domestic servant? I think a servant ought to woik only as many hours as the mills girls—that is 9 hours. It ought also to be trade compulsory for a servant to be allowed Sundays off. The clergy are agitatit gto have the Sunday trading stopped. Let them see that their own servants do no work on a Sunday. Then again woman ought to please herself whether she wears a cap or not, as it is a badge of servitude ; let laws be made for the servant as well as for mill girls and let the social stigma be removed. Then we shall perhaps have no servant problem to solve. The servants should have their bedrooms away fro:n the scene of their labours, as t!..ese poor creatures are often put in a damp bed- room, or a co.!d attic to be made sufferers all their lives. Let some good Christian people send a Bill to Parliament to improve the lot of toe poor servant. No wonder girls won't go to service. I don't blame them.— Yours &C.
JOHN CAMERON, Rock Vila, Willis-street Warrington.

At Staveley Parish Church on Satenrday, the marriage took 'Place of Kenneth Houghton, only son of Mr and Mrs Glover, of Lowton House, Lowton, and Mary Belle. elder daughter of the late Mr George Washing- ton Ireltiod. of Kendal and Staveley, and of Mrs Ireland, of Elf Howe, Staveley. div.head: MODESTY OF HAROLD SMITH.
div.p: THE MODESTY OF HAROLD SMITH.

Sir,—lf there is a man anywhere who does not need to pray "May the Lord gie us a good conceit o' oursels," it is surely our youthful member. His speech in the House on Tuesday last, in moving a reduction of the vote ( n the Civil Service Account, in order that he might censure the Home Secretary, is worth read- ing. His words " when they found people inciting to violence," were suitably met with cries of "Ulster," and his further magnaLimons offer to produe his alter- nitive method to Mr McKenna's humane determine- Con not to let any of these misguided women die of 8-If-enforced starvation, when and not until he (Mr Harold Smith) becomes Home Secretary, was met with the suitable response "Heaven help us," and further he was told that his chance of ever becoming Home SPcretary was as remote ts "The Greek Kalends." Mr McKenna's definition of the difference in character and tone between the speeches of Lord R Cecil and Mr Harold Smith was dignified and crushing, viz, that the two speeches were "entirely different in tone, temper and argument; Lord R Cecil had been as fair, frank and courageous as Mr Smith's was the opposite." Perhaps after a few more snubbings of this kind our Member will learn that, after all, moderation in speech and a reputation for courtesy and good manners are worth striving tor. It is worth noting also that in this same speech Mr Smith announced himself as an Anti-Suffragist.—Yours &c,
ELECTOR.

div.head: RECTOR AND THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. REPLY TO COUNCILLOR H. ROBERTS.
div.p: THE RECTOR AND THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. REPLY TO COUNCILLOR H. ROBERTS.

Sir,-1 have just seen in the public papers my letter to the chairman and members of the Education Committee. He says they are not aware of the mental distress of the parents of any of the children. If they are not they ought to be, for they have refused to receive a deputation of parents requesting denominational religious instruction for their children. Would those parents have tequested this teaching if they had not earnestly desired it and when it was refused can it be doubted that they were distressed? The chairman should be more careful in his utterances.

It is now necessary to speak out. Bearing in mind the difficulties as to hours, rooms and teachers attendant upon instruction in various faiths, and recognizing the value of the syllabus permitted in the Council Elementary Schools, I tequested the com- mittee to intrcduce it into the Secondary. The answer is practically this: The Bible may be read for five minutes each morning to 200 scholars of various ages, without comment or explanation except so far as to make the passage intelligible. Is this, I ask a worthy treatment of the Bible ? Is it, I ask, worthy of Christian men? Is it, I further ask, satisfactory to Christian pareuts? if not, let them rise and protest. With them, not the Committee, really rests the p tver to say what shall be the character of the instruction given in our schools. They are responsible for the education of their children and with them rests the responsibility, a real and great one, of seeing that those who will be leaders of this town in the next generation are brought up in the fear of God and with a sound knom ledge of life and the teaching of our Lord.—l am, Sir, yours FREDERIC W. WILLIS, The Rectory, Warrington, March 206, 1913.

div.head: MR. PARKER ON PROFIT-SHARING.
div.p: MR. PARKER ON PROFIT-SHARING.

Sir,--1 have read with interest the letter of Mr Chailes Dukes on Co-partnership and Profit Sharing in your last issue. The differences between Mr Dukes and myself are fundamental and are revealed in the following from Mr Duke's letter : "We are opposed not only to profit sharfog, we also are oppAied to profit exaction." "A man who sets out to support it must be . _

prepared to justify rent, interesi,-and profit." In these . words Mr Dukes clearly speaks as a Socialist, as one who believes that interest on stored up labour in the form of capital is robbery, and that profit representing the remuneration of those who work the business and take the risk is alai) robbery. The two points are fitting subjects for academic debate, but would take us very far outside our present subject. The Socialist who is out to destroy the present system naturally opposes anything that will improve it and of course any form of association between the worker and the employer. In my letter confined my remarks to workers generally, I did not for a moment contemplate that the scheme would have any attraction to Industrial Socialists. I am not therefore difipased to be side-tracked into a barren and necessarily lengthy correspondence on Indust ial Socialism.

The most important, vital, and practical part of Mr Dukes' letter is that in which de deals with the effect of co-partnership. It is," he said," to increase the intensity of labour by lessening the labour employed compared with the output." Mr Dukes goes on to emphasize his point and tells us that by increased efficiency fewer men will be employed and unemploy- ment will be increased. Now this line of argument is as old as the hills and has been applied in all sorts of curious directions. It was brought to the front by the Luddites in their campaign of machinery smash- ing, for just as according to Mr Dukes, efficiency, the product of co-partnership, would reduce employment, efficiency the result of mechanical appliances would do the same, hence smash the machines and smash co-partnership. One of your correspondents a short time ago contended that temperance from an economic point of view was a bad thing for the workers because it increased efficiency, and added, "and that this proves clearly then that if teetotalism is adopted we shall have another 15 per cent. added to the already 9 per cent. unemployed." It is significant that the increased temperance habits of the people in recent years instead of increas4ng unemployment have been followed by a substantial reduction. We can find another example of the same idea in many of the arguments of tariff reformers. Their object is to increase employ- ment by the creation of work, which they imagine would be the result of keeping out goods made abroad, and this irrespective of the reduced efficiency measured by the product of, say, ten per cent. It is singular why those who believed with Mr Dukes do not throw in their lot with the Tariff Reformers for they are out to make more work, and their reasoning runs on the same lines. Now the mistake I think Mr Dukes and many others make is in looking on work as an end in itself, and not a means to produce the necessaries of life. The argu- ment is based on the asuniption that the call for labour is a fixed quantity, and hence our friend's con- tention is that it is well to spread this limited amount of work as widely as possible. If his assumption be correct he is quite logical in opposing co-partnership, temperance, Free Trade, use of mechanical appliances, and anything that makes for efficiency which lessens the local labour factor in the production of a definite product. The demand for labour depends primarily upon our wants and the means we have of satisfying them. In nine cases out of ten any industrial concern which increases its efficiency by economies in labour production (paradoxical as it may sound) the call upon . labcur is increased. But whether this is so generally when you localize your outlook or Lo, it is true as a whole.

lam prepared for Mr Dukes agreeing with me in the general argument, but raising the objection that I am only right when thinking of wealth (or its equiva- lent the comforts of life) in the mass, but not if the increased wealth be followed to its several recipients. In other words claiming that the products of increased ( fficiency go largely to the wrong party. If I am anticipating his arguments aright this seems to me the strongest reason that can be given for co-partnership which i designed to divide the results of increased efficiency. But the increased share which the pro- ducer gets is only one side of the shield ; it is the most apparent but the least important. Where there is free competition the efficient manufacturer cannot retain either for himself or his workmen the main part of the result ( f efficiency, which is always greater than the' extra cost. Be has to part with it by lowering his price of the article produced in competition with other manufacturers who are likewit-e increasing their efficiency. For example the cost in labour by the introduction of machinery has probably reduced tbo selling price of a man's pair of boots about three shillings. The gross saving may he four shillings, but sixpence may be absorbed in power end interest. The buyer of this boot has therefore three shillings to spend on some new want. Suppose however, by adopting the principles of Mr Dukes, by a system of "ca-canny " by smashing boat machinery, by Tariff Reform raising the puce of leather, the saving of the three shillings and sixpence is lost, then every boot buyer has to pay three shillings more. Does this not mean that it is equivalent to the reduction in wages of every man who buys boots? Or to put it another way the three shillings formerly saved can no longer employ the men who have been engaged in making those things which the extra three shillings demanded. Has Mr Dukes ever thought out the ultimate ffect of his opposition to those things which make for efficiency? I have gone into this question at some length because it is vital to the issue. If Mr Dukes is right and efficiency is had for the worker, then of course he is wise in resisting any form of profit-sharing. On the other hand, if Jam right then it is worth considera- tion. Yours,. etc.,
CFIARLES E. PARKER. Penketb. March 18th, 1913.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, March 22, 1913,
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, March 22, 1913,
The Chairman : There was oue in the Church porch. /Or Jenkins : Was that the only one. The Chairman : I think ro.
Mr Lomas : I don't see why other people should be allowed to apeak and ask questions when I am not. The Chairman : When did you ask a question? Mr Lomas: Just now.

The Chairman: I was reading something at the time. Mr Lomas: Are these gentlemen who are objecting thinking of going on the Council. I scarcely tnink it Is the thing for a member not going on the Council to bother about it and put the Council to the expense of a poll. The Chairman: That is closed now.

The miautes of the last annual meting having been read, the Chairman remarked amidst laughter "We will now proceed to discuss parish business." Mr Nicholls proposed a vote of thanks to the parish councillors and paid tribute to the work they had done.

Mr Leach seconded and said no one could have worked hatthr than Mr Lister-Kaye for the modification of the sewerage scheme, and on every occasion be was supported by the whole of the Council. Mr Lister-Kaye replied on behalf of the whole Council and said they had done as much as they could in regard to the sewage scheme. Mr Fox said they found themselves in great difficulties six months after they had been elected. Mr Jenkins resigned and it was a great blow to them to lose such a brilliant village statesman. (Laughter.) When they came to corsider, it was no wonder that they failed to reach the high standard of morality set by that particular tower of righteousness. (Laughter). Mr Ashton : We were a bit disappointed in the last Council. At the commencement we did think Mr Jenkins would have purified the Council from some- thing which he said was radically wrong. Instead of that 1 rather think that the last Council did very little better than the previous Council. Mr Kaye : They have proposed a vote of thanks to us. Is Mr Ashton in order.?

Mr Nicholls: I did not mean to slight any member. I proposed the vote of thanks in ail sificerity. Mr Jenkins had had time to alter his mind. If I read correctly, wise men alter their minds out fools don't and apparently Mr Burrows (who had interrupted Mr Nicholls with a cry of " piffla ") is a fool. (Laughter).
RATE DEMANDS. FAVOURITISM ALLEGED.

The question as to when the rates shall he paid was raised by Mr N Cook, who said he had been informed that several parishioners had been summoned for non- payment of rates. He wanted to know when the last day was for paying the rates, befcre summonses were issued. He found on the rate paper that the rates were to be paid by the 25th March. He bad been informed that people had received sunamonses on the &Li March and he would like to know if power had been given to the clerk to issue those summonses before the expiration of the 2r.th. (Hear, hear). Mr Lister-Kaye, as one of the overseen, said he sup- posed he was responsible in some way. The rates were not due on the 25th March hut "On Demand." If they were not in by the 25th, the matter went to audit and there was a row. Tney were left until the last court day before summonses were issued. He did not like the work, but someone had to do it. Mr Cook held that the rate papers were very mis- leading in regard to the last day for payments of the rates.

Mr Hankey said they made flesh of one and fish of another. They forced the rate in one case and not iu another. If it was necessary to isque summonses before the last court day prior to the 25th March, why not force them all to pay or appear, and not let some have more time. He knew there was favouritism going on. They should compel all to pay,not excluding any. (Hear hear). Mr Hankey said they wanted to know was there a definte date fixed for the payment. Mr Kaye: It is on the notice" On demand." Mr Hankey : Why can't you demand it from all the ratepayers and not favour one above another? Mr Cook: Could we fix a day when they shall be paid? The Chairman : 1 don't think we have any power of that kind. _ _ _ _

A rate paper was read and it was pointed cut that payment should be made" on demand." Mr Kaye said it was no great catch to be an overseer. The Clerk said they could not deviate in any way from the demand note. Some of the people paid up before Christmas. Everyone was treated ailike. Mr Hankey : Is it true some have been summoned and some have nA ?
The Clerk : No, it is not so. After further discussion, the matter was dropped, the Clerk having explained that they c,uld not in say scay alter the present system.

div.head: STORMY MEETING.
div.p: STORMY MEETING.
GRAPPENHALL CRITICS OF THE
PARISH COUNCIL.

The storm clouds again burst over the annual meeting of the ratepayers of Grappenhall which was ' held in the schoolroom on Monday evening. An I exceedingly large number of ratepayers attended. The, rector, the Rev H V Pigot, was elected to the chair. Amongst those present were Mr Charles II Hoult (clerk), Messrs A Lister-Kaye, W Lomas, F Fox, F Burrows, J Carter, F L Garside and J Bradford. The first business was the election of ten parish councillors and 19 nominations had been received. The voting resulted in the election of the following :—Messrs A Lister-Kaye (75), F Aylmer Frost (62), John Bradford (62), W Winstanley (61), R W Wild (581, Albert Earweker (56), Francis M Appleton (55), W H Wooding (53), C F Read (43), and Edwin A Allen (38). The other candidates %ere :—Messsrs W Lomas (35), Nathan Cook (34), Frederick L Garside (20), Joshur Carter (18), Francis Ellison (18), G A Leach (18), Frank Fox (17), W II Haitley (11), and F Burrows (9). Before the result of the voting was made known, Mr F A Jenkins said he would like to ask the candidates a question. There was a report current in the village, tnat of the ten gentlemen elected by the ratepa}ers to watch over their interests during the past three years, only two were opposed to.— At this stage the Clerk was conversing with the Chairman. Mr Jenkins evidently resented this for be remarked : " Will you kindly allow me to say what T have to say, Mr Clerk, without any interruption at ? I shall be obliged it you would keep still whilst I am speaking." Gmtinuing Mr Jenkins said : Only two out of the ten were opposed to the very expensive sewerage scheme which was put upon the parish. A Voice: I move you are out of order. Mr Jenkins: I um in order. Am I not Mr Chairman?

The Chairman : You are in order in putting a question to the cand,dates. Mr Jenkins : I think you will find all the members of the old Council have been nominated to-night. The Chairman : You are in order in asking a question. Mr Jenkins: Just so. lam going to ask a question. I want to know if it is a fact that only two out of the ten candidates nominated to watck over the interests of the ratepayers were found to.protest against the very expensive sewerage scheme put on ua by the Rural District Council ? No dowbt the late cnairman can answer that question if the candidates do not. Mr Burrows : The scheme was not launched during the lifetime of the late Council, out in 1908, and the, rate of remuneration the engineer was to be paid was flied by them. if the members did not know about it or did not think about it it was their own fault.
Mr Bradford : But, Mr District Councillor, you have not been attending these meetings as you ought to have done.

--The Chairman : You are out of order. Mr A Lister Kayo: There was a public meeting of ratepayers called in regard to the sewerage scheme, and it was their unanimous opinion that the scheme should be opposed for a more modified one, and they informed the Council of that opinion. As a result, at the next meeting of the Parish Council they tried to get a elm- mittee together, but he believed he was right in saying that Mr Bradford and himself were the only two present who would act on that committee. Mr Fox: I think we were all pretty well opposed to the scheme and I should like the minutes of that meet- ing read. As far as his memory carried him they were unanimous that the scheme was too expensive and that they were all in favour of a modified scheme. tie thought that was the wish expressed at the ratepayers' meeting. (Hear, hear.) Mr Burrows : I endorse what Mr Fox has said. Mr Jenkins: It will be interesting to the ratepayers to read that minute if such a minute is in existence, and satisfy the ratepayers on the point. The Clerk: Tne business is the election of Coun- cillors. Definite questions should be put to definite candidates and answered by the candidate only. Mr 0 A Leach : A meeting of the three garishes of Grappenhall Latchford Without and Tiff:3lwatt was called with the distinct view and no other, of modify- ing the whole scheme with the object of making it economical and inexpensive. It was not the wish of, the Council that the scheme should be launched irrespective of what it might cost the individual rate- payers. A Voice: I think we are getting out of order. Mr Leach 'las not asked a question. Mr Fox : Could our assistant overseer read the minute? Mr T.,each : I would like to say in fairness to myself that Mr Jenkins put the question to any member of the old Parish Council. I was a member of that Council and have a perfect right to answer the question myself. Mr Jenkins: I should like Mr Leach to tell the rate- payers how long he was a member of that Council. Mr Leach : I might say, Mr Chairman, that I was a member for longer trian Mrienkins. (Applause). Mr Jenkins: If Mr Leach was a meinuer fur 16 years then I admit I was mistaken. Mr Leach: You were dealing with the old Council not with the history of the parish. (Laughter.) Mr Nicholls : We are getting out of the question. Will the assistant overseer read that minute. The Chairman: That does not come in the business at present. Mr Nicholls: Tam quite satisfied sir. Mr Jenkins- -he minute is in existence I should like it to be reau. If it cannot be read then let some acknowledgment be made. The Clerk advised the chairman that the minute could not be read. __

Mr Lister Kaye : All the ratepayers were given an opportunity to oppose this scheme. Mr Bradford and himself, he continued, had shouldered the job on the committee. All the members present at toe meeting were in favour of opposing the scheme but he did not know whether they had no time to go on the committee or not, but they did not join it. Mr Fox : DJ you assert that no member of the late council besides yourself and Mr Bradford worked in any way to get the scheme modified. A Voice: I rise on a point of order. Is it right for Mr Fox to ask Mr Kaye a question on that minute. The Chairman : Yes. Mr Burrows: He says it was before the Parish Council. Mr Fox : Is Mr Burrows in order in asking a qnes..ion before mine is answered ? I should like to as Mr Lister-Kaye if he asserts that no other member besides Mr Bradford and himself acted against the scheme to try to get it modified ? Mr Lister-Kaye : I said the whole Council were with us, but when it came to the working part on the committee there were only two of us who would act on the Committee, and that probably the other members had not the time to come on the Committee. Mr W Lomas: It has been said " Get on with the business of electing the fresh parish conncillors, and then we can argue and fight points out." When the result of the voting was read out. Mr W Ashton, who had been most persistent all the evening in demanding a poll, said that he along with several other gentlemen, had not voted at all. He demanded a poll. This was seconded. Mr Leach said the voting that night was anything but legal, inasmuch as votes had been recorded by people who were not ratepayers in the parish. Mr Jenkins: I don't think we can act on that ex-parte statement. I think if Mr Leach had seen any- one voting who was not a ratepayer, it was his duty to object at the time. Mr Leach : If --- Several Voices : You are out of order. Sit down. The Chairman: We are discussing the question of the poll being demanded. Mr Burrows: I support the demand for a poll. I consider this meeting a " packed " meeting by Mr Jenkins.

Mr Nicholls: You can have a dozen polls. We don't object in the slightest degree. Mr Leech: Mr Chairman, you do not allow me to go on. If a poll had not been demanded I should have demanded that non-ratepayers leave the room and that a second poll be taken. The Chairman : You would have been too late. Mr Leech: Oh no, I should not. (Hear, hear, and a Voice : " Stick to him.") Mr Bellian : In fairness to everyone it should be pointed out that if a poll were carried out it would be expensive to the ratepayers. He felt sure that the members elected would serve the Council in a proper manner. _ _ .
The Chairman : If five ratepayers demand a poll they can have one. _ _ _
Mr Jenkins r May I ask for the rule stating that five can demand a poll. Mr Ashton : There are above five. Mr Jenkins: I beg your pardon, I addressed the chairman. .

The Chairman: According to my reading of the Act five can demand a poll. Mr Jenkins : Will you kindly read the section, sir ? The Chairman : I have given my ruling. A Voice : Are themoishole of the ratepayers of demanding a poll. The Chairman : I don't think so.

-- Those who demanded the poll were Messrs George Ashton, T Burrows, 0 A Leach, F Buirows and Ernest Mr Lomas : Am lin order in asking a question? The Chairman : No ! The returning officer, Mr Ashton, will fix the time and date of the poll. Mr Jenkins : How is the Rural District Council appointed now ? Is there not some departure in that business The Chairman : We have nothing to do with that here.
Mr Jenkins : Since when? The Chairman : Nominations were sent in on Thursday last. Mr Jenkins: Was there any public notice announcing the notice required.

div.head: SOAP TRADE PATENT CASE,
div.p: SOAP TRADE PATENT CASE,
JUDGMENT AGAINST MESSRS. GROSFIELD

In the Chancery Division of the High Court on Tuesday, the reserved juegment was given in the case brought by Messrs Joseph Crusfie,d arid Sons, Limited, of Warrington, against, Techno-Chemical Laboratories, Limited, and Nib o Testrup, of London. The action was alleged infringement of Dr Norman's patent of 1903 for the conversion of unsaturated tatty acids into saturated compounds. The process enabled whale and similar oils to be used in the manufacture of candles, margarine and soaps, as it removed the strong smell. The plaintiffs put the commercial value of the patent at a very high figure' and even the defendants admitted that it was worth £250,000 per annum. Toe real plaintiffs to the action were said to be Oessrs Brunner Mond and Co., and the real defendants Messrs Lever Brothers, of Port Sunlight. Mr Justice Neville, in giving judgment, said that a patent action was not, in nis opinioJ, different from any other kind of action. Although the evidence of scientific) witnesses might be very useful in assisting the Court on technical matters, the question as to the state of public knowledge and as to the true c,nstruction of the patent was for the Court to decide. There had been a great improvement in recent years, but there was still a great deal of time wasted by calling unnecessary expert evidence. His Lordship went on to dt scribe the patent in question, and pointed out that the claim made was for a liquid process (if producing the resalts set out in the specification. Dr Norman claimed a process which could be applied to any unsaturated commercial acid with a catalyst not only of nickel hut of iron, copper, or cobalt. But the patentee did not make any express reference in his specification to several very important points ; he simply referred to the papers written by Sabatier about the time of the patest, and relied on the state of puLlio knowledge. He (the judge) had come to the conclusion that the patent as sot out in the specification would not produce the results claimed tor it unless one applied with it thing's which were not indicated therein After point- ing out various matters which were required for the success of the process, and which were not indicated, his Lordship said that by n claim so wide as in the pre- sent case the patentee did not safficiently describe a process that could be successfully worked. Therefore the patent was bad from insufficiency, and tbe action must therefore be dismisssd on that ground, with costs. _ _ _

_ Mr Walter, K.O (for the plaintiffs), said the Cour had no power to avoid the patent in the present pro ceedings, and no reference to the ground on which the patent was bad w.s therefore necessary. Mr Jenkins, K.O (for the defendants), agreed that was so. The Judge : Then the order will simply be that the action is dismissed, with costs. With the consent of counsel for the plaintiffs the defendants were given costs on the higher scale, includ- ing the costs of three counsel.

div.head: FLETCHER, RUSSELL AND CO.
div.p: FLETCHER, RUSSELL AND CO.
A Prosperous Year.

The twenty-first annual general meeting of Fletcher. Russell, and Co, Limited, g,is engineers, ttc, was held on Wednesday at the offices of the company. Mr George Perkins presiding over a good attendance. The Chairman said there had been a steady improve- ment in the position of the company, financially and otherwise. A much larger business had been done, owing to some extent to the coal strike, and this, coupled with the many economies which had been effected, accounted for the satisfactory results achieved. Large depreciations had been allowed for, including extra depreciations especially in the pattern value and Pendleton property. In addition to the dividend of 5 per cent. on the ordinary shares, that £4,500 be transferred to the reserve fund, and that the balance' namely, £3,057, be carried forward. The total value of the property had decreased from last years'a total by the sum of £6.505. The additions during the twelve months, including a large new moulding shop, %ere £4,227, and the depreciations and writings off .1:10,7:33, thus the amount of £6,505 just mentioned, was the difference between the additions and the depreciations and extra depreciations. Cash in hand and at bankers I had increased by £11,923, due to the increased business, a very satisfactory feature of the balance sheet. The National Insurance Act had given them a great deal of extra clerical work to do, and although they had only had a few months' working of the Act, they could see that the expense of it practically meant a loss of 1 per cent dividend to the shareholders. The labour question was still causing some trouble. They along with other makers, had to give a further increase of wages to all workmen this year. The com- pany got advances on the prices of their goods last year, which were still being maintained in order to cover the increase in wages and the increased cost of all materials.

Mr Edmund Rowson said that it seeme-I to him a strange thing that the trade unions, on evory possible occasion, should offer opposition to the employer, and instead of working baud in hand for the good ot the ceuntry, the employers; and employees, they seemed fit to fly in the face of the employers.

div.head: LIBERAL WOMEN.
div.p: LIBERAL WOMEN.
A WARNING AGAINST THE CONSCRIPTIONIST AGITATION.
REV. W. COOPER
AND MR. HAROLD SMITH, M P.

There was another enthusiastic gathering of members of the Women's Liberal Asiociation in the Bold-street schmaroom On Tuesday evening, the occasion being a tea meeting and clncert in connection with the Town Hall and Bewsey Wards. Over 2CO sat down to tea, the arrangements for which had been made by the ward captains (Mrs Lindley and Mrs Pemberton), and the hon secretary of the association (Mrs Edmund Osborne). Members of the committee assisted at the tables. The subsequent meeting and concert was pre- sided over by Mrs Dodds (vice-presido-nt), and amongst others present were Mrs Clarke (Liverpool), the Rev W Cooper, Councillors F Lindley, j Dickenson, J Skelland and J Snsw.

Mrs Clarke devoted the greater part of vu interesting address to the suffrage quest ion, She said she was exceedingly sorry that s.rrie ef the ardedt spirits of the movement were going to such extremes, and that they had very deplorable rut rages happening daily. She did not, think such conduct Min helping the suffrage movement at, all; in the contritry it had a hindering effect. (Hoer, hear.) The Cause had been advocated for years, aid she believed that, the militants of six or seven years; ego did help to draw people's attention to the movement. E'en yet, if they had a meeting purely on the suffrage question, it. was largely the idea that there Was going to be some fun that drew a large audience. The end, however, did not justify the means, end one could not help feeling great regret that the militants did commit such excesses. At the present moment it became many of them who had the cause really at I earl to point out that the majority of women who did wish for the vine, did not ceunterittnee these tactics. She understood there were about 38 suffrage societies, only two of which were confes,edly militant. Those two, however, had the bulk or the money and enthusiasm It therefore behoved women who wished to agitate in a peaceful and constitutionnl way to put just as much enthusiasm into their work. Dealing with the bitter hostility of tue militants to the Liberal Government, Coe speaker said that if the Conservatives were returned to power they would certainly give them a measure of women's suffrage, tint it would not be a democratic measure. It would probably strengthen the hands of the Conservatives, but what would the workir g classes have to hope from a Conservative Government? She hoped and believed that the Liberal Government during the next session would give facilities for a Suffrage Bill and help it through. (Applause.) Mrs Clarke went on to advance arguments in favour of the enfianchisemeut if women, pointing out that there was a great field out- side the home in which women could exert a very powerful influence. She showed how the development of industrialism had forced women more and more into the labour market, but they had no voice in the I/INS under which they laboured. One object lesson to women in demanding the vote was the success of the Labour Party. Until that party went into Parliament the working men had very little consideration. When they realized the necessity of direct representation and found a party powerful enough to make their voice heard, they found that their grievances received mere attention. Mrs Clarke touched upon the great, influence which women could wield on such questions as temperance reform cud the alteration of the Poor Law, if only they poseessed the vote. Alluding ti other political issuses, she referred to tne c rnscriptionist agitation. We in England had been very happily placed in not having c iescripion up to the present. (Hear, her.) There wits, however, a very strong section of the Conservative party, and she believed 130nle Liberals too, who tlaoright that conscription would be a good thing for us. She thought it would be the very saddest thing that could happen. (Hear, hear.) We needed is strong navy ; our very life depended upon it. Supposing, however, that we had a large conscriptionist army, if our Navy were destroyed and we could not get our food supply, the army would be like so many [(musts devouring the land. What good would it be without the protection of the Navy ? The 1 growth of militarism, as expressed in the saying "We've got the ships, we've got the men Rad we've got the money too," was always an inducement to put our finger into someone else's pie We did not want that ; we had got is big enough pie of our o an. (Hear, hear.) There was 1.0 real necessity for coLscription, arid anyone who knew of tale great evils that ban resulted from that system on the Continent, would be very sorry to see them in dear old England. She hoped that at the next election they would de nothing to return to power a party that wits going to bring about dearer food and conscription. (Applause.) The Rev W COOPER said he wondered whether all present knew that the NI.P for Warrington was Mr Harold Smith. (Laughter.) Some folk seemed to be very much afraid that that little fact might be over- looked—(laughter)— and so if Mr Smith chanced to make sonic remark in the House of Commons, the rnagnifiying glass was applied to it and it appeared very prominently in certain local newspapers. P, however. they read the daily Press would probably find that Mr Smith was not regarded as the imp.raant personage that some imagined him to be. Ceuncillor Roberts recently ventured to ask Mr Smith a question or two and he (Mr Cooper) was rather glad he did. There was is book which some people liked, and in it there was a character named Harold. But he was always called "Childe Harold." (Laughter.) He did not kn. w whether some of them thought that might fit their local M.P. Mr Smith said he wanted an opponent and be (Mr Cooper) had been wondering what he meant by that. Dio
he' want someone to meet him a,r,d have -a

round with the gloves at the local noxiug booth ? (Laughter.) He was afraid Mr Smith would cut a queer figure. (Laughter ) Did he want someone to engage in newspaper controversy with him, because it ,:cetirred to him (the speaker) that Mr smith ought to finish off those with wnom he conimenc ,d an argument before calling for anybody else. Ile seemed to forget that now he was M.P. for this important borough, he was expected to represent the borough and not call for opponents. Although Party men had put him in. be should remember that he represented the borough and net become bad tempered because soi,ebody ventured to ask him a question or two. Mr Smith had not vouch,safed any reply worth considering but had given plenty of ablve. However, Mr Smith was not in the most enviable position. He was in the House of Commons along with an opposition which was in a distinct minority. He felt bound to say and do some- thing, and as he could not do it in the H. use of Commons he had to come r'ow n to Warriugton and, at meeting of hi si,pporters, call for an opponent. He might, think that was sear, but if that was the only sample of what he c,uld do for the constituency, it was time they reo,mri eeded him a cliange—(laughter.—and he believed they would do- it when the next e ection came. (Applause ) Continuing, Mr COOPER said he supposed that when they opened the next morning's naper they would find new delimit inn of tariff reiortr, becaus Mr Bonar Law was spEakingt in Manchester that night. The more spteches Mr Law made, the better it was for the cause of Liberalism. (Apphatise.) Each tie fe o ened his mouth, he got foot well into it— (iaughter)—Find all his party were in doubt as to the Meaninl ,•f what he had said. T e present position or tariff reform was .eyoncl the comprehension if any person. Mr Bonar Lew would tell them it was one thing and Lord Derby would tell them it was ano, her, while at Kendal the Conservatives were a.tually running a Free Trader BY their candidate. (Laughter.) The rosmetivres which had taken place in that constituency showed the sorry predicament in which the Tory party found iislt ; for Colonel Weston had in turn declined to repudiate Free Trade or to denounce Horne Rule and the Insurance Act. He (the

speaker) had a suggestion to make to the Torie?. Thsy recently held a dun-Ting exhibition in Warrington,which was one of the best. eovertisetnents for Free Trade he had seen for a long time. div.head: ALLEGED MASKED BURGLAR AT WIDNES.
div.p: ALLEGED MASKED BURGLAR AT WIDNES.

At Widnes, on Monday, Joseph Jackson, Prince's- street,was charged on remand with hurglariously enter- ins 38, Salisbury-street, and stealing jewellery,the pro- perty of Arthur Hughes, value £5 18s. Superintendent lioster said Hughes was the manager of a local co-operative store, and retired to bed shortly after midnight. He heard a noise shortly after, and went downstairs, but saw nothing wrong. Later, his wife aroused him, and standing by the bed- side, with a mask over his face was Jackson. Hughes closed with prisoner, who was held whilst Mrs Hughes went for the police Sergeant Davidson, who resides opposite, took( him into custody. Upon him several articles of jewellery were found, an electric flash lamp, iron chisel, skeleton doorkey, glass-cutter, table-knife, piece of rope,and a bottle containing liquid to quietest dogs. When charged, he said "1 don't remember having a gold pendant, but the other articles 1 have in my pocket." Joseph Jackson was further charged with breaking and entering the lock-up shop of William Gordon, Victoria-road, and stealing a gold bangle the property Agues Gordon, and a number of pipes, ciearette and cigar cases, match boxes, &c., valued £6 fis and also £l2 19s 21 in money, the property of William Gordon. When prisoner was arrested on the previous charge some of the articles which were found in his possession led to his being arrested on this charge. Superintendent Fuster said Mr Gordon kept a sub-post office and tobacconist's shop. On February 2 last the place was left secured and abut nine o'clock the tollowiug day the shop, was found to he in a state of great disorder. Au entrance had been effected by the back window. The raoel of the door leading to the shop was found to have been bored round by a brace and hit, and forced. The b.ace and bit was found at prisoner's home, which exactly corresponded with tne holes bored in the door. Joseph, when charged with the offence, said he got the matchbox from a friend, but if it was going to be robbery he would tell them nothing about it. Prisoner subsequently admitted the charge. Pursuing inquiries, Detective-sergeant Davidson visited the house of his brother, Thomas Jackson, and found several of the missing articles hidden in the coalplace. Thomas Jackson, of Hood-lane, Sankey, was charged with receiving a quantity of goods, knowing them to be stolen. _ _

Agnes Gordon, 93, Perkin-avenue, Nottingham,identi- fled the gold bangle. Further evidence was given by William Ashworth and William Gordon. I.lle latter caused some merriment when the suplriatend tat asked him if the property was his. " Yes," he replied, " prisoner was not a bad judge, either. He took the best in the shop." Mr Steel, of Warrington, who appeared for Thomls Jackson, pleaded for leniency, and asked that he should be treated as a first offender.
Prisoner were committed for trial at the Asslzes.

div.head: Borough Police Court
div.p: Borough Police Court
SITURDAY.—Before Metiers R T Fairclough (in the chair) and A J Jolley, Alderman Tinnion, Councillor
Locker and Mr T Per-u-berton.

"ALL SHE COULD GET."—Mary Flannery, 35, Lloyd- street, pleaded guilty to stealing during the past six months /rom the pawnshop, 18, Lovely-lane, a large quantity of articles, value .C 3 13s. 7d., the property of Stubbs Stores, Ltd.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner was a customer at the shop, and apparently on each occasion she bad visited the premises she had taken all she could lay her hands on.—A fine of £3, including costs, was imposed.
COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs Roger C Parr (in the chair), H Roberts and W Fairclough. BIT A POLICEMAN'S FINGKRS : SCENE AT ButcroswooD.—Andrew McLoughlin, Lime Kiln Farm, Burtouwood, was charged with being orunk and dis- orderly and with assaulting PC Moulding on March 17th—The officer stated that on Monday he was called to a disturbance at the Limerick Hotel, Bnrtonwood, and found the prisoner, who was drunk, using had language and wanting to fight the landlord. As the man refused to go away witness arr.ated him and in a struggle Mc Loughlin got witness's fingers in his mouth and only the use of the truncheon would make him louse his hold. A piece was bitten out of one finger and he had been treated by a doctor for the injuries.— William Price, licensee of tbe Limerick Hotel, said they had refused to serve the prisoner because he was mad drunk and was using obscene language. The policeman was sent for and the struggle ensued as described by the last witness.—Prisoner was fined 5s for the drunkenness and lOs and costs for the assault or fourteen days. CARELEbs BUT CRIMINAL—Percy Collier, 190, Common-road, Earlesto 4n,was summoned for taking matches into pit No. 2 of the Collins Green Cilliery Company at Burtonwood en the 7th inst.—Mr Darlington of Wigan, who appeared for the Company, stated that when the men reaciied the bottom of the shaft they were searched and it was found that the defendant had a box of mhtches in his possession. It was nothing but carelessness but it was criminal care- lessness and the Company, who felt they must stop such a practice at all costs, asked that such a penalty might be imposed that would nut an end to it.—ln inflicting alma of 20s and costs, Mr Parr reminded the defendant tnat he endangerei oth,tr men's lives by his are lessuess.

div.head: BRITANNIC ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED.
div.p: BRITANNIC ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED.

This old-established Company, as will be seen from the abstract of Accounts published in our advertising columns, has experienced another highly satisfactory year. Notwithstanding a substantial increase in the amount distributed by way of claims, the net result of the year's transactions has been the addition of £313,051 to the accumulated funds of the company. In their report the directors refer with special pleasure to the results of the annual valuation reported by Mr Ackland, which enable them to announce an increased bonus to participating policy-holders in the ordinary branch and an allotment of bonus to claimants under industrial policies. 'lhe premium income in respect of life assurance amounted to £1,245,335, being an increase of £28,077 over the previous year. The total premium income amounted to £1,2:)1,069. The gross income from all sources amounted to £1,383,614, being an increase of £40,407 over the gross income for the previous year. The accumulated funds, inclusive of capital paid up, now amounted to £3,286,905, being an increase for the year of £313,051. The claims (inclusive of surrenders) paid during the year an ounted to £602,199, and included £128,917 paid under maturing endow merit and endowment assurance policies. The total claims paid by the company up to the 31st December, 1912, amounted to £8,761,989 The annual valuation of the company's policy liabilities has been made by the consulting actuary, Mr Thomas G Ackland, FIA,F F A. On the present occasion, the valuation has been on a specially stringent basis, the policies in all classes in the ordinary branch having been valued by a strictly net premium method, whilst in the industrial branch the whole of the policies have been valued by the mortality table known as the " English Life Table No 6 (Males)," deduced from the mortality experience of the population during the modern period 1891-1901, which recent investigation shows to be closely in accord with the actual experience of the company. It is believed that the company is the first thus to adopt this up-to-date table in its valuations. After making full provision for the policy liabilities on this drastic basis, a gross surpluaof £95,342 is brought out. The sum of £lO,OOO has been added to the investment reserve fund, raising it to £75,000, and the sum of £5 COO has been added to the staff pension fund, increasing it to £15,000, Out of the remaining surplus, the directors, acting upon the advice of the consulting actuary, declare the amount of £56,420 available for distribution amongst the partici- pating policyholders in the ordinary branch and the shareholders, which will provide a reversionary bonus at the increased rate of 32s per cent. for the year to all participating policyholders in the immediate profit class, and make adequate provision for the policy- holders in the accumulated profit class. It is also pro- posed to allot a cash bonus at the rate of £5 per cent. upon sums assured under industrial policies of five years duration and upwards which become claims by death or maturity during the year commencing 10th l‘iarch,l9l3, and terminating Bth March, 1914, except in Cases where additions have already been made under the terms of the policy. The local superintendent of the company is Mr T Boyd, Midland Buildings, Winwick-street, Warrington'

div.head: GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT ST. HELENS.

At St Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, a local inquiry was held by Mr North, a Local Government Board Inspector, into an application by the Corporation for sanction to borrow £430 for works of street improve- ment. Mr Andrew (Town Clerk) said that by the local Act churches and chapels were not charged for the sewering and paving of the streets alongside their build ings, and the £430 had been expended for thoFe pur- poses. Alderman Foote (chairman of the Finance Committee) ridiculed the holding of an inquiry in respect of so small a sum, but the Town Clerk replied that it was necessary by Act of Parliament.

div.head: Wycliffe Congregational Church Livingstone Centenary Service
div.p: Wycliffe Congregational Church Livingstone Centenary Service

A Epecial set, i.;•e in recognition of the ceutentary the birth of David Livingetone, the great explorer' was held at the NVycliffe Congregations! Church °II Sueday morning A special order of service, includieg hymns and psalms which were connected with partt. cubir epochs in the life of the hero of the 05;: Contineut. bad been arranged. The choir effectiveli rendered as nu anthem Bishop Walsharn How's" For the saints who from their labour rest." There woo large congregation. The Rev T T JAMES after a reference to tllet shadowy heroes of bygone ages, said the" thy they commemorated one who so reeentli played his part that they possessed about him awealtAn of positive information. There were many men eu" women in England still who had listened to the voice of David Livingstone, and whose eyes had rested 00 that e which strong, rugged o ftaticee, heroic thatc missionaryepa the Dark Continent. It needei no weaving of imagine: esinewy esp l o r flegr o u rt; tive minds to provide a picture of the man, no recount.' to the prnegyrics of partisans, or the rhetorical device° of mere word spinners ; there were simple uncontre- vertible facts waiting for all who cared to seek tiler-3' It eas but forty years ago that the tangled forests 1' down A f rica formed the field where Livingstone 10 d•iwn his life, and through the clays th, had passed since then, the eloquence of 1;1! \vitt e.s hid not lost its charm, nor the wcncle• of his triumphs palled upon tue minds of There was one point to emphasise and that was OP David Livingstone began and finished his work er missionary, and that at no period in the whole storY °A his days did he cease to feel that he served and toile' lin that capacity. Certainly be was a great explorer.; The great waterways of Central Africrethe great intent' lakes, the greet routes for the future direction of trad! aid commerce, the whole lie of the country from nortP to south and east to west, from the very centre to the sea on either side, these things Livingstone made tbe_ knowledge of the world. Nor was that all. It, was On the mere course of the Zambesi or the wonder 01 Victoria Falls that put the race in his debt. It wl,l the wonderful revelation of the kind of land it was. was no desert after ell,it abounded in grassy plains flo' f.-rtile soils, forests of endless variety, and population° vast in number and various in custom, life and speecl?i I* hat was the discovery of a Contieent and men kuee; and drew their maps afresh,and marvelled at the tenacityd doggedne,s and perseverance with which Livingstone h' almost single-handed,riciriched the knowledge of nein; kind. Livingstone stood in history as more than the grt explorer. His name was for ever hound up with tb story of human liberty. He waged incessant war f°: the freedom of mankind. The history of Africa sct', dark with the horror of the slave trade. Very eariY his contact with the strange new land Livinestol begin to realize the blight of slavery upon it. He how material civilization was bringing in its train, n,°,, the uplifting, but the absolute degradation of human"?.: It became more to him thin arty feud or battle between" tribe and tribe, for that was the curse of the white v 36„ upon the black, and with a love and sacrifice whic" never feared to pay the cost he made the cause of slaver his own. There was something beneath tue explorer and the humanitarian ; there was the missioner 4 of the Cross. That he was from first to last and IP_ the way between. The whole plan of his exploratiols sprang out of a missionary enthusiasm.

div.head: MARRIAGE BY BARGAIN.
div.p: MARRIAGE BY BARGAIN.

----- _ _ Another echo is to be' found in "The three knights from Spain." Here comes three knights all out of Spain, We have come to court your daughter Jane. Our daughter Jane she is too young She has not learned the Spanish tongue. Whether she be young or old, Tis for her beauty she must be sold. Turn back, tarn back, ye Spanish knights, And rub your spurs till they are bright. Our spurs are bright and richly wrought, For in this town they were not bought.

This sounds a different note. The three knights state their errand to the parents of the maiden. A bargain has to be made with them. She has a marketable value because of her good looks, and "for her beauty she must be sold." Here also we are in a curious and unfamiliar world, but the song undoubtedly reflects what once was ordinary usage. Nor are these the only children's games which contain pre-historic fragments. In one at least we seem to have Marriage by capture—the process by which desirable maidens were forcibly carried away by raids and in trials of strength. The game has the innocent title " Gather- ing Nuts in May," but commemorates things far less innocent than the title suggests. A. M.

THE MAN WHO KEPT HIS WORD. David Livingstone had several happy little nick names given to him by the natives of Africa. One of them meant "The man who laughs with all his body," and described Livingstones hearty laugh very well. Another name they applied to him was "The man who keeps his word." This name was one he deserved and I am this week going to tell a story which will help to show how he won his immense power over the hearts of the Africans. In his desire to find a highway for European trade which could be rightly carried on, Livingstone engaged twenty- seven natives as porters to go with him from Linyanti in the interior to Loanda on the West coast, promising that he would return with them and see them all safely to their homes again. They passed through many different tribes on the long journey, which took many months, and as they had no stores of food for themselves and no presents for the natives (except a small amount of coffee, cloth and beads), they had a very hard time. Heavy rains and constant wettings caused fever and dysentery, and mosquitos attacked him furiously. One savage tribe he met declared he should not pass unless he gave them an ox, a gun and a man; but as for giving up one of his men for a slave he said he would sooner die, and for this his timid followers were very grateful. In spite of weariness and fever he did what he could as a missionary. Finally he reached Loanda, a poor ragged skeleton, and was kindly received by the Portuguese and nursed back to health. It was a time of suffering and distress. He had been separated from his wife and children for two long years,and had earned, if ever a toiler did earn, a period of rest. Most unexpectedly there appeared in the harbour an English ship whose captain offered to take him to the home land where his family, and rest, and well-earned honours were waiting- for him. We can think how he must have longed to go. He had not even had a letter for many months. But he had promised the black followers who were with him that he would take them back to their homes. So, without hesitation, he turned from the prospect of seeing his own dear ones, and started back to trudge on aching feet two thousand miles and be lost to communication with home for two long years more. He nursed the men through their sicknesses and saw them safe home again. They reached home in rags and poverty,having parted with all they possessed on the way. Did he not earn fairly the title which the natives gave him of "The Man Who Keeps His Word " ? " We trusted you," said certain of the blacks who had been left at another time with a promise of his return. "The Tette people often taunted us by saying, 'Your Englishman will never return ' ; but we trusted you, and now we shall sleep." The poor burdened hearts were quite won over. They turned to him as the flowers to the sun. Often indeed their devotion was embarrassing, but Livingstone, with a touch of humour, used to say that there was a real remedy. When a native could not be got rid of he threatened to have him washed. But after be had said it, he would laugh "with his whole body," and the natives who were embarrassing him by their affections would cling to him the more closely.

FELICITATING PA. My pa says when he was a boy, W'7, all he'd get was just one toy--- A jumpin'-jack, or pop-gun, when 'T 'uz Christmas-time where he live then. He never looked for any more— He didn't 'spect a whole toy-store !

My pa says 'at in those days Folks did things dirrent, anyways. He says he never got a stack 0' tcffee—more 'n he could pack. A stick o' toffee's all he got An' he'd think that was a lot. My pa, he says when he's a child Folks didn't all try to go xsild, An' make their children think they'd get Enough to run their pas in debt. 0' course, it wasn't from their pas, But always came from Santa Claus. He tells me that I should be glad I don't have Christmas like he had ; He says there's lot he was denied, But he learned to be satisfied ; He never dreamed, he says, that boys Should have a whole room full of toys. I tell my pa I'm awful sad About th' hard times that he had, But that he's really lucky now— He's in our fambly, anyhow, An' that he shouldn't raise a fuss, But be real glad he lives with us. WILBUR D. NESBIT. THIS WEEK'S STORY. WHY HE WAS ARRESTED.

A man who said he was "tired of motor- ing" sold his machine to a guileless friend. A week later his friend approached him with a troubled look upon his face. "Look here Jack " he began "I don't want to say anything disagreeable_but when you sold me that car you said you had been arrested six times through motoring in it. I thought it must be a flyer, but look here upon my word I can't get it to go more than 5 miles an hour and it breaks down every 500 yards. Do you mind telling me how you came to get arrested? " "Certainly my dear fellow" said the man who had got rid of the car "It was for obstructing the highway."
