provide the institution with £5OO which was urgently needed for the purpose of installing a new heating appratus in the old building and improving the equip- ment of the operating theatre. Mr ROuER C PARR (hon. treasurer) seconded and the proposition was agreed to. THE OFFICERS.

The election of officers then took place as follows : President, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., C.V.O. ; vice- presidents re-elected with the addition of the Very Rev Father Whittle, Mr J H Smethurst and Alderman Burton (chairman of Ulm Workingmen's Committee) ; Iron treasurer, Mr Roger C Parr ; hon. auditor, Mr C Jackson Holmes ; non-c:lnsulting surgeons, Dra E A Fox and G W Joseph; hon surgeons, Drs E E Dowdeo, E J Fox, G H Joseph and A Hodgkinson ; hon. assistant surgeons, Drs G Binns, C Robinson, F H Seger and R Wilson Sutherland : hon. dental surgeon, Mr El H Taylor ; Board of Management, re-elected with the addition of Mr J J Whitley and Mr L A Voisey. OPHTHALMIC SURGEON.
Dr E J Fox WAS appointed hou opthalmio surgeon at he institution, in addition to his duties as hon surgeon.

THAN KS. The customary votes of thanks were accorded to officials and organizing bodies. Mr A J JOLLEY, in returning thanks for the Hospital Sunday Committee, expressed regret that this year the offertories at the various churches hail shown a slight tendency to decrease instead of increase. Dr Sutherland responded for the hoe surgeons, Mr J H Smethurst for the Juvenile Ball Committee, and Mr J Moore Murray for the Children of Warrington Cot Committee. ACT TO MAKE NO DIFFERENCE. Mr W P RYLANDS, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Workingmen's Committee, said it was a great source of satisfaction to have it reported that toere was a confident feeling that the Insurance Act would NOT MAKE THE SLIGHTEST DIFFERENCE in the amount that workingmen were prepared to subscribe to the institution. He believed the working- men realized that the services rendered by the Infirmary were something quite apart from and additional to the benefits they would get from the Insurance Act. Those services were rendered not only to insured persons— indeed only a comparatively small proportion were insured—but to their wives and children. Consequently It wss upon voluntary subscriptions that the Board of Management must depend to the largest extent for support. Mr JACKSON HOLMES seconded and the vote was accorded, Mr G WALKER responding. BUSINESS AND PLEASURE. The Rev H V PIGOT proposed a hearty vote of thanks to .the Million Penny Fond Committee who had,he said, by their Old English Fairs made money raising a very pleasant occupation —not for themselves, because they had to w ,rk hard night and day, but for the patrons of their enterprises. (Hear, hear). Dr SUTHERLAND seconded and said it was a great acquisition to the Infirmary to have such an absolutely first-rate Xray apparatus as the Million Penny Fund Committee had assisted to provide. Mr H COLLIE, in acknowledging the vote of thanks, said that if ever the institution required the assistance of the committee again they were prepared to give it. (Applause).

"AN AIR OF REPOSE." A vote of thanks was accorded to the Mayor for the use of the Council ChAmber, the Rev H OGDEN, who eecondod it, remarking that there was an air of repose about the meeting which would have captivated the Mayor, had he been present. (Laughter). Sir GILBERT GREENALL : He is not used to it. (Laughter). Sir Gilbert Greenall was thanked for presiding, on the proposition of Councillor tt ROBERTS seconded by Mr JOHN FAIRCLOUGH.

They were thankful for those generous gifts, and they appreciated them very much. They were only sorry that they could not see their way to continue those donations during 1912. If they put those three items together they found they amounted to £l2s,and,deduc- tiug that from .Cl4B Ils, it only left them with a deficiency of .E 23 us from 1911. (Applamse.) That was gratifying and ought to be satisfactory to everyone. As they all knew, the past year had been a most trying and critical one. They were faced at the commence- ment with a national coal strike whin for magnitude surpassed anything we had had before. After detailing the hard times experienced during that period of want the Alderman continued that it was plain to be seen that their contributions to the Infirmary suffered as a consequence of that strike. The strike ended, but their troubles wore not ended. A short time afterwards they had other troubles arising out of the Insurance Act. He had nothing to say for the merits or demerits of the Act, that was neither the time or place, but he was bound to say that the Act had materially interfered with the subscriptions to the Warrington Infirmary. They received information that a number of workingmen had ceased to subscribe to the Infirmary on account of the Act and meetings were held at the various works. Mr Hampson who had done them yeomen service worked exceedingly hard and the result was that,-without exception, the workingmen in the town had renewed their subscriptions. (Applause). If it had not been for the coal strike and the Insurance Act their subscriptions would no doubt have amounted to £1,500, a sum they had tried to raise for a good many years. After eulogising the work of the Infirmary and appealing for support and encouragement, Alderman Burton concluded that the patients at the Irfirmary would be more and more looked after as time went on. LOW WATER MARK.

Mr J H SMET:IITRST seconded and said he was suffi- ciently optimistic to believe that they bad seen the low water mark in regard to the contributions. (Hear, hear). He had every confidence in the workingmen of Warring- ton and particularly the Workingmen's Committee con- nected with the Infirmary. The year had been a most trying one not only for the workingmen but for the Board of AldtlPgement. It had been trying for them in more ways than one and particularly so with regard to the changes which had come about through the National Insurance Act. He advocated the idea that the contributions to the Infirmary should be deducted from the wages of The men. if the cause was thoroughly explainel to them the workers would not grumble at the amount being deducted from their wages. After remarking that they could not understand some of the readings of the Insurance Act, he said they had to recognise it was now an Act of the land —(hear, hear)—and every one of them must do their utmost to make it go along and see to it that the various other institutions suffered as little as possible. He could not see, however, that any system could compete with the present hospital system in the way of efficiency. There was a deficiency in contributions all over the country; they were not the only institution which suffered in that way. They were a long way from the time when they would have to threw up the sponge. (Hear, hear.) As long as they got the support of the workingmen they would continue in the good work they wore going. Dealing with the Warrington Infirmary and Its future, he said that special efforts had been made in the past few years to bring the institution to a higher state of efficiency, and in regard to tbat the tone of the hospital Was never higher. (Applause.) Ho paid a tribute to the honorary staff and spoke of the improvements they were going to make in the future. They had a splendid resident house surgeon who was ably backed up by his assistant who became inoculated with his superior's ideas, that they must give the greatest attention and extend the greatest civility to patients. They also wanted civility from those who Game to the Institution. They would be surprised If they heard f 301310 of the rude things some of the people said to the resident staff. The nurses also did their work well. They had a nursing staff which was second to none iu the manner in which they tried to do their work for the benefit of the patients. He paid a compli- ment to Mr J Daintith and Alderman Burton, who represented the committee on the Board, and concluded with the remark that both employer and employed must do their best for the Infirmary, and they would do their beet for the patients. Mr J FAIRCLOUGH supported and said he was grateful for the cheque which they had given him.

div.head: INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY.
ANXIOUS YEAR BUT SATISFACTORY
INCOME.
INSURANCE ACT AND WORKINGMEN'S CONTRIBUTIONS.

Although the past year has been one of some anxiety for the Board of Management of the Warring- ton Infirmary, there was a consensus of opinion that the statement of accounts submitted at the annual meeting of governors held at the Town Hall on Mon- day afternoon was very satisfactory. The debit balance of £BB9, with which the year began, has been more than halved and, while the ordinary income has shown a slight increase, there has been a reduction of £56 in the corresponding expenditure. The Board of Management strongly appeal to the public for con- tinued support to enable them to maintain the voluntary character o;f the hospital. "Under no other system " said Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, who pre- sided " could we have the same sympathetic and zealous service on the part of the hon. surgeons or the same devoted attention by the Board of Management." The probable effect of the National Insurance Act on the finances of the institution has, of course, occupied much consideration and a scheme by which the Infirmary shall receive some assistance from the funds of the Insurance Committee, is at present before the National Insurance authorities. There was a good attendance at the annual meeting and the spirit of confidence displayed augured well for the future working of the institution.

div.head: YEAR'S WORK.
div.p: THE YEAR'S WORK.

In their 103rd annual report the Board of Manage- ment stated that the number of patients treated in 1912 was 12,333—an increase of 100 on the previous year. In the year 1907, before the extension was completed, 547 inpatients were treated, as against 1,053 in 1912. The average number of beds occupied was 56.31, as against 56 for 1911; the average cost pr bed amounted to £62 12s 11d, as compared with £63 13s 4d in the previous year. The year began with a debit balance of £839 18s 6d, and closed with a reduced debit balance of £423 17s 101. The ordinary expenditure was £1,723 17s Gd, a decrease of £56 Os 41. With the exception of the items under surgery and oispensary, which had been reduced by £222 is Id, ordinary expenditure had increased, in conse- quence of the advance.in cost of provisions and ttn greater number of in-patients treated. The Board tendered their special thanks to the honorary surgeons for the intereA they took in the purchase and use of drugs and surgical rf quirements, ahich resulted in so considerable an economy in this department. There was an extraordinary expenditure of £72 for paintiog the exterior of the Infirmary Buildings. The ordinary income was £4,320 4s. 10d , an increase of £3B 17s 7d. The income from investments was £837 131. 81., an increase of £l3 12s. 11d. The annual subscriptions were £l. 15d 18s., a decrease of £l4 9s. Congregational collections were £217 03 id, an increase of £6 4s sd.lt was gratifying to record that the income from the Working Men's It,firmary Committee was £1,397 9s. 10d an increase of £166 Gs. 9d.Special thanks were tendered to the committee. The Board were pleased to report that £941 13s 41 was received from the Centenary Million Penny Fund Committee, being the balance of the million pennies (£4,166 13s 4d),ln addition,this committee had a surplus of £431 9s 101, with which they provided an up-to-date X-ray equipment, new mortuary, additional drug store accommodation and pathological label atory accommo- dation. These acquisitions greatly increased the efficiency of the Institution, and brought it up to the latest hospital standard. Toe 13,ard, in tendering their grateful thanks to the Centenary Million Penny Fund Committee on the c3mpletion of their task, felt certain that on some future occasion they might be able to rely upon the services of all who, in any way, assisted to bring abut such a magnificent result. The Endowment Fund was increased by the receipt of the following legacies :—The late Mrs Margaret Neild, £228 12s ld ; and the late Mrs Elizabeth Hartley, £5OO. The balance of £lOO required to complete the amount of £5OO for the endowment of Cot No 1 was recived from the Children of Warrington Cot Endowment Fund Committee, in Warrington Corporation Mortgage Bonds at 31 per cent per annum. In addition, Cot No 2 was provided and payment of £25 made for its maintenance

for the year. In commemoration of the services given by 'Air Charles White for over half a century, a bed in one of the wards was named the " Charles White Bed " ; and in recognition of the services rendered by Mr W Peter Rylands, in connection with the recent extension of the Institution a bed in one of the new wards was named the " Rs farads Bed." The year provided a time of great anxiety, but the Board considered the statement of accounts submitted very satisfactory. Every effort was made to make the equipment of the Institution as efficient as possible. The National Insurance Act had been in operation for so short a time that it was impossible to forecast the effect it might have. To judge by present indications there would he an increased damand made f r in-patient treatment, which was the most expensive department. It was increasingly recognized that horpitals were an absolute necessity. The Board, therefore, earnestly appealed not only for continued and increased contri- butions from those who already subscribed, hut for annual subscriptions and -lonations from those did not now help in this noble work.

div.head: INCOME APPROACHING EXPENDITURE.
div.p: INCOME APPROACHING EXPENDITURE.

Sir GILBERT GREENALI, in his presidental addreFs, laid stress on the fact that the ordinary income of the institution was now approaching the ordinary expendi- ture. In 1908, after the extension had teen opened, the deficiency on the .year's work was £1,200. In conse- quence of the ready response to appeals for additional and increased annual subscriptions arid the incroasA interest displayed by the Workingmen's Committee, the nominal income had gradually risen until it was now only £403 12s 8d below the norm3.l expenditure. It was a

div.head: MOST ENCOURAGING SIGN
div.p: MOST ENCOURAGING SIGN

and led them to hope that the inhabitants of the town and district would not fail to help a charity which was doing such beneficent work. They regretted that the annual subscriptions were £l4 loss than in previous years, as a steady and increasing subscrip- tion list was one of the most reliable sources of income. They trusted that those subscribers who hal withdrawn or decreased their annual contributions, under the special circumstonces which prevailed last year, might be induced again to help the institution in its efforts on behalf of those who fell by the way in the battle of life. Expressing special thanks to the Workingmen's Com- mittee, Sir Gilbert said he was pleassd to learn that the systematic form of contribution was now in vogue in practically all the workshops in the town. The Board would welcome the formation of another committee to obtain contributions from employers and places of business. Allusion was made to the Icas sustained in the death of many valued friends, including Mr Charles White, Mrs Pickmere, Mrs W II Bleckly and Mr Frederick Monks, each of whom rendered conspicuous service on committees and did everything in their power throughout a long life spEnt in the district, to help the institution.

HOW TO COMMEMORATE THE KING'S VISIT. Mr J H SMF.THURST (chairman of the Board of Man- agement), in moving the adoption of the report,pointed out that there was a &crease in the payments by private and ordinary patients. He invited the people of Warrington to inspect the conveniences which were placed at the disposal of the better-class people who required special attention and he felt sure more people would he disposed to take advantage of the private wards. The institution had not received quite so ranch money from the ordinary patients in voluntary payments simply because, although more people had been attended, they could not afford to pay to the same extent as in pre- vious years. There was also a reduction in the pence obtained from the out-patients' department, largely due to the fact that during the coal strike the Board, as far as possible, forgave the payment of any money for dressings &c—a concession which was of great benefit to the poor. In face of the general out- cry which had been raised in hospital quarters as to decreased revenue they in Warrington ought to be extremely proud that during the last year their receipts had more nearly approximated to their requirements than in previous years. (Applause.) He appealed to the firms who had curtailed their contributions seriously to consider whether, as the days went on and their prosperity increased, they could not continue their former support. A large number of subscriptions had been sent in from various works without any reduc- tions whatever. With regard to the workingmen's contributions he appealed for greater interest on the part of employers in making systematic deductions from the wages. In no ease had the workingmen declined to have contributions deducted, and it was only by reason of indifference in certain questions that the money was not always sent in regularly. The Board of Manage- ment hoped to get a substantial contribution 'from the funds available under the

div.head: NATIONAL INSURANCE ACT!
div.p: NATIONAL INSURANCE ACT!

Some time ago they approached the local Insurance Committee with the request that they should seriously consider the position of the Infirmary. Certain schemes had been submitted to the head authorities in London' but up to now no definite reply had been received. The Board of Management had decided that, for three months, no change should be made in the system of treating patients, but a record was being kept of the number of insured persons who received attention. During the month of February they treated 118 cases in the accident department, which, at 2s 6d per head, worked out at £l4 10s. In the in-patient department there had been 24 cases, representing an expenditure of about £l2O. The Board had decided to pay consider- ably more money to the senior house surgeon during the next twelve months in order to stir up increased efficiency in the institution and to strengthen confidence in the management. Finally Mr Smethurst suggested that a tangible commemoration of the visit of the King to Warrington would be for the townspeople to

div.head: WORKINGMEN'S EFFORT. _ A Deficit in the Contributions.
div.p: THE WORKINGMEN'S EFFORT. _ A Deficit in the Contributions.

The conti ibutions to the Infirmary from the Workingmen's Committee for 1912 are £l4B us less thao the amount handed over in 1911. In some quarter 3 the deficit was attributed to the call made on the workingmen by the Insurance Act, it being argued that employees would not submit to the double deduc- tion from their weekly earnings. To clear away this impression we need only give an extract from Mr H J Hanipson's (hon. secretary) financia statement:— " During the year we have made it our business to find out from the various employers the effect of the Insurance Act on the Infiimary contributions. The opinion of a great majority of the employers was that no workingman had refused to contribute to the Infirmary." Therefore, in spite of the coal strike and the Insurance Act the workingmen of Warrington. have shown their loyalty to the Infirmary, and the actual deficit on their contributions was only , the balance of £125 being due to other organisationa not extending the same support as in 1911 The annual meeting of the Committee was held in the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon the Mayor (C .uncillor Dr Joseph) presiding over n large attend- ance. There were also present :—Alderman Burton (chairman of the committee), Mr G Walker (vice- chairman), Mr John Fairclough (chairman of Finance Committee), Rev H V Pigot (member of the Board of Management),Mr JII J 'lampoon (hon. sect etary of the committee and secretary to the Infirmary), Mr W Daintith (one of the two representatives on the Infirmary Committee). —Letteis of apology for non- attendance were read from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Councillor II Roberts, Mr Roger C Parr, Mr W Peter Rylauds, Mr F W Monks, Mr H Collin and Mr C Jackson Holmes, Mr. W. P. Rylands wrote expressing his sorrow at noting a slight falling off in the total subscriptions, hut hoped it did not mean any slackening of interest. It must be remembered that the Infirmary covered ground far outside the Insurance Act, and its import- ance to the workingmen of Warrington was as great as ever. There was too little in the Insurance Act to take the place of the Infirmary, and while the Insurance Committee would be competent to make a contribution to the Infirmary in payment for services rendered, a far greater part of the work done was not covered by the Act, and the cost of the Infirmary must continue to be met by voluntary effort. In his opening speech, the MAYOR said he could heartily commend the workingmen for the efforts they made in favour of the Infirmary, and also upon the fact notwithstanding the football match (although football was healthy and enjoyable if they did not get any damage done to their bones), they were present to take an interest in the institution. He was glad to find that so many gentlemen had not bowed the knee to football. Having quoted figures ,a to the number of patients treated during the year, showing that since the extension of the institution, the wcrk had practically doubled, the Mayor said there was no doubt at all that the Insurance Act did not make the least pro- vision for such treatment as patients received at the Infirmary and until some provision was made by the Act the Infirmary would have to go on as it was at present, supported by such efforts as the workingmen would laudibly make and by voluntary con- tributions on the part of others. Not only were workingmen liable to accidents and therefore more within the scope of the benefits of the Infirmary, but their wives and children met with accidents which required similar treatment. Workingtnen might say "We pay so much to the National Insurance Act and we cannot afford any more." It was a pity if that was the case bat he was very glad to hear from the secretary that so far as he knew

NOT A SINGLE WORKINGMAN had refused to pay what he could towards the Infirmary. He thought that was a gratifying faot, that the workingmen, although they had an additional sum taken from their wages weekly, were still making further sacrifices in order to support the noble institution, the Itfirmary. (Applause). Mr J U J 'lampoon (hon secretary of the committee) said that for the first time during the eleven years he had been with them he had to submit a redoved balance sheet but he thought they were all very proud of the returns,having regard to the adverse circumstances they had bad to contend with during the year. (Hear, hear.) The contributions from the various works amounted to £I,L 57 10s. 31 .as against £1,248 12s 31. f or the previous year,and witti contributions from other sources came to £1,265 lOs 4d.as against £1,413 103. 11d. for 1911. After expenses of £l6 its. Gd. had been paid they had the sum of £1,248 18s.10d. to hand over. The amount they con- tributed in 1011 was £1,397 9s. 10d. which showed that their contributions for 1912 were down by £l4B 11s. The first time the work the oontributed over £l,OOO was in 1910 when the figures were £1,014 18s. 10d. Daring the past year they had made inquiries with regard to the effect the Insurance Act had on contributions. The opinion of a great majority of the employers was that no working men had refused to contribute to the Infirmary. (Applause.) The adverse balance sheet was not owing to the working men but to other circum- stances he would not mention there.—Mr Hampson then handed the cheque for £1,248 18s. 101. over to Mr J Fairclough (chairman of the Finance Committee) amidst applause. EFFECT OF THE COAL STRIKE.

Alderman BURTON, in moving the adoption of the balance sheet,said they all recognised it was not theusual balance sheet they had had to submit,Their usual balance sheet they would find generally showed a gratifying increase in the subscriptions, In regard to the decrease of £143 us, if they would examine the balance sheet they would find that upon the whole they had come out fairly Eatifactorily. He had heard, although he could not vouch for the accuracy of the statement, that certain employ- ers had added £5O to their employees donations to the Infirmary. That was in 1911 but they had not done it in 1912. Then the Warrington Charities Committee handed them the sum of £5O in 1911 but nothing in 1912. They received £25 from the Warrington Football Club in 1911 but nothing in the past year.

div.head: OFFICERS.
div.p: OFFICERS.

The following officers were re-elected : Chairman, Alderman Burton; vice-chairman, Mr G Walker; hon auditor, Mr C Jackson Holmes; bon secretary, Mr J H. J Hampson. Mr A C BINKS moved the re-election of the hon. auditor, and said he would be glad to see next year some of the Insurance Companies who dealt with works, and workpeople coming forward and volunteering to help. They did nctlwant to press them into the service,but to get them to help an institution whici was such a good reserve for them.

div.head: VOTES OF TEIANKS.
div.p: VOTES OF TEIANKS.
Votes of thanks were heartily seo3rded the honorary surgeons, the PreEs, Mr Down's Band, Crosflelds' Band and the Warrington fale Choral Union.

div.head: MERCILESS JUDGE.
div.p: A MERCILESS JUDGE.

div.head: WORKINGMEN AND EDUCATION.
div.p: WORKINGMEN AND EDUCATION.
ARE TOO MANY SUBJECTS ATTEMPTED

"I do not go in for the exploitation of child labour. I think a child should be kept at school as long is possible." So said Mr George Walker in giving his report as member of the Education Committee repre- senting the Workingmen's Committee of the Infirmary, at the anunal meeting on Saturday afternoon in the Town Hall. Mr Walker said on behalf of his colleagues on the Sites and Buildings Commit tee that whether in the selection of an architect, school, or of school sites, he could bear testimony to the fact that there was no other influence at work than that which made for the good of the whole community. He deeply regretted the criticism of the Town Ccur.cil from time to time, as "the man in the street," not knowing the foots of the case, could not always sift out the good from the bad. The only interest the Sites and Buildings Corn- ' mittee had was to do the best it could for the town. He regretted that in four years that Committee load worked so slowly that they were now only opening the fourth school. They had not moved very rapidly. Although the cost of the schools in the aggregate was very considerable, they must remember that payment was extended over a period of from 30 to 50 years, and thAt did not make a difference of 24 in the £ on the rate. Referring to the Education Committee he sometimes thought that they did not get value for the money spent. Children leaving school did not answer his ideals,and he regretted that some of the elementary subjects were very badly taught. The schools attempted too much. If the elementary schools could look more to the purpose for which they were designed—elemen- tary subjects being well taught—they would have totter results. That criticism was not his alone, and when it alsO came from such a high authority as Sir Henry Hibbert, who said that the education given did not realise hI E; anticipations, one felt justified in making it. How could they teach 23 subjects in 20 hours ? (Hear, hear.) They were likely to have a new Education Bill, and it was very probable that the school age of children would be increased. He was not one of those who went in for exploiting child labour, but there were certain circumstances under which a child was better released from school at a certain age and sent to work. There wero also circumstances when parents, for financial reasons, not always the best, desired to get a child away from school before the committee thought it ought to be reasonably exempted. But the Bill to which he had alluded was likely to get attached to it a compulsory clause compelling the attendance of young people at evening classes until they were 16 years of age. They wanted to make education attractive and get the young people enthusiastic.

div.head: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
RELIGION IN THE SECONDARY SCHOOL.
Chairman's Sharp Reply to the Rector.

A letter from the Rector of Warrington (Rev Canon Willis) with reference to the scheme of religions instruction recently adopted for the Secondary school, called forth a spirited reply from the Chairman (Councillor H Roberta) at the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee on Monday evening. There were present :—Aldermen J SmethurA and A Bennett, Councillors 1' Birtles, J Dickenson, J Wilkinson, J T Locker, R Henshall, E Osborne, Revs G C Briggs and Father N Wilson, Mrs C Jackson-Holmes, Messrs A J Jolley (deputy-chairman), H Kingdon, C E Parker, J Upson, C H Unsworth, J Jarman, G Walker, E Plinston, J Moore Murray (director of education), and R B Roberts (assistant director). Tbe letter from the Rector was as follows :

"I feel so strongly and deeply on the subject of religious instruction in the secondary school that I cannot let the matter rest where it is. and wtite now to ask if you will allow the head master to give two lesons a week on the Bible instead of using the allotted time of fifteen minutes each morning for a hymn, prayer and Bible-reading. You have given him 90 minutes a week, lie could easily devote 50 minutes to two good lessons and spend the other 40 in a hymn and prayer each day. If you will agree to this I am quite sure you will relieve the minds of many religious parents who do not, like to complain, but are greatly distressed at the result of your deliberations." The CHAIRMAN: I should suggest in regard to this letter, which I must say surprises and pains me very considerably—l think it is absolutely uajustiflable that it should be referred to the School Management Committee for consideration and report. When the Rector talks about not being able to allow the matter to rest where it is, I should very respectfully suggest to him that we are the Education Committee and we are responsible for what goes on in our schools. I say it with all respect and with great regret too, that the style or manner of attempted dictation to us which this letter conveys, in view of what,the Committee has tried to do to meet the wishes of the Rector and those whom he alleges he represents—well, to say the least of it, it is not a generous response on the part of the Rector. We are utterly unaware of the mental distress to the parents of any of the children on this very important subject. We have not had the slightest intimation from any parent, from first to last, that he or she was in any sense or degree dissatisfied with the character of the religious instruction given iu the school. Altogether I think the time has come when we have got to assert our position. (Hear, hear). Mr C E PARKER seconded the proposition to refer the letter to the School Management Committee which was agreed to.

A RESIGNATION. Mr L Greening wrote resigning from the committee, as be was unable to attend the meetings. The resignation having been accepted with regret, Mr Josiah Longlaud was selected to succeed Mr Greening. Alderman SMETHURST suggested Mr C Jackson Holmes but the DIRECTOR said Mr Holmes did not wish his name to go forward. SUCCESSFUL EVENING SCHOOLS.

Mr UPsoN, in moving the adoption of the Minutes of the School Management Committee, called attention to the fact that the Government grants in respect of the committee's evening schools were considerably in excess of those earned last year. It was satisfactory to know that those grants had been gained by increased efficiency and good work. If there was one part of the committee's work of which they might legitimately be proud, it was that which was done in the evening schools and technical institute which was one of the most successful—if not the most successful school of its kind in Lancashire. (Hear, hear). ALDERMAN BOLTON PILLORIED. A CURIOUS VOTE OF THANKS.

An amusing interlude was provided by a resolution of the Sites and Buildings Committee according thanks to Alderman Bolton for his services during the past year. Mr PARKER drew attention to the vote of thanks which he said was right enough, but he wished they could get a chairman of that committee who would attend the meetings of the Education Committee regu- larly. He did not know whether Alderman Bolton had been unwell or whether there was any other cause for his absence, but that was an important committee which had to deal with eubjects ot considerahla moment. Either Alderman Bolton should attend or the committee should kindly suggest to him the advisability of elect- ing a chairman who could be present at the committees. Mr UPSoN said the vote of thanks to Alderman Bolton discounted all similar resolutions of other committees. It made them appear to be absolutely formal whereas, speaking for the School Management Comelittee they had no intention whatever of its being regarded in that light. The thanks they offered to Canou Stevenson were most sincere, but he could not think the resolution of the Sites and Buildings Committee bore in it much sincerity. The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps it is an evidence of that gratitude which is a lively sense of favours to come (Laughter). - -

s Mr-Jou:EY : May I respectfully suggest that one of the grounds for thanks is the tact that Alderman Bolton has not attended? (Liughter). Couucillor HENSIIALL : I may point out that that skpect was emphasised at the committee mesting (Laughter). _ .
Th; HAIRMAN : It is not a new discovery, then. Mr WALKER: I think no-one doubts the sincerity of tho committee in tnia matter.

The CH Al RMAN : Certainly not. Mr WALKER : You who know Alderman Bolton will know that tie deserves as touch thanks for his non- attendance as he does for his attendance. (Laughter). The CHAIRMAN : In view of the explanation.— Mr. KING DON : Would it not be as well if somoone formally conveyed the resolution to the absent Chair- man ? Mr JanmsN : May I ask if these gentlemen are aware that there are reporters present? ... _

- The CHAIRMAN: I think that is one reason why the remari,s have been made. (Laughter). It relieves any individual member of the committee of the invidious- ness of conveying to the Alderman the pleasantries we have indulged in. (Laughter). I was going to say that in view of the numerous explanations tendered, we may now unanimously pass these minutes. (Laughter). The committee did as suggested. THANKING} THE CHAIRMAN AND D EPUT Y-CHAIR MAN.
Alderman SMETHURST.proposei a vote of thanks to
Councillor Roberts for tin -ability with which he had presided over the deliberations of the committee during the past year. Mrs JACKSON HOLMES seconded.

Councillor BIRTLES, in supporting, said that when Councillor Roberts undertook a duty he did it faith- fully and well, lie not think they would find his name on any committee whose work ha did not diligently attend to. The vote was carried with acciammation.

The CHAIRMAN, in responding, said it would be impossible to find a body of individuals more deeply or intelligently interested in the work which they had undertaken than the members of that committee were. He did not think be would be doing his duty if he did not take that opportunity of thanking Mr Murray and all the members of the educational staff. On every occasion when be had wanted information or assistance, it had been most readily and generously given at the earliest possible opportunity. He did not think he was exaggerating when he said ttat committeo were particularly fortunate in the class of official they had appointed from time to time to serve them in the very important and responsible duties which Mr Murray and his staff had to carry out. The town owed them quite as great a debt as it did to the Education Committee itself. _ _

Alderman BENNETT proposed a vote of thanks to Mr Jolley, the deputy-chairman. He said it might be considered insidous to say that the Education Com- mittee compared very favourably indeed with a certain other body which he would not mention—(laughter)— but the work it performed was tremendously important and it was carried out with efficiency and dignity, largely due to the fact that it was presided over by such able gentlemen as Councillor Roberts and Mr Jolley. Mr UPSON, in seconding, said the vote was tendered "in no Boltonian sense." (Laughter.) No member of the committee took his duties more seriously than Mr Jolley. Mr JoLLEv, in reply, said he had occasionally tired to prevent their proceedings becoming too serious. (Hear, hear).

div.head: CHALLENGE.
div.p: A CHALLENGE.
REV. A. M. MITCHELL AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTION.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Vicar of Burtonwood, writes as follows in the current issue of his parish magazine: —The County Council Triennial Elections are now over. Among the most interesting and excit- ing of the contests was that for the Winwick Division between our Vicar and the local brewer. Mr. Mitchell did not actually capture the seat but he went very near doing so and won a splendid moral victory over a strong combination of forces and a conglomeration of interests. The victory is ours, the seat is theirs. Et was a brave effort determined upon and engaged in at the last moment, supported by an intelligent and discriminating public opinion throughout the Division. If the campaign had been entered upon earlier and if again money and motors had been avail- able to anything like the extent on the other side, the seat would have been wrested with ease from the retiring Councillor. The polling, 521 and 441, reveals weakness and strength, weakness as showing no advance in the Forshaw poll (518 last election) ; strength as showing an increase of 169 in the con- te4B6 three tingc years poll (272 in 1910) A majority of 2o has been reduced to 80. The position, therefore, is this—Thu drink traffic as represented by the holder of the seat has reached its high water polling mark—it has polled its last man. Despite the frantic efforts and manifold manceuvres to drag or drive voters to the poll the total number stands at par and nothing that this unwelcome representative can do will increase his poll or his majority. To change the opposing minority into a big majority will be the easiest thing imaginable at the next triennial election.

Citizen life has been stirred by this election; the County Council is now better " understdnded of the people '—they begin to realize their duty not' to allow anybody to represent their Division—they now ask for the most intelligent and sincere, the most reputable, reliable representative that may be had. After criticising Mr Forshaw's absence from tbe division "at the critical moment," the Vicar pro- ceeds : —Mr Forshaw must not think the people of the Winwici Division are mere children to be played with, whose intelligence and commonsence can be set aside as of no moment.

We tbrow him down a friendly challenge. We ask him in the not wholly satisfactory position in which he has placed himself to resign his seat and to contest the division afresh with his late opponent. We ask him to come from out the shadows of pyramids and screens of Egyptian mummies to meet us in the open, in person and no longer by deputy, to abandon the unmanly shelter of the petticoat. We hope the challenge will be accepted and at once. A. personal contest is but fair, it is the right of the electors. Let the people see—let the people hear, and leave them to judge betwixt man and man. "Please vote for father " may be very pathetic and, withal effective but it is not Eenee, in an electioneer- ing campaign—when, that is, there is nothing else to 'be said except this—the amazing audacity of anyone presuming to oppose one who conceives a tlounty Councillorship to be in the nature of a vested interest, "my inviolablp right" from which "hands off, please."

div.head: ANALYSIS AND SYNTHESIS.
div.p: ANALYSIS AND SYNTHESIS.

Most people know what is meant by Analysis, but Synthesis is not a word in such common usage as analysis. The one is the exact opposite of the other. Clever chemists can tell by analysis what is contained in certain substances. But never, despite the closest enquiry of man, does Nature completely reveal her secrets. The most learned men acknowledge that Nature is the only true chemist who has ever worked in synthesis manner. Take the example of a simple household comm)dity like the little Greek Currant. By analy,is it has been found that it contains Grape Sugar, the best of Nature's pure nutriments, a little tartaric acid, and other substances, enti ely beneficial to health. Yet even with that accurate knowledge no one could make a Currant. It must grow and be ripened by the glorious Grecian sun, whose rays pour into it the marvellous virtues it has always possessed. Not only analysis, but the greatest doctors, including Sir Francis Laking, the King's Physician, are firmly convinced of the beneficial effects of eating Currants. If only you could make Currants,a vast fortune awaits you, but if you eat them, good health and a well- nourished body are yours. So perhaps it is as well to benefit by the analysis without troubling about synthesis. An entirely new and interesting little book, telling you all about Currants, and giving recipes for a great vaillety of sweet dishes which can be made with Currants,has just been published, and your Grocer will give you a free copy on request. The book is called "Home Recipes for Cooking Currants."

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO CHESHIRE.
div.p: ROYAL VISIT TO CHESHIRE.
County Council Arrangements.

The Chairman of the Cheshire County Council (Colonel George Dixon) at a meeting on Saturday alluded to the visit of the King and Queen to Crewe on April 21st. On the previous day, he said, the clerk, Dr Hodgson, and he went to Crewe and met the Mayor of Crewe, Mr Turnbull, and other Crewe gentlemen. Certain arrangements were made, but there were a good many other arrangements that would have to be made. Tkey had to go to the County Dairy Institution at Worleston and make arrangements for the reception there and it required ,a good deal of detailed arrangements and some little expense. They were going to share the cost of the decoration of Crewe Station and a small bit outside the station, and they also would have to decorate Worleston Institute. He moved—" That a humble address be presented to their Majesties on behalf of the County Council, and that the common seal of the Council be attached thereto."

The Vice-Chairman (Dr Hodgson, of Crewe) seconded and the resolution was carried with applause. The Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Mr W McCrackm were appointed a sub-committee to deal with the local arrangements. The Chairman said that the King after receiving the addresses from that Council and from the Crewe Town Council would go through the railway works, then tbrough Crewe, and on to the Worleston Dairy Institute.

div.head: Rev. A. M. Mitchell on the Problem of Slumdom.
div.p: Rev. A. M. Mitchell on the Problem of Slumdom.

The Rev A M Mitchell, vicar of Burtonwood, writing in his parish magaz,ne, makes an interesting comment- ary r,n "The Animal Baby "and baby shows. Latterly," says the vicar, " some daily papers have been full of picture babies, babies ! babies ! every day, babies ! babies ! on every page, babies rule the Press. The Baby Show threatens to become a hardy annual. It is a moot question whether or not these Baby Shows are unmixed blessings, whether or not they do the work they claim to achieve. There are many who deprecate, and with some reason, the cultivation of babies as possible prize winners, who object to their being exhibited in public places, to be inspected, criticised, ticketed as prize winners or labelled as 'commended,' as are show horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, dogs and puppies, cats and kittens. From the baby standpoint, the Baby Show may not be really advantageous. On the whole the ultimate effect is not likely to be good. It is not desirable to have babies fed, fattened, and increase 4 in weight just for exhibition purposes. Size and fatness, bulk, and weight do not necessarily stand for health and stamina. The gross baby is not generally the best fighter in illness. The very fat baby like the adipose adult (or Christmas bullock), is a burden to itself. Physical development may be at the expense of soul and spirit, it may tend to grossness, animalism, and nothing more." Slumdom, it is to be feared, will be little influenced by the Baby Show movement. Baby culture demands dwelling-places—the abolition of slums.

div.head: SUICIDE'S PATHETIC FAREWELL MESSAGE.
div.p: SUICIDE'S PATHETIC FAREWELL MESSAGE.

An inquest was conducted by Mr F A Jones (deputy coroner) at Warrington on Tuesday on the body of Robert Thomas Griffiths (45), warehouseman, White- cross Works 25, Wakefield-street, who was found hang- ing in his bedroom on Monday. The widow stated that her husband had been rather a heavy drinker and when intoxicated he was of a most peculiar temperament and used filthy language in the presence of the children. He had accused her of going with other men ; allegations which were untrue. About six weeks ago he had a spell of heavy drinking and she left him. She obtained employment as a weaver at Blackburn and was informed of her husband's death by telegram. She knew of nothing else, except drink that could have caused him to take his life. Harry Griffiths, deceased's son, said that during the last three weeks his father had not done any work and had been drinking heavily. He agreed with all his mother had said. He returned home the previous day and on going upstairs for some cigarettes he saw his father in a sitting posture banging by the neck with a piece of rope fastened to the bedrail. His hand was resting on the floor but the greater part of his body was suspended. A neighbour named Armitage cut the body down. In reply to the Coroner, witness did not know where his father got his drink. The Coroner : You should have tried to find out and given notice to the persons from whom he got it. The following farewell message, which was written on a piece of newspape,, was read : "To my wife, from her broken-hearted husband. I cannot stand it an' longer, so farewell for ever. God bless the children. T Griffiths." .
A verdict of" Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was returned.
WHAT ARE ATTERCROPS ? AN ILLUSTRATION AT A MEETING OF LANCASHIRE AUTHORS.

The Lancashire Authors' Association held a re-union at Blackburn on Saturday, and abtut sixty dialect- writers were received by the Vicar of Blackburn, the Rev T R Sale. In a short address Mr Sale said he valued the Association because it was a means of keep- ing in the language some of the oldest and most interesting words. He came across one remarkable example many years ago. As chaplain to Bishop Moor- house he paid his visit to Hoddlesden, a village in the hills near Darwen. In looking through the church he noticed some black-looking objects in the corners of the walls. He asked the sexton why they bad those things in the churcb, and the sexton said, " Do you mean them attercrop nesses ? " He knew that "nesses" were nests, but he bad never heard of " attercrops " before. " Are attercrops tbe same thing as spiders ? " he asked. "Of course they are," was the reply. More than two years later he was looking up something in a Norwegian dictionary, and accidentally discovered that " attercrop," or something like it, was Norwegian for spiler. There was not the slightest doubt hat the word was brought over here by some of our Danish ancestors.

div.head: GUARANTEE
div.p: GUARANTEE
The Examiner, Saturday, March 22, 1913.
WOMEN'S GHAT.

The Gifts of Easter.—The shops have not been lack- ing in enterprise in order to encourage the custom of giving presents and sending cards at Easter, and the Easter egg, in all its possible varieties, has been seen everywhere in the shopping centres. Novelties in shapeiand colourings have not been very striking, but the chief interest attaches to the contents of the egg, which may have cost an)thing from two shillings to £2OO or more. Costly gifts of je;rellery are of course wf loomed by the lucky recipients, and are all very well for those with wealth which enables them •to spend endlessly, but the general opinion appears to be that modern life affords so many occasions for present-giving tqat it is unnecessiry to make Easter another Christmas in this respect. Formerly the custom of giving presents at Vastortirle was almost universal. It was the one great occasion of the year for young people to air their new clothes and finery, and to some extent this is still the case, although perhaps less sl in the South than in the North.

Lady Emigrants.— If we attached the same import- ance to doing things by method as is the care in Germany, we should long ago have had a Government department where intending emigrants of all classes could obtain the fullest information about the Colonies. What is wanted is some official central bureau where all the facts are ascertainable, as regards climate, cost of living,_ distances, prospects salaries, drawbacks, advantages and general conditlons, which those who advepture themselves across the seas may expect to meet with. As it is, tbe educated woman who is look- ing to the Coloni?s, for hope and opportunity, has to get this information where and how she can. Simi can obtain help, in this direction, from the British Women's Emigration Association at the Imperial Institute, which publishes a magazine called the "Imperial Colonist." There is the Colonial Intelligence League, of which Princess Christian is prole- ident, giving special attention to emigration as it concerns gentlewomen. Tee Assistant Superintendent of Emigration for, Canada, will also afford detailed information about Eastern or Western Canada, and the Young Women's Christian Association has branches in the Overseas Dominions, where the lady seeking a non-resident post may obtain usefnl advice and assistance. From all these sources ieforma- tion may be obtained from people who know facts, and it is not, of course, wise for the woman especially if she has no capital and is looking for some occupa- tion, other than that of homg-help, to start without having definite ideas as to what she is most fitted for. and the condition of life she is likely to meet with. The Crawling Cure.—Crawling on hands and knees over the floor 18 the latest "beauty "fad. We have had many extraordinary crazes of this kind. Skipping digging, rolling over and over, going up and down- stairs, and carrying weights on the head, are but sometof the things that have been recommended as excellent forma of hygienic exercise. All of them have had their support for their theory from the medical profession. Some years ago crawling exercise was adopted in the London Hospital, where it has been found to greatly aid the treatment. for spinal weakness and it. is said to produce excellent results in cases of stubborn inciigention. This return to monkey fashion progress will help to confirm the evolutionists in their views regarding the origin of man, but society women are not cencerned with such matters. They have taken up that "crawling cure" to improve their health and figure. Tne Bulgarian Style.—Every season has its sensa- tions, and this spring Bulgaria has quite unconsciously furbished the greatest in the world of modes. Fashion and great astronomical bodies have one thing in COLUlLoll—thby revolve in cycles. The cycle of soft refined semi-tones, in fashionable colours came to an end just as the war cloud burst in the Balkans, and for want of a better term, the primary colours, bright red, green, blue and orange, that of anotaer cycle, were ()Med Bulgarian. The greater part of the gorgeous embroideries bearing this name are made in Switzer- land, and only a very few of the others resemble those wore by the Bulgarian peasants. But brilliant " Bulgarian " colours enter into every class of embroidery, passementerie and galon, into headgear trimmings, collars, ribbons, feathers and flowers. This stale was teutatively introduced last year, and there is every reason to believe that it will last throughout the summer, and perhaps extend its reign through next autumn. Weighted Draperies.—A great many skirts will be dtarad or tucked up on one side, leaving one foot and Rutile uncovered. The crossed drapery gives the same result. The good and pleasing effect of the new draperies depends on the way in which they are weighted. Grains of lead are largely used for this per- peso, more especially in the arrangement of tunics which do not add to the size of the hips. Some tunics have long points, and these are held down by heavy tassels. The necessary weight is also- obtained by leaded braid or tape' the latter being used chiefly in the hem, or is concealed elsewhere. This braid is frequently employed to produce the clinging or peg-top effect of skirts at the foot. Very few draperies set well, if not weighted where the folds are gathered together. Tabs, coat basques and sash ends are all weighted to keep , them in place. Blouses, Tunics and Sleeves.—A blouse or tunic, in a soft lostrous silk, is never lacking in charm, and since the makers of modes have decreed that silk attire is to be specially favoured during the spring and coming summer, there is no doubt that the lovely fabrics in silk prepared by manfacturers will be almost universally worn. A new long sleeve which appears on this season's model blouses, is put into what looks like a very short magyar. The arm hole is very large and is outlined with a strapping mid way between the shoulder and elbow. The Masculine Dinner-Jacket.—Thie may be worn with a black or coloured skirt of tweed, coating, or any of the heavier cloths. It has a seamless back, is straight at the sides, a roll-over collar, and is completed with one of the new waistcoats under which is worn, and showing above it a simple bleuse devoill of trimming,of some very thin transparent material. The coat is more often in black than in colours, and in that case the waistcoat is also black, and fashioned in a rich ribbed plain silk. The sleeves are finished with cuffs, from which depend delicate ruffles of Valenciennes lace. A noticeable feature in all the new 'bodices in Paris, is the open throat, which will doubtless find favour over here also. - -

This Season's Washing Dresses.—Bordered fabrics are among the newest designs. They never go really out of fashion. In cotton goods the Terry cloths have borders of an isolated motif, embroidered in the brightest colours on a wlqito ground. These are delightful materials. Another new catton cloth has a broad velvety stripe on a grenadine ground. As a pale sand shade so popular last year will be much worn this coming summer, cotton tussores in natural colourings are sure of a vogus. This summer's washing dresses are chiefly noticeable for the beauty of their embroidered trimmings fashioned from the materials of which the gowns are made. Linen, lawn, voile and sponge cloth are largely used for these dresses, and insertions worked on the latter material have the effect of multi-coloured macramO lace. •

SUGAR BEET GROWING IN ONTARIO. During the last ten years the beet sugar indnstry has arisen in Ontario. At the present time it is a very important industry, which is returning to the farmers large sums from small acreage. As is the case in fruit growing, Ontario produces by far Oa majority of sugar beets grown in all Canada. The Dominion last year manufa'ttured sugar from Canadian grown beets to the amount of 29,877,8571b5., and of this amount there was manufactured at the Ontario factories in Wallaceburg and Berlin no less than 22,572,791105. The acerage devoted to beet grow- ing was 10,761 acres. There are yet thousands of acres of as equally good soil which will come under cultivation for this particular purpose, for the returns are good. The average price obtained at the Wallaceburg factory was 520 per ton, and at the Berlin factory 616 dollars; this was due to the difference in the percenage of sugar cant, but the Wallaceburg are raised one ton more per acre, thus equalising tba returns. 1 hese factories utilize their by-products for cattle feed, and it is now used quite extensively by many dairymen and stock raisers, and forms an excellent rad, n along with ordinary diet. The growing of the sugar beet is in many instances just a side line with farmers, who are able to handle a few acres conveniently with their other crops. The prospects are that in the future this industry will develop very much. Cultivation is not difficult and the average returns are well over £lO per acre.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
FOOD AND THE FADDIST.

What was said at the conference called by tke Mayor in view of the Health Week reminded me of a few things which I will try to set down quite briefly. In a speech at Oxford some time ago, Mr Seebohm Rowntree observed that you can't put energy into Et man except through his alimentary canal; and Arch- deacon Madden has since added (at Liverpool) that the physical happiness of most people depends largely on good cooking, cleanliness, and sweet domestic peace. It is when you come to consider what it is best to cook and prepare for the said alimentary canal that the discord begins and we have Babel once more with us. I have myself heard a lady lecturer declare in all solemnity and earnestness (with a man in the chair, too) that it was possible for one to get drunk on mutton chops. I think that, next to that, the funniest experience I have had of vegetarian gatherings was when the pre- sident of one apologised foi baying relapsed by e.xplaining that his doctor had insisted on his return to a mixed diet, though he wished the faithful to understand that he had done so solely for beabh reasons ! What unspeakable faddists there are in the world, to be sure such as those who laboriously rise at a given hour the year round, although not obliged to do so ; those who, whatever the weather, dare not close a window, or who purposely and deliberately go insufficiently clothed, or take a daily cold bath even if they have to break the ice to get at the waters, thine who (to get back to the everlasting food question) dare not touch new bread, although they have no experimental knowledge of stomach trouble of any kind; those who go in for the fasting cure nowadays so assiduonsly preached by Upton Sinclair ; those who consume only raw food, mostly vegetable; those who have a horror of drink- ing with meals; those who hold that drink is really more important than food, and that you shculd drink deeply; those who tell us to eat fish in abundance as brain nourishment; those who declare that it contains no nourishment whatever, and that we ought not to touch it but one might go on extending the list almost interminably. As someone has remarked, there was never a time when so many people were reading books about health as at present. Mr Fletcher has taught us to go on chewing everything we put into our mouths—except water—until it has become an absolutely flavourless fluid. Ms Eddy has told us that disease is only a sort of sin. Mr Miles has set us all proteid-hunting. Somebody else,has forbidden us to wash; and a great number of other people have told us that as long as we have breath we shan't die. Meanwhile, it is well for our Mayor and his supporters in the good work to "formulate a scheme for giving lectures to working class mothers on the subject of cooking during health week." More power to his Worship's elbow. BREACH OF PROMISE.

An answer in the legal column the other week sAt me thinking of the subject as a whole. Britain is a sort of Tom Tiddler's ground for a lady plaintiff in a breach of promise action, and quite the reverse for the aggrieved male. - In France, Austria and Holland, one in the position of the former must prove to what extent she has actually suffered in a pecuniary sense. In the United States the law as to this varies very consider- ably. Germany and Italy have simple and effective methods of dealing with breach of promise, but John Bull continues to blunder along in the old ruts. As a contemporary once put it :—Be, in effect, says to any young man who has suddenly jilted a girl " This lady says you promised to marry her ; a letter or two which I have read almost prove i that you must have done something of the kind ; anyhow, she's a lady, and I take her word before yours, so pay up just as much as you can afford." But if a man raises an action for breach of promise of marriage and it happens on occasion, John Bull chuckles and laughs, and sags: "Fancy a great big man like you suing a little woman like this ! It's a scandal; you ought to know better. Is chivalry dead within your breast? Anyhow, it is a womaa's privilege to change her mind, but as you seem to take it badly, and as she has clearly jilted you why, I don't mind awarding you one farthing damages with costs to the defendant, of course." Britain' in short, is the place for a lady to sue for damage/ for breach of promise ; as for a man suing, why, he's laughed out of court, and voted an idiot. IMPROVED BOOKING DESIRABLE.

The other afternoon our busy and excellent Mayor conducted an open conference in the Council Chamber with the object of stirring up interest in the question of food and cooking so far as the wage- ,earners in particular are concerned. Of course the ladies attending wr- re themselves one and all com- petent and beyond reproach in that re,pect, and not like young Mrs Justwed. "What's the matter, dear?" asked Mr Justwed, as he came into the bcuse and found his wife crying as if her heart would break "Pm Bo discouraged." she sobbed. " What has bothered my little ife ? "I worked all the after- noon making cu,tards because I knew you were so fond of them, aid and— —" Here she began weep- ing hysterically again. "And what darling ?" "Ai.d they turned out to be sponge cakes !" Seriously, of course, one has only commendation of the work initiated last week. No doubt there is plenty of scope for it, and nothing but good should re,ult. I well remember when the Oldham Education Committee arranged to rent four cottages in that town in which to train school girls in cookery, housewifery and laundry work, under similar conditions to those which prevail in the working class homes of the town. Mr Hirst, the chairman of the Committee, declared that Oldham was lagging behind in these matters. Well, that was two or three years ago, therefore it can hardly be pretended that in the very modest scheme which the Mayor and his supporters hope to launch as the result of last week's conference, Warrington has acted with precipitate haste. PURE FOOD.

This incidentally the subject of last week's story in the Children's Corner— is a kindred topic. I have previously written pretty strongly with respect to adulteration, and need not now "pile on the agony." , The opinion has been expressed that Tennyson was not drawing on his imagination when he wrote that "chalk and alum and plaster are sold to the poor for bread." lam convinced, however, that things are by no means so bad as that nowadays. There are upon the Statute Book many admirable statutes which aim at the protection of the public from the dangers aris- ing from impurity in food, and there are many com- petent officials whose duty it is to secure the observ- ance of these statutory provisions. But it is sti- gested by Mr A G Moore, secretary to the National Pure Food Association—the object of which is to secure by every p-is3ible means the purification of every form of national food, solid and liquid. that we have by no means reached the limits of statutory protection; and that the association, while not trespassing upon the field of activity of the many very competent officials concerned in such matters, may discharge useful public purposes. I have no quarrel with this; all the same I think there has been decided improvement of late years, and that even those traders who otherwise might feel "so dispoged," are finding that after all adulteration does not pay in the long run. I believe it is just over twelve months since a lecture was delivered by Mr Ellis Richards at Queen's College, London on " Old and new ways of testing frauds." One reporter said Mr Richards shwa ed that, " according to his revelation no ordinary article of common diet is really safe from tho depredations of the dishonest manu- facturer and tradesman." Upon this Mr Arthur J Giles, of the Federation of Grocers' Association, pertinently wrote that if the lecturer really made such a sweeping statement as this, one wondered how it was that the annual reports of the Local Government Board show each year a decrease in the percentage of adulteration discovered in this country. The writer went on that a further statement as to " boric acid sausages dumped on country folk in large numbers" might be pictusesque, but hardly accurate in its inferences, inasmuch as sausages con- taining boric acid are so labelled, and country folk at least are able to read. By the way the other day I dropped in at a cafe for a cup of tea, and in accordance with recent legislati the precise proportion of preservative added to the cream supplied therewith was set forth for the infor- mation and protection of the consumer. To resume for a moment. One other sentence put down to the credit of Mr Richards was that " it was very difficult to detect real coffee berries, for Americans were manufacturing by the million imitation berries made of burnt wheat." To this it was retorted —" As coffee is an imported article, surely neither your reporter nor Mr Richards seriously asks your readeis to believe that the Customs allow imitation berries made of burnt wheat' to come into this country for consumption?

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION.

The annual general meeting of the above association was held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Thursday latit week, Mr F Emson in the chair. The SECRETARY (Mr F H Longshaw) reported a satis- factory state of affairs, showing that the membership was still increasing, and had reached to almost 100 per cent. of those eligible. Mr BOWEN (the Sports Secretary) gave a resume of tile doings of the Sports Committee with regard to rounders, football, cricket, and swimming, and appealed for general support in this branch of the Association.

After the presentation , and adoption of various other reports, the PRESIDENT-ELECT (Mr J Cann) took the chair), and on behalf of the members presented the retiring President (Mr F •Emson) with an illuminated address, as a recognition of his eight years' service as Press and Parliamentary corres- pondent. In the course of his presidents! address, . Mr CAN g;ve some interesting reminisences of the early day s of compulsory educati n and showed in a very strong light the evils of the methuds adopted in those days of allocating Government grants. The training of the old-time pupil teffhers was referred to. They were generally chosen at the age of eleven or ta elve from ' the pick of the school and tried as monitors. If they liked teaching as well as study they were at the age of 13 presented fur a candidates' examination and. having passed were " bound " for five years. Their day was made up as folio : Lessons from 6.30 to 8 a.m., teaching from 9 to 4 plus an hour or two extra just before" show day" aad then study at night. It is interesting to note that these pupil teachers might be responsible for 90 children. it was pointed out by the speaker that for many years the teacher was tossed about by varying methods and echemes. Even in these days when'teachers are supposed to be trusted and are "captains of their own quarter-decks," they are still the victims of imposed schemes and regulations. A reference was wade to the latest, the Montessori System and Dcctor Geraldine Hodgson's "The theory of the primrose path," was quoted in support of the speaker's criticisms of this system. The address concluded with an el gent appeal for more rational methods in education and greater sympathy between education authorities, inspectors and teachers.
On the motion of Mr STANSFIELD, seconded by Mr NEWBURN, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded the President for his addresi.

The following officials and committees were appointed : 7-Vice-president, Mr G Nevrburn ; secretary, Mr F 11 Longshaw ; treasurer. Mr J Upson; Press and Parliamentary Correspondent, Mr S J Price. Committee: In addition to the above officials the Misses Orton and Bro:les, and Messrs Armstrong, -Bowen, Jeffery, Knowles, Parker, Stansfield and Emson ; secretary of Ladies' Bureau, Miss Orton ; representalice n Health week _Committee, Mr J W Parker; auditors, Messrs Armstrong and Glover; Advisory Committee, Mrs Stansfield and Messrs Newburn and Upson; Sports Committee, The Misses Ewart and Turnbull and Messrs Bowen, Kilburn, Mee, Minards, Price, Sinclair and Whitehouse.

div.head: NATIONAL UNION OF TEACHERS The Easter Conference.
div.p: NATIONAL UNION OF TEACHERS The Easter Conference.

The National Union of Teachers, comprising 55 County Associations, 519 Local Associations and 78,034 members, will hold its forty fourth annual Conference at Easter in Weston super-Mare, by invitation of the Local Urban District Council. There will be prelimin- ary gatherings and excursiona from Thursday, March 20th, and the Conference will be open on Monday, March 24th, and close on tbe bllowing Thursday. Conference will be Welcomed by the Chairman of the Urban District Council; Captain Sandys, M.P. ; Mr J C Hanle, M.A., Chairman Somerset Education Com- mittee ; Rev Preb Norton Thomson, M.A., rector of Weston-super-Mare; the representatives of the Free Churches, and of the Trades' Council. A public reoep- tion will also be accorded to the Conference by the Deputy-Lieutenant of the Comity and Chairman of the Urban District Council. Over 2,003 delegates have been appointed to attend the Conference by the various branches of the Uaion, and representatives of Teachers', Associations in Belgium, Germany, Holland, Ireland, Sceiland, and the Co-operative Union are also expected to , attend. .111 r A W Dakers, B.A. (of Newoastle-upon-Tyne), the president-elect, will deliver his inaugural addrets, de:-.1- ing with current questions of great educational interest. . The Vice-President, Treasurer, and members of the executive for the ensuing year will be elected, and the result pf the poll for the place of Conference in 1914 will be aon9unoed. Debates upon the questions of rural education, age of exemption from school attend- ance, medical inspection and school clinics, chilireu's courts, acting teachers' certificate, training of teachers, supply of teachers, teachers' salaries, employment of c,rtificated as unoertilicated teachers, women teachers in' boys' schools, parliamentary franchise for women, &c. will take place during the public sessions, and there will be sessions tor the consideration of private busi- ness and matters domestic to the Union.

The I. ird High Chancellor, Viscount llaldane of Cl an, has ciasentoi to address the Conference, and it is expected that he w,ill speak upon the subject of educa- tion extension at.d retoirn, which have been announced as being among the plans of the Government An extensive exhibition of school publications, appa atm, &J., will be held. Tne Natiintl Tealperance League will entertain representatives to breakfast on the Tuesday. On the Thursday the ‘;ountess Walcegrave will receive the purses contributed ny the Narious branches of the Union towa.ds the maintenance of the 0 phaniges and other benevolent institutions connected with the Union, and will present trophies awarded to the Branches contributing the largest amount per member, &c. Sectional meetings will be held on the Tuesday of Easter week, at which papers will be read dealing with (1) The Staffing and Improvement of Rural Schools (2.) Inspection versus Examination, (3) Transfer of Children from Primary to Secondary and Technical schools. Additional features of the conference arrangements will be a presentation to the retiring president, re-unions of former training college students, meeting of secretaries of local associations, meetings of the National Federation of Class Teachers, the National Federation of Church School Teachers, Secondary School Teachers, Evening School Teachers, Rural School Teachers, N an-collegiate Teachers, a busin iss meeting of women meinters of conference, a ladies" at hone" and a conference ball. The a nual meeting of the Teachers' Provident Society and of the Teachers' Benevolent and Orphan Fund will take place, and members and officials of education committees will meet and discuss papers on the small schools problem— staffing, curriculum and financa. Facilities for chess, golf, &c, will be provided, and motor car trips and visits by coach, steamer, or train to places of interest in the neighbourhood will conclude the week's proceedings.

div.head: DROWNED IN A RAIN-TUB.
div.p: DROWNED IN A RAIN-TUB.
RETIRED FARMER'S SUICIDE AT CROFT.

Mr F A Jones (deputy coroner), conducted an inquiry at the Swan Inn, Winwick, on Tuesday, into the circumstances surrounding the death of John Daxon (60), retired farmer, Oven-back Farm, Croft, who was found drowned on Monday in a rain-tub in his farmyard. . . . . .

The widow stated that she last saw her husband alive at 945 a.m. the previous day when he left the house and went into the yard. At 10 o'clock she went to look for him and not being able to find him, she called Ellen Peace, a neighbour, who searched until 11.30 when she said she had found deceased in the rain-tub. Witness said deceased had been suffering from nervous debility for two months and had been attended by Dr Sephton. lie had been depressed but had never threatened to take his life.

Ellen Peace deposed to finding the body. The deceased was in an upright position in the tub which was a very tall one. It was impossible for the deceased to have got in by accident. Ho had not been fetching water as there was no can near and the water was let out of the tub by a tap.—" Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was the verdict returned.

Until nine or ten years ago the old school was apparently considered sufficient for the wants of the inhabitants From time to time valiant efforts were inrle by the managers to extend it in order. to cope with the growing number of children Addition after addition was made to the old school until it could be extended no further and unfortu- nately every addition that was made encroached upon the playground which was already far too small. Having referred to the steps which led to the opening of the girls' and infants' departments of the Bolton school, Mr Briggs said that in spite of the fact that the school in Wash-lane was from that stage the boys' school only, it was again overcrowded within twelve months. A .few years ago the building was con- demned as insanitary and hopelessly inadequate to meet the requirements of the rapidly-growing population. Referring to the eminently cordial relations which had existed between the school managers and the Education Committee, Mr Briggs said his own experience of the Education Committee had been a most happy one from first to last. He believed that authority wished to be perfectly fair, and to
