There was every reason to suppose that a very bright future lay before that beautiful new school. He doubted if a better school building existed anywhere—certainly he was convinced that no better existed in Warrington. (Applause.) It would have been difficult to choose a more desirable site, for it was not only open but dry. Paying a high tribute to the loyalty and enthusiasm of the staff, Mr Briggs said the managers of Ctalst Church school never did is better stroke of business than when they appointed Mr Turton as head- master live years ago. (Applause). He had more than fulfilled the high expectations they formed ot him, for he did not think they could find a keener, a more capable or a kinder Mtn. (Applause).

THE IMPORTANCE OF A WISE SELECTION. Councillor HENRY ROBERTS, before proposing 8 vote of thanks to the Rev C Briggs, said he would like to express how deeply their sympathies went out to the Queen Mother in the terrible news which that day's tress brought to them of the assassination of her beloved brother the King of Greece. Queen Alexandra had gone through the very deepest of the waters of sorrow, but one of her greatest consolations must be in the tact that the people of this great nation sympathised with her as a woman and as Queen in a way whicn did them credit but which was as little as they could possibly do for her in her great trouble. (Hear, hear.) Speaking to the vote of thanks, Councillor Roberts said Mr Briggs had only recently joined the ttducation Committee but he said, without hesitation, that his fellow-members appreoiatPd him as is most valuable colleague. (Applause.) They knew he was a ' man of broad sympathies and deep beutimeat.' that he only wished to see fair-play all round and, 'is he had very properly said, that was the policy of the Education Committee. Without fear or favour or anything which should alter their proper course, they desired first the interests of education and they did their duty on those lines, no matter whether the school was denominational or undenominational. The managers of the Bolton School, the architects, the builders and the Education Committee might he equally congratulated on the excellent addition to the Bolton School which those new premises had given them. A few months ago he had the honour of opening the Evelyn-street Council School, and he then referred to a subject which was extremely important—the early age at which so many of the children left school for work. lie would like to appeal to the parents present to do all they could to keep their children at school as long as possible and not allow the TEMPORARY DIFFICULTIES OF THE FAMILY PURSE to overcome the future interests and welfare of the children. He knew how difficult it was—nobody knew better—lot many parents he would not say burdened with largo families, because he was one of those who thought that large families ought to be, if they were not, a dis- tinct blessing to the parents, but he knew the difliculty i that parents with comparatively large families had n

making both ends meet end keeping everything as it ought to be at home. On the other band, when a child bad got to thirteen years oi age and it was a question of whether it should go to work at thirteen or four- teen, he thought that extra twelve months—or six months, at any rate—was well worth a little extra effort and personal srctilice on the part of the parents. One of the disadvantagss under which they bad laboured in Warrington was that many children when they left school bad no prospect of securing suitable employment. Parents in humble circum- stances, unless they had a certain amount of influence or association with people better off than themselves, could not get their children into the kind of employ- ment that would be best for the children in the long run and also most suitable in compliance with the parents' own wishes. He hoped before long there would be established in Warrington a Juvenile Emoloyment Committee. It was not the fault of the Education Committee that such a committee was not already in operation. They had de3ided that it was extremely important, in the interests of children leaving school, that thare should be some machinery by means of which they might be introduced to suitable avenues of employ- ment in order that they might not be turned out merely to sell newspapers or take up some temporary employment which might carry them on for a year or two until they were utterly unsuitable to take up more responsible positions. The Education Committee had tried to get such a committee appointed, but unfortunately some of

THEIR FRIENDS IN THE TOWN COUNCIL who were impressed with what they considered to be economy, on the score of the possible cost of working the committee, had been able to frighten the majority of the members with the bogey of the rates so that the committee had not yet come into existence. On Mon- day evening a representative of the Board of Education sketched out for the Education Committee a scheme in regard to which the necessary expenditure would be extremely small and if the committee adopted the policy of appointing a Juvenile Employment Committee he hoped the ladies and gentlemen present who were connected with the electorate of that ward would bring sufficient pressure to bear upon their representatives in the Council that they would not dare to do anything else but vote in the Council for the establishment of that extremely important and useful committee which would keep a full record of all children leaving school and assist them to secure suitable employment, it would keep an oversight of the children for a con- siderable period and the end of it would be that they would have a better chance in life than their parents had before them. (Applause). Mr R T Fairclough, in seconding, said the Juvenile Employment Committee would do much to prevent youths degenerating into corner boys. He believed that boys needed as much training with regard to their employment as they did in scholarship in the schools. The money spent on education was likely to he thrown ,way in rainy cases if no control vas exercised over the children after they had left school. Mr Kerslake supported and aid the managers of Christ Church School bad acted in a self-saorificing way, in the interests of the children. Ilowever well the scholars had clone in the old school, they had now to live up to the new building and that could not be done except by all-rouud effort. The vote was heartily passed. Mr Jolley proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Pierpoint for presiding. He said that Alderman Pierpoint and he were old friends and antagonists in more ways than one, but the friendly feelings had outweighed the others. Alderman Pierpoint had been a champion of progress in the public life of Warrington for merry years past. In a humble way he (Mr Jolley) had tried to be something in the same line, and there was no direction in which social progress in the best and highest sense of the word could be effected more surely than by the provision of additional and better means of education all round. By providing that new department, the committee had taken another great step forward—and he hoped that, for the good of the town, it would only be one of many steps. (Applause). Councillor Henshall seconded. Having referred to his own school days at the Parochial Schools, under the headmastership of the late Mr John Dewhurst, the speaker impressed upon the scholars that the true object of education was not merely to make them clever but to Rominaskne.Ft:rhuenmerlo)ertstsearinbos ..y,,anrd gin!egrirs. A eatests oneknowolf the old eis to be wise and the highest wisdom is to be good. ( Applause.)

J Moore Alurray supported. He said if all the school managers in the town attended to their work like the managers of the Bolton School, the dnties of the Education Committee would be much lightened. The vote was warmly aonorded and the visitors then proceeded to inspect the building.

div.head: Borough Police Inspection.
div.p: Borough Police Inspection.

On Monday afternoon la-t Lieut. Col. Eden, H.ll. Inspector of Constabulary, made his annual inspection of the Warrington County Borough Police Force. Col. Eden was met at the Chief Constable's Office, on his arrival, by his worship the Mayor, and several other members of the Watch Committee. The whole force, with the exception of a few men on duty, were paraded in the large drill room at the Police Build- ings, the mounted contingent forming up in front of the Police Station. The latter numbered eight and looked most smart and military, several of tile men having served in " crack " cavalry regiments. In all there were on parade, the Chief Constable, ' Chief Inspcctor, four Inspectors and between sixty and seventy Sergeants and Constables The Government Inspector made his usual carefu inspection of the men, clothing and equipment. Drill followed and was gone through in a smart and credit- able manner. Afterwards Colonel Eden made a tour of the offices, cells, etc. and later went carefully through the books and records of the police establish- ment. The local force, which now Includes a fairly large propo, tion of exceptionally tall men, many of whom have served in the Life Guards, looked exceed- ingly smart, and the Borough may be congratulated in having ft thoroughly efficient police organization. It is understood that Lieutenant-Colonel Eden expressed himself well satisfied with all he saw.

div.head: HUSBAND AND WIFE SHOT AT YORK.
div.p: HUSBAND AND WIFE SHOT AT YORK.

George Frederick Ogram and his wife Alice were found dead in bed at their house in Emerald-street York, on Wednesday, with bullet wounds in the head. Ogratu in his right hand grasped a revolver. He was the manager of a wine and spirit stores. He and his wife were both about 40 years of age, and had apparently lived happily together.

div.p: WIN WICK.

ELECTION OF PARISH COUNCIL.—Tho election of Parish Councillors for Winwick-with-Hulme and Orford took place in the schoolroom on Monday evening. The Rev Canon Penrhyn presided over a good attendance n parishioners. There were eleven candieates for six seats, the first six being elected. Messrs W G Wallace, farm bailiff (80 votes) ; P Longton, farmer (75) ; It Hambleton, shoemaker (59) ; .1 Shaw, farmer (59) ; _

, Norman, clerk (51) ; A Alker, farmer (47), M Meehan, and G Milner,Asylum atten-,, ants; W Morgan,electrician W P Dean, farmer ; and S W Rodgers, labourer The Chairman said he was pleased to see that all the retiring members had been re-elected, and be was sure they had always tried to do their best for their parish. He was glad, also, to see that Orford had a representa- tive, and he congratulated the meeting upon the very amicable manner in which the election had been carried out. A vote of thanks to the chairman was proposed by Mr W G Wallace and seconded by Mr P Longton. Mr Li Harnbleton supported, and said that be disagreed with a previous speaker who had said that the Council had not a great deal to do. He contended that there was a lot to be done, and he thought that if they were to do their work fearlessly, they would receive more respect from the road committees and others. DEATH OF MR A. DEAN.—The death occurred, on Saturday morning, after a short illness of Mr Alfred Dean, of Hermitage Green. He had An attack of ihfiuenza and then erysipelas, which carried him away, after a good deal of suffering. Mush sympathy is felt for his widow, whom he has left afterabout five months of married life, and his family. He was for a number of years one of the bellringers at the Winwick Parish Church, and was well known and respected.
" The Old Clock on the Stairs" and "A Fancy," by Mr Arthur Appleton ; and the solo "Alone on the Raft," by Mr B Edwards. lhere was a very good attendance.
PETTY SESSIONS.
WEDNESDAY—Before the Hon J E Cross (in the chair), Messrs John COXOD, Samuel Davies, 8 W Gould and W G Groves.

MISCELLANEOUS CASES.—Alfred Johnson was sum- moned for being the driver of three horses and a timber carriage and failing to have a lighted lamp attached to same in Booth's Hill, on February 22nd at 11.35 p.m. He was fined is Gd or 7 days. John Garvey was charged with having ridden a blo3cle on the footpath in Heatley road, Warburton, on Februar) 25th. This transgressing cost him 2s 6d,

MOTOR CYCLIST FlNED.—Another case brought bolore the Court by the police was that in which Hugh Bannerman, the driver ot a motor cycle with side-car attached, was summoned because he failed to produce his motor driver's license when requested to do so by Sergeant Washington at Heatley Heath, Lymni, at 3 p.m. on March 12th.—He was mulcted in the sum of £1 8.4 6d including coAte. BRICK WORKS LODGERS.—Thomas Gibson, Patrick McNlann, Fred Davies, Arthur Leigh, George Parkin- son, Benjamin Gaskell, John Ward, Richard Farrell, and John Bridge w-,re charged with lodging in a brick works at Statham, lATIIIM, on March 19;ti, without visible means cf subsistence. Thomas Gibson was sentenced to 14 rays inpri,onment, George Parkinson, Benjamin Gaskell, John Ward, Richard Farrell and John Bridge to 7 days, whilst Petrick McMann, Fred Davies, and Arthur Leigh were discharged. MR G L WELFORD BUMAIONED.—Mr G L Welford who has repeatedly lieured as a passive resister of the Education Act, of 1902, was again summoned for non- payment of the poor rate, £4 lOs and costs 3s 6d. He sent a letter to the clerk of the magistrates, in which he stated tbat as lone as the existing law remains in force be should continue to make his protest by refus- ing actively to pay the rats. He also said that his absence from Court did not mean a want of respect for the magistrates. The summons was withdrawn on payment of the rate and costs.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
THE LYMM BILL.—In the House of Commons on Monday, the Lymm Urban District Council Bill was read a second time.

THE NEW HIGH SHERIFF.—As OUT readers will no doubt remember, we reported in our issue of November 16th last that Mr Alfred Watkin, of Daneb .nk, Lyrnm, had, along with other gentlemen, been nominated as High Sheriff for Chesbire.—We are pleased to announce that at a Council h.ld on Monday for the annual appointment of Sheriffs, His Majesty the King selected Mr Alfred Watkin as the Hign Sheriff for county Chester.

LECTURE AT THR GRAMMAR SCITOOL.—On Saturday night Mr Arno Schmidt gave a lecture at the Grammar School on his recent visit to Egypt and the Soudan. Many beautiful slides depicting the scenery &0., includ- ing some flue pictures of the Nile, were shown on the screen by Mr W l!tioss, jun, who operated the lantern in the place of his brother, Mr C Moss, the latter having sustained a rather serious accident earlier in the day. Several bones in the back of his hand were broken through the back fixing of the engine of a motor car.

HOTRICULTURE.—The second of a series of Horticul- tural lectures by Mr R G James, of Holmes Chapel College ,was delivered on Friday of last week. Ha dealt in an exhaustive manner on the planting,pruning, and fruit-bearing qualities of various varieties nof apples and pears. Mr James said that Cheshire was very favourable for fruit growing and mentioned that farmers were taking a greater interest in its cultivation Mr James's next lecture will be held on March 28th, subject," The rose,and its cultivation." - - - -

LOCAL BUFFAIoES.—Tha chief attraction in the shop window of Mr F A Morris during the past few days has been the exhibition of some Buffalo Jewels, which have a connection with the interesting presentation ceremony that took place at a meeting of the Lymm Lodge, No. 1529, of the R.A.0.8. held on Monday night at Ye Old Fleece Hotel, " Sir " John Taylor presented Primo J Wilcock with a Propaganda Jewel ; the same Brother receiving a Primo Jewel at the hands of "Sir" Thomas Davies. " Sir" Walter Miller also gave a Primo Jewel to Bro J R Burn. Bro A E Atkinson was the recipient of a Primo Jewel from the hands of Primo J Wolfenden. There was a good attendance, many Warrington representatives being present. Capital harmony was rend ered by Primo Csoper, and Bro Craig, Morris, and Spencer. AT THE PARISH CHURCH.—At the Lymm Parish I Church on Monday night after a short service bad been conducted by the Rector, the Rev G B Thurston, ALA, an address on" How the Jews kept the Passover in the days of our Lord" was given by the Rev J J West, M.A, the secretary of the London Society for Promoting Christianity amongst the Jews. Mr West who had a table spread with various vessels and foods which bear closely upon" The Last Supper" rs as able to illustrate his address in a most vivid manner, throwing light on several passages of Scripture and on various Jewish customs. A collection in aid of Church Missions to the Jews was taken up. It was most unfortunate that several other meetings being held on the same evening prevented more persons from hearing a most instructive and interesting address. WESLEYA.N SPECIAL SERVICES.—As mentioned in our previous issue the special services that were held at the Wesleyan Church . last week have been continued into the present week. Prior to each night's service open-air meetings have been held. Last Saturday night a fellowship meeting was conducted, in which a number of Latchford friends took part. Mr Weston, the missioner, preached on Sunday morning and evening, and presided over the musical service held in the afternoon. Under the leadership of Mr H S Brown, organist and choirmastert an augmented choir gave a praiseworthy rendering ot Stainer's " Crucifixion." Mr Arthur Greenough, on Walton Church, was a pleasing tenor, whilst th baritone solos were admirably sung by Mr Ernest Walker, of Warrington. Ile collection at this service was in aid of the expenses incurred by these special services. On Wednesday evening a " Faith tea was provided, when a most bountiful supply of all manner of gifts was received. .Later in the evening the last service of the Mission, which was well attended, was held. Mr Weston preached a powerful sermon on the story of the ten virgins, and on the word " Ready," exhorting his congregation to " Be ye ready also." His farewell words of commendation and counsel to the Christians present were most solemn and helpful. A supper and testimony meeting brought a suc.essful mission to a close. This week's solos have been sung by Miss Jones, Miss Winstanley, Mr Weston and Mr T Newton. THE FUTURE OF LYMM GRAMMAR SCHOOL.—A meeting of the Secondary Schools Sub-committee of the Cheshire County Council was held at the Crewe Arms Hotel, Crewe, on Monday, when the following minute of the Lymm Grammar School was confirmed: Presented the following report, dated 15th February, of the Chairman, and the Rev J Grant Bird : "On the Ist instant we met the Rev G B Thurston (chairmen) and Mr Ridgway (hon clerk to the governors in conference at the Lymm Grammar School. We were then assured : (i) That the governors were able to maintain the school as at present on the present income. (ii) rhat further cspital expenditure would probably t e necessary shortly. OM That the governors though not very desirous, are willing to transfer the school to the County Council provided the following two conditions are observed, viz., (a) That out of the school's present income there be provided a scholarship or scholarships from the school to the university ; and (b) that the Articles of Government of the school, if and when transferred to the County Council, provide for the retention on the Governing Body of three ex-officio membess named in the existing scheme. The former of these conditions was urged as a strong means of induc- ing pupils to remain in the school longer than they do at present ; the latter condition does not appear to be insisted upon by the majority of the governors." Resolved : "That the above report he received, and that the Secretary for Higher Education report on the financial questions raised in the report." ' CHRISTIAN ENDEAVOUR ANNIVERSARY.—Last week end the Christian Endeavour Societies of the Lymm Primitive Methodist Church celebrated their anniver- sary. On Sunday the preacher was Mrs Johnson- Wright, of New Zealand, a former Sunday school scholar. In the morning she spoke of the" Love of God," John iii., 16, and in a concise manner showed what a power this love was in the world. In the after- noon she addressed the scholars on her old associations with the school and made touching allusions to her old teacher and fellow-scholars. At the evening service Mrs Johnson-Wright spoke to the splendid congregation present on the text a I. Chronicles, xxviii.,_ 9. After explaining the circumstances that led up to the utterance of the teat the speaker spoke of the choosings of God and then led on to the responsibility of individual souls seeking God "while He may be found." At this service the choir rendered the anthem " Glory to Thee, my God, this night" (Gounod), the solos being taken by Miss M J Appleton, and Mr 11 Clare. Mrs Wright also spoke at the Sunday evening lantern service. On Monday evening the lsdy members of the society and friends, under the direction of Miss Welford,the hon secretary, provided a most acceptable repast after which a public meeting was held. The President, Mr W T Moss, was in the chair and in his address gave a brief review of the society's history since its formation nineteen years ago. While expressing his thankfulness for its past success he hoped that it would do even better in the future. He announced that Mrs Johnson- Wright had promised to hold a series of Mission services at Lyme], to commence shortly. The principal speaker was Mrs Johnson-Wright, who, in talking about her connection with this Sunday School and Church during her early days said that her brother,her sister-in- law, and herself were all witnesses of the good that had come from them. She trsoed up the influence that Lymm had so prominently played in the chief events of her life, and ssid that if only the workers of those bye- gone days could see the harvest that their seed bad brought forth they would be delighted beyond measure. She told the Endeavourers and workers not to be discouraged, but to persevere, as the future rested upon their efforts.—The Rev R W B Whiteway also took part in the meeting. Variety was added by a pretty duet "I am Jesus' little Friend," sung by Elsie and Florence Wibberley ; excellently given recitations

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.
ANNUAL PARISH MEETING. A POLL DEMANDED.

The annual parish meeting was held in the Council School. There was a fair attendance of the ratepayers and the Parish Councillors present were Messrs J Ball (chairman), S Walsby, H E Southern, R W Copple and the Rev H I Wadeson, also A Marsh (clerk), Mr J Ruffley presided. The following six gentlemen were elected on the Council out of 10 nominations : Rev W H I Wsdeson and Messrs J Ball,L Birchall, H E Southern, J Rigby and S Welsby. A poll was demanded on behalf of the defeated candidates by Mr J Hankinson, supported by the required number of electors and the probable cost, was estimated at about .£l2.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

NO POVERTY IN THE TOWNSHIP. The annual meeting of ratepayers took place in the Great Sankey Board Schools on Monday night, Mr George Clarke presiding. The voting on the seven nomination papers banded in to the Chairman resulted as follows :—Messrs W H Ireland, 28; William Furness, 27; William Taylor, 26 ; Ralph Long, 23 ; Joseph George Pownall, 22 ; Stanley Fair, 21; and Arthur Harry Lowe, 15. The first six candidates were elected to serve on the Parish Council for the ensuing three years. A general discussion took place, and Mr Furness said they were in a happy position to be able to say that there was no district in the whole District Council where there was so little poverty, and there was not a single person in receipt of poor relief All the work on the Parish Council during the past three years had been done without involving a single penny on the rates.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PARISH MEETING.—The annual meeting of rate payers took place in the Council Schools, Penketb, on Monday evening. This being the year for the election of councillors great in -,erest was taken in the event and a large number of parishioners put in an appearance. At the outset Mr J B Aitken was voted to the chair ; 15 nominations were sent in for seven vacancies. Several questions were put to the candidates by the audience respecting matters of interest to the village, viz., children going to school at four years of age instead of playing on the main road with the possi - bility of being knocked down by motor ca a or other vehicles passing through the village ; the recrea- tion ground also was discussed, all agreeing that some; thing should be done to make it more convenient for children to play thero. Other items were raised, and several of the candidates spoke in reference to the d ifferent points raised. The voting took place with the following results :—Messrs B Routledge, 80; J G Withinshaw, 53 ; J Woodward, 50; Dr Murray, 49 ; C Wozencroft. 49 ; G Faulkner, 44 ; J Ditchfield, 43 ; W Davies, 42 ; Miss Tinsley, 40 ; Messrs W Woods, 38; J Midwood, So; H Pownall, 26 • P 0 Garnett, 22 ; W W Shaw, 12; H Hunter, 11. The Chairman declared the first seven duly elected Afterwards a poll was demanded by the required number of parishioners and the chairman said that a poll would take place.

div.head: HATTON.
div.p: HATTON.

HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY'S POSITION. A credit balance of £49 2s lid was stated to be the financial position of the Hatton Horticultural Society at the annual general meeting which was held in the Parish Room on Friday evening of last week, when tha Rev T T Lee Jones presided over a large attendance. The Secretary presented tie statement of accounts, which were passed, showing a balance at the bank of £49 2s lid. The Hon. C F C Cross was elected president and Messrs R L Warbur ton and John Done were elected chairman and vic e-chairman of the Committee of Management, Mr William Blackshaw being chos en trustee to act with Mr Warburton. The committee were re-elected en bloc with the addition of Mr H Taylor, of Preston Brook. Mr J G Hatton was unanimously re-elected secretary THE LAST SHOW. The Secretary,in his report stated that the eighteenth annual show, which was held on Saturday, August 17th, there were 33 garden entries, 646 of produce, the latter being an increase of 60 compared with the previous year. The poultry exhibits numbered 68, being exactly the same number staged at the previous show. The Committee regretted that this section was not growing or doing anything like co well as anticipated. There was a lout on the -ear's working of nearly £6, chiefly accounted for by the same amount taken at the gate, which only realized £B. Thanks were accorded those who had best plants, and also the judges. After a lengthy discussion it was decided that the society's district extended to a six miles radius and also that the show be held on Saturday, August 16th.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

WESLEY GUILD.—Mr and Mrs Gipsy Evens, of Liverpool, paid their annual visit on Monday evening. The proceedings were opened by the Rev E Morgan, who then callea upon Mr Duckworth to preside. In the course of a short speech, the chairmsn remarked upon the pleasure of again welcoming Mr and Mrs Evens to a guild meeting. Mr Evens spoke on the subject" The romance of finding buried treasure" and drew parallels from the story of the sinking of the "General Giant" with a large amount of bullion aboard many years ago. He also made allusion to the ingenious attempts now proceeding to recover some of the treasure. The story of work connected with the Liverpool Wesleyan Mission came in quite naturally and a collection in its interest was made. Mrs Evens spoke of her branch of mission work and sang a solo, " Stepping into the light." ANNUAL PARISH MEETING.
The above meeting was held on Monday evenlng in the Church of England schoolroom their being a large

- I number of ratepayers present. Tbe chair was occupied by Mr R Denham who stated the order of procedure in the conduct of the business of the meeting. There were eight nominations for the seven places on the Council. The following were the candidates— Messrs W Putter, R Denham, W S Howard, W Price, J Critchley, G Walker, J Lythgoe and C Harrison. All were elected, with the exception of the last named gentleman, in the order given. Mr George Mather presided during the election, and upon resuming the chair, Mr Denham presented some interesting facts regarding the suggested sewage echemes. It appeared that, if the leaser scheme were adopted thereby only including a portion of the town- ship, an annual increase of :2a in the I: on the rates would result. If the whole scheme were adopted, incurring an expenditure of over £15,500, the annual increase on the rates would be 3s Gd in thee.

The position was very fully discussed by various ' speakers and a resolution proposed by Mr Guest seconded by Mr P II Bennett in the following terms was carried "That in view of the fact that either of the schemes submitted by the Rural District Council, will cost in the first case considerably more than the rate- able value of the township, this meeting cannot approve of either of the proposed schemes and agrees to resist to its utmost the enforcing thereof, and that any ac.mmulation of seaage matter in the brooks of the the township, be removed by the systematic cleansing of such brooks." The question of the provisions to cope with possible outbreaks of fire was discussed, hut a proposition to provide telephonic fire alarms in various parts of the township was negatived.

div.head: DARESBURY.
div.p: DARESBURY.
DARESBURY RIFLE CLUB.

The annual meeting of the Rifle Club took place in the Council School on Saturday evening. Mr Seeker presided over a good attendance. Amongst those present were :—Messrs C H Tinsley, C Shepherd-Cross, J Armitage (Walton Lea), G Davies, W J Bleckly, Airs Bleckly, the Rev 'l7 Lee-Jones, &c. In the absence, through illness, of the Rev W S Adams (honorary secre- tary), the Vicar acted as secretary (pro tern). Letters of apology for non-attend.nce were read from Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., C.V.0., Messrs J J Whitley, J Burder, W Sloane and R 1 Wynne-Jcnes.

div.head: FINANCIAL.
div.p: FINANCIAL.

The financial statement submitted by Mr Cross, showed that the total receipts for the 3,ear amounted to. £69 Os Id, expenditure £56 8 11d, leaving a balance at. the bank of £l2 lie 23. as against £4 18s 3d for the previous year. The accounts were approved, the opinion being that they were very satisfactory. SEC RET ARY'S REPORT.

The Vicar read the secretary's report, which stated that there were 79 members last year, and that as many- as 42 took part in at least one club match or competi- tion during the season. Others had attended for practice only. The club had a very successful season, and the winning of the Astor Cup for the county of Cheshire was the greatest success, after which came the winning of the se;:ond place in the C.R.A. Cup at Urruston. The" Greenall "Challenge Cup was won by J Ravenscroft, with a very narrow margin, merely a decimal point over Albert Ryder and J H Grosvenor. The Townships Challenge Cup Wft3 won by Newton,and the Novices' Cup by Arthur de Prez. The following officers were elected :—President, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, C.V.O. ; vice-presidents, the Rev T T Lee-Jones, Messrs J E Seeker, J J Whitley and C Shepherd-Cross (bon vice-president) ; hon secretary, the Rev W S Adams; hon treasurer, Mr C H Tinsley ; captain, Mr G Walworth ; statistics officer. Mr J Wright; committee, Messrs W J Bleckly, Ade Prez, H Potts, J Ravenscroft, B Ryder, C Ryder, T Speed, G Walworth, Stephen Whitlow and J Wright.

div.head: PRESENTATION.
div.p: PRESENTATION.

Mr Shepherd-Cross, the founder of the club, who is taking his departure from the district, was presented with a solid gold cigarette case, suitably inscribed. The Vicar, in making the presentation, alluded to the many good qualities of Mr Shepherd-Cross. Mr Cross assured them that the gift would constantly remind him of the seven happy years he had spent in the district. (Applause.) Mr Armitage proposed that the beat thanks of the club he given to Mr James Ryder for placing the quarry at Iheir disposal as a shooting range. This as seconded and carried.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
NEW RUNCORN PICTURE HALL.

At Runcorn on Monday, Mr 3 Laycock applied Mr cinematograph licence for the New Palace Theatre' erected in High-street. The Chairman of the Bench (Mr Norman) said the magistrates had inspected the- premises. They unanimously agreed to grant the licence. While they did not wish to harass the manage- ment with regulations, they hoped the lighting 'would be so arranged as to prevent any cause of complaint from women and children. The bench would keep ars eye on the place for twelve months, just to satisfy themselves. COLONFL HALL WALKER'S CRITIC.

WIDNES LIBERAL CANDIDATE ON PENSIONS. The chief speaker at the yearly meeting of the Whiston Reform Association of the Widnes Parlia- mentary Division on Saturday night, under the chair- manship of the Rev J D Allan, was Mr J B Martindale, prospective Liberal candidate. Mr Martindale, ssho had a cordial reception, made

several critical references to the sitting member, Colonel Walker. In the House of Commons in 1908 he said Colonel Walker voted against old age pensions, an I now, five years after, he was saying what a grant: thing the Old Age Pensions Act was. It was a pity he failed to have the perspicuity which the Liberal Government showed in 1908 when they passed that measure into law. If the country was to be intelligently governed they must have people at the head of affairs who could take their courage in both hands when realising what the count, y act,,ally wanted. The banner with the strange device which Colonel Walker had to place before them was not " Excelsior," but " Turn the Government out" (laughter). He was, however, prepared to fight him on that issue, to see whether or not the Liberal Government was considered to be deserving of another term of office. When the Conservative patty were in power their principal feat was the passing of that epoch-making measure of Distress Committees which gave one man an oppor- tunity of digging a bole and another man to fill it up again. (Laughter). The Tories did not attach their flag to a mast, but to a weather-cock. (Laughter).
INEFFICIENT TERRITORIALS FINED.
Five Territorials were fined 308 and costs each at Lambeth Police Court on Wednesday for failing to make themselves efficient.

div.head: MR. HAROLD SMITH, MP.
div.p: MR. HAROLD SMITH, MP.
"A POOR ATTEMPT TO COPY THE STYLE
OF HIS BROTHER."

Mr Harold Smith, M.P., raised a discussion in the House of Commons on Tuesday, on the Home Office treatment of suffragist prisone, s. Ile moved a reduc- tion of the salaiy of the Home Secretary in order to call attention to the question. Criticism of tie Home Secrstar3's methods (says the " Manchester Guardian ") took exception both to his leniency and to his E see ssi ye severity—to his ineptitude and inefficiency, as Mr Harold Smith put it, in encon:aging the women to snap their fingers at the law in their war against society, and to his harsh- ness in resorting to the cruel and barbarous process cf forcible feeding. In stating his case Mr Smith rather spoiled it by an over-indulgence in small personal gibes. "I hope lam not waking the Home Secretary." he remarked at one point, resenting the Minister'n drooping attitude. And as if this were not withering enough, he presently went Cu to advise Mr McKenna either to devise some new method of suppressing mob law or to make way for somebody who would. " Let him exercise his talent—his rely great talent—for failure in some other place." Invited by Mr A F Whyte to say what would be done if be were Home Secretary, Mr Smith discreetly replied, "1 will tell you when I am," which, as Mr Whyte retorted, was a way of postponing the solution to the Greek Kalends. "And Heaven help us when i comes," piously ejaculated Mr John Ward. When the House got into Committee on Civil Service Estimates (says the " Westminster Gazette,") Mr Harold Smith, in an inconclusive speech, raised the interminable problem of the suffiagettes. Be sought to reduce the Home Office Vote by £lOO in order to call attention to the state of affairs in con-: nection with the meetings of suffragettes and the treat- merit of suffragettes in prison. Mr Smith's condemna- tions of people who incite others to defy the law were greeted with loud cheers from the Liberal benches, and he discreetly made no retort to the obvious question " What about Ulster ?" Mr Smith's plea is that " Something ought to be -done," but he did not suggest what. He denounced the Suffragettes. He denounced the forcible feeding of the Suffragettes. Be asked for some remedy, and did not say what. In a poor attempt to copy the style of his brother, the hon. Member advised Mr -McKenna to exercise his talent for failure in another department. His speech was aptly summed up by Mr A F Whyte, who said that when the h( n. member commenced his speech he thought he had a good case, but he com- pletely spoilt his case by the manner in which he presented it.

div.head: MURDER OF THE KING OF GREECE.
div.p: THE MURDER OF THE KING OF GREECE.
Warrington's Sympathy with the Royal Family.

Warrington's sympathy with the Royal family in the shadow cast over it by the a-sassination of the King of Greece was appropriately expressed by the Mayor in the following telegrams : "His Majesty King George V., London. —lnhabitan ts of Warrington humbly offer to your Majesty their deep sympathy cn the lamented death of his Majesty the King of Greece.—Mayor of Warrington." "Her Majesty Queen Alexandra, Marlborough House, London.—lnhabitants of Warrington deeply deplore the death of his Majesty the King of Greece and humbly tender to your Majesty their deep sympathy. Mayor of Warrington." The followirg replies have been received : "Windsor Castle. Mayor of Warrington. The King sincerely thanks you and the inhabitants of War' ing- ton for your message of sympathy. Starnfordbam." "Buckingham Palace, The Mayor Warrington. Queen Alexandra desires me to express to you and the inhabitants of Warrington her grateful thanks for the kind sympathy in the terrible b as she has sustained through the assassination of her dear brother the King of the Hell cues. Private Seereta, y."

div.head: LECTURE ON THE PASSION PLAY.
div.p: LECTURE ON THE PASSION PLAY.

Those who attended the Rev Father Jackson's lecture on " The Passion Play at Ob.rammergan " at the Hippodrome on Sunday evening, must have marvelled that such an idea as attempting to prohibit it was ever entertained by the Watch Committee. Although the building was crowded in every part, the demeanour of the audience was all that could be desired, the exhibition of the sacred pictures and the unfolding of the simple but deeply moving story of the Passion being followed with reverent attention. The lecturer described the various scenes of the wonderful play with a restraint which enhanced rather than detracted from the poignancy of the narrative and the significance of every incident, and in particular the blending of Old Testament prophecy with New Testament fulfilment, was powerfullY brought home. The devotional effect was increased by the sacrea music interspersed by the boys of St. Mary's ch,,ir, under the conductorship of Mr John Eckersley. The Mayor (Courcillor Dr Joseph) and numerous prominent townspeople were in the auoience. Before the lecture began Father SWARBRECK expressed the pleasure it afforded Catholics to see such an unexpectedly large audience, which would enable St. Benedict's schools to be kept on and religion to be taught in them. No better subject than the Passion Play could have been selected for an appeal to the public in that direction.—On con- cluding his lecture, Father JACK.ON thanked all who had assisted in the organisation, especially Mr Macnaghten, the managing director of the Hippodrome, and Mr Turpin, the manager.

LYMM COUNCIL VACANCIES. TO THE EDITOR OF THE EXASHNER. Sir,—As one who watched with considerable interest and amusement the evolutions of the party who so strenuously opposed the C. tineil on the waterworks questi n I am amazed to see that these people are not opposing a single one of the retiring members at the elections next month. Especially would I point out the singularity of these proceedings in the Heatley District where the strength of the opposition was supposed to lie. There you have a Councillor retiring and from the fierce denunciations, fiery eloquence somewhat mixed) which paeeed for argument at the waterworks meetir gs, it was generally expected that the representatives of the wards would surely be opposed when next they sought re-election. What has become of the gentleman who made special enquiries from Chester respecting the much debated ifootne and who made scrupulous examinations of dry water tunnels ? Surely such zeal deserves to shine in the Council and not merely in a rail. ay compartment. We are then to believe that the electors are to be denied the inestimable privilege of recording their votes because, their would-be leaders are men of words only. Lymm and district is cursed by having a large number of residents whose only object in life is to criticise and condemn and who never by deeds help those who are, so far as possible, doing their best for the di-trict. If these people cannot " screw up " courage to run in opposition to the sitting members let them cease their carping and return to their gardens to contem- plate what a lot of woik authorised and unauthorised s done by.

div.p: The Exanainor, -,aturdav, March 22 1913.
reasons which have ;ed to the abandonment of the "closed &or " sttitule, and the desire in many quarters to enter upon overtures 0 the borough with a view t, joining forces.

Mr IA-estbrOnk readily consented to outline the pros arid cons of the question as they present themselves to hon. At the outset he pointed rut that on at least two occasions the question of the amalgamation of Stockton Heath or alternatively the appl cation for Urban pewers had received careful and painstaking coneideration at the hands of the Parish Council as a whole or from a special co nmittee appointed (Zr? hoc. A maluaroarion was on both occ esions ruled out as then being inopportune, while the question of Urban power.; was exhaustively gone into and unanimously repnried to be out of toe question, the chief ground bring that the whole of the establishment expenses would be thrown upon the ne et area, which must necessarily be elm Avveat restricted, turd that there would not he a sufficient saving in the contributions to minty and other expenditure under the present system to co riperreate f 1- the change. "As was intimated by more than one speaker at the parish meeting " continued Mr Westbrook "the question of the amalgamation with Warrington has recently occupied the attention of the members of the Council, and there can be no doubt that it has become a more general topic of discussion owing to the reoent rise in the local rates. In toy opinion it would be incorrect to say that any large number of people in the parish have suddenly become 'converted' to . the idea of jAning ariington, but at the same time circumstanczs have cauied even those who were at one time strongly opposed to the union to incline their ears more attentviely to tire proposal. These circumstances, of course, include the iisi; g rates and it hems also become appareLt that, va hit the increased population of the village, the questi. n of burial ground accommodation will in the not very disraut future become a pressing one. Many are also of the opinion that street lighting amid sanitary matters would be more efficiently dealt with if the parish were a part of the borough. 'Then, of course, there was the crowning incident of the absent lirebell which, by being unhung,appears to have caused the minds of many to °notate unhinged. Personally and I think I could say that every man on tne Council would be wide-awake enough to agree —if it can be shown that there is a a advantage to be gained by joining the municipality, we should fall in with and support the idea. But to this, as to all que,tions, there are two sides. Something was said the other night abeut getting differential rating. The value of this differential rating will, to my mind, be very much depreciated, if Warrington gets the idea that Stockton Heath is hungering and thirsting to be taken in. Even if you want to sell your horse, it is not prudent to let the man in the market know that you are too anxious to do so." Mr WestbroJe went on to suggest that the special parish meeting which is to be held on March 31st, might do well to decide on the appointment of a com- mittee consistiug of the new Parish Councillors and other protninent ratepayers to give further careful coneideration to the question. nee .disclaimed any attitude of peYsonal hostility tewards the Corporation of Warringten, but said that, having been elected by the ratepayers of Stockton Heath, he had always taken the line that Stockton Heath people were entitled to have their battle fought as stroogly and per i ste utly as Warring ton people were to have theirs. In lighter vein Mr Westbrook called attention to one aspect of .the amalgamation project which had not received public mention. " The inclusion of the parish in the borough" he said "would bring the two village public houens within the jurisdiction of the borough licensing law and would consequently enable them to remain open one hour longer each eveoieg. This point will b 3 viewed with varied feelings by at least two sets of parties, and the rabid teetotaller will have to decide whether be will prefer to suffer all the ills to which he considers himself subject by uou- inclusion, or be a party t ) allowing the publicaa an extra hour in which t dispense his beverages." Mr Westbrook expressed the opinion that what- ever Stockton Heath itself might say on the question of amalgamation, a strong tight against it vvouid undoubtedly be put up by the Cheshire County Council and the Hum corn Rural Distiict. Council, to both of which authorities St ,ckt in Heath is a very valuable ratepaying asset. If the Warrington Corporation did move in the matter, they would be well advised to seek the inclusion not only of Stockton Heath but of Latchford Without and Walton Inferior. ." It is considered by some " continued Mr West- brciok " that Stockton Heath owes something to Warriugton bec else toot of its residents find employment in the Borough. I have, however, never been able to follow that line of reasoeing as an argu- ment in favour of amalgamation. Warrington owes something to Stockton Heath, in that she provides it with such a valuable lung of pure air and good sleeping accommodation for so many of its workers. It cannot, however, be denied that there is a general feeling in the parish that the matter should be gone into, nut personally I do not think the overtures should come from Stockten Heath in the first instance. A nifferential rate—such as was granted when Wilderspool was severed from the ' tow eship of Appleton, as it then eras -should certainly be asked for as one of the terms on which Stockton Heath would favourably regard the proposal Every ca,e must be taken that the irritation of the recent rise in the rates does not cause us hastily to jump out f the frying pan into the fire, because there are indications that the rates of Warrington are likely to continue their upward tendency." 1.1- Westbrook regards the question of Urban powers as being, for the present, outside the range of practical politics. It must, however, be borne in mind that the more the traffic on the Ship Canal increased arid the. longer Warrington Corporation was apparently careless as to the serious blecks caused by the Wilderspool cross- ing railway gates, the greater would be the tendency to keep people on the Stockton Heath side of the Ship Canal and for the village to increase in importance as a 'shopping centre. The time might come when Stockton Heath would have grown into a sufficiestly large bulb that,with Latchford Without plus Walton Inferior ar.d a portion of Grappenhall and Appleton, an area could be constituted which would justify the establishment of an Urban District Council.

div.p: PROPOSED AMALGAMATION WITH WARRING TON.
A Striking C

Should Stockton Heath seek amalgamation with the borough of Warriugton ? A few years ago any such question would have been regarded by most of the dwellers in the Cheshire suburb as unworthy of serioui consideration but it is obvious that the force of cir- cumstances has at last brought incurooration within the range of immediately practical politics. There is bitter dissatisfaction at the constantly increasing rates, due to a large extent to County Council expencdture on new schools and roads, and many of the inhabitants are disppsed to argue that the village would benefit con- siderably by throwing in its 1 t with the municipality which controls its gas and water supplies, as well as its tramway service. An alternative project which has occupied the attention of the Parish Council is that art Urban - District, consisting of Stockton Heath, Latchford Without and Walton, should be formed, but we hear that the-majority of the village ruleis are now converted to the idea of amalgamation with Warrington as probabiy presenting the mole economical and efficient solution, that is, if the move can be wade without undue precipitation or loss of dignity. The question was the chief topic of debate at the annual parish meeting on Monday evening al,d, so desirous were the ratepayers there aasembled to wake a a test at the forthcoming elections, that it was decided to hold a special meeting to argue the prcs and cons on Mon, the 31st inst. Mr T DEAKIN, who introduced the Etf,ject, frankly declared that the time was opportune for them to approach the Corporation of Warrington with a view of taking Stockton Heath over. Look- ing at the question from the ratepa)ers' standpoint, the rates of Stockton Heath were only about Is. 10d. below those of Warrington.. If they formed an Urban District their rates were ' bound to increase to that extent end they might hive to go to Warrington in the end. Then they would have all their establishment charges to meet. They had been told that it took about three years to get a reply from the Local Government Board on some questions although he understood that in Warrington it took only three months—so a great deal of time might be

lost by a small community like theirs. Stockton Hew h was no longer a village but a town. The time was opportune to ask for incorporation. He believed the WARRINGTON COUNCILLORS HAD SO MUCH AUDACITY that they believed Stockton Heath would go and kneel to them and beseech them to take them over. (Laughter.) Iu the event of amalgamation Stocktou Heath would no doubt have a diffeleatial rate for some years, and if the Council allowed them the rate they were paying now, they could gain iu the end, becau,e he understood their rates were bound to go up still further and no power on earth could atop them. If they amalgamated, toe extra halfpenny on the train fare to Stockton Heath would probably be immediately knocked off. They already obtained their gas and water from Warrington and they would probably get them at the same rate as residents within the borough if they joined Warrington. It would mean a saving to the parish all round and they would have representatives on the Corporation to safe- guard their interests. With all respeJt to the coun- cillors, who had managed the affai-s of the village so long, he thought they would have better management under the Warrington Corporation. He proposed that a referendum of the village be taken on the question. Mr Griffin suggested that the candidates for Parish Council honours should fight the election on tie amalgamation question. Ile believed it would be a grand thing for .he district if it were taken over by Warrington. It was bound to come and delays would be dangerous. 'the Chairman said his private views co-incided with those of the last speaker. A month or two ago the Parish Council devoted an evening to the question and their unanimous opinion was that some effort should be made. They were very glad that the question had been brought forward so that it could be deuided at a parish meeting or by referendum. The Council was entirely in the hands of the parishioners. Mr G Davey-Smith said emalgamation was a big ques- tion and would require a great deal of discussion. He suggested that a special meeting should be called to thrash it out.

Mr A Bottomley said a rate of 6s 2d in the in Stockton Heath could not be compared, on equal terms, with one of a like amount in Warrington. It they took a house in Stockton Heath, rented at £3O per annum, 121- per cent had to be deducted to arrive at the rateable value which consequently came to £23 51 That meant that on a rate of 6s 23 in the £, the amount payable would be 261 times 6a 2J. The deduction on a similar house in Warrington would be 15 per cent,which would bring the rateable value down to .C 25 10s. The rate would therefore be only *.-:sil times 63 2d, as against 261 times in Stockton Heath. Mr Harold Houghton said it was evident that th.re was considerable feeling on the question of inclu, ion in the borough. Ile suggested that when the election took place, the voting paper should bear the qnestion : " Are you in favour of approaching the Warrington Corporation for inclusion in their area ? The election I of Parisi) Councillors and the question of amalgamation could then be decided at the kaate time, if such pro- cedure were legal. The Chairman : It cannot legally be done. The two questions are entirely separate. Mr J W Bouchier proposed that a special meeting of ratepayers be called to discuss the quet.tion and instruct the new Parish Council as to the steps to be taken. He was quite in accord with everything that bad been said with regard to incorporation with tanr- ringtou. It ought to have been done years ego and the parish would have been in a much better position to-day. Mr John Lord seconded, and expressed the hope that each of the candidates would attend the parish meet- ing and give the ratepayers his viects on the proposal. Mr J Hallows said the Parish Council and Parochial Committee,to amen almost were in'favonr of approach- ing Warrington. They were, however.feeling their way very gently because they did not want the Warrington Corporation to feel that they wished to rush into their arms. "Feelers" had been put out to ascertain the best way of going about the matter. It was the unanimous feeling of the Council that something should be done, Mr Griffin asked whether it was proposed to hold the meeting before or after the election ? If it were deferred until after, another three years might elapse before action was taken. The Chairman pointed out that it Was necessary to

div.head: MAYOR'S ViEWS.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S ViEWS.

A representative of the " Examiner " wh waited upon the Mayor with the ol,ject of ascertaining his views on tht• amalgamation question found him very sympathetically disrosed towards the project. His Worship pointed out that some eighteen months ago at the invitation of Dr Parker,he atteuded a meet- ing of the association which has been respon,ible for the development of Stockton Heath Late. Some of the residents of the village took occasion to air their grievances and his Worship then strongly recom- mended them to come w.,thin %Vat rington's jurisdiction " I btdieve" said the Mayor "that the beietiis of amalgamation would be more immediate in the case of Stock-ton Heath than of W iniugtoii. I maintain that Warrington couiparea favourahly witn most towns in the cour,t,y in regard o amtation—in fact it may claim to he something of a pioneer. div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT'S SATISFACTION.
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT'S SATISFACTION.

Alderman Bennett also views the proposed amalga- tiou in a very fitendly light. To our rrporter he sad: " I naturally heard of the resolution of the Stockton Heath patish meeting c% it') great pleasure. Several weeks ago I brought the question of the extension of the borough before the Town Courcil and suggested that a committee should be appointed to go into the whole subject. After some discussion, it was un2ni- mously resolved that a special meeting of the General Purposes Committee should he convened with that object in view.

1 _ " In my o, inion, the time is more than ripe for a considerable extension of the borough b uudaries and many obvious mutual advantages at once suggest themselves, both in re' erence to Warrington and all the other localities concerned. Apart from such queltions as the supply of gis and electricity, better sewerage arrangements and improved tram services, the matter .is vitally important in connection with the town p!atining movement. Warrington has already decid,d to town-plan the whole of its undeveloped area, but in order to make a complete and comprenen.ive scheme, with a due regard.tvolie probandities of the fttur e. it is highly necessary to. consider a much wider area than that which it fits been found possible t i include !ri the present plan. It isouly by the harmonious and earnest co-operation of the inhabitants of all the area affected, that the best use can be made of the Act and the future growth of the town maored out on lines that are really worthy of its imp Attune."

div.head: "THE HEATHEN'S" STANDPOINT. Mr. H. J. Westbrook on the Change of Front.
div.p: "THE HEATHEN'S" STANDPOINT. Mr. H. J. Westbrook on the Change of Front.

Thr,se who are familiar with till history of the official relations between Warrington and Stockco, Heath, well know that until quite recently the powers that be in Stockton Heath have scorned the idea of throwing in their lot with their neighbours on the other side of the Ship Canal. So recently as March, 1900, a special committee of the Parish Council presented a report in which they came to the conclu- sion " after full consideration of all the present cir- cumstances, including the question of a differential rating for a certain number of years, that no sufficient advantage would accrue to this parish by its inclusion within the administrative area of the County Borough of Warrington."
The chairman of that special committee was Mr H Westbrook, and a representative of the " Examiner " called upon him on Thursday t) gather some of the

div.head: AN OPPONENT.
div.p: AN OPPONENT.

In conversation with an " Examiner reporter, one of the largest property owners in Stcckton Heath, who is closely in touck with public affairs, said that while he was naturally in favour of the developtnent of the district to toe fulle-t extent, he thought it was a mis- take to press for inclusion in the borough. The rates of S ockton Heath were still t!-; in the less than those of Warrington and he believed there was every prospect of the borough rates advancing still further. Warrington was not able to offer Stockton Heath any- thing tangible cxcept possible concessions with regard t , the cost of gas and electricity. Stockton Heath already had an adequate sewerage scheme of its own and a great part of the debt indurred on that under- taking had been paid off. He was of opinion that the County rate had about reached high-water m irk, for the village would not in future be called upon to meet ruch abnormal expenditure as the provision of the new school had recently entailed. As the advance of public expenditure Was largely due to the duties imposed on local authorities- by new legislation which applied equality to town and county, be believed that any p saille further increase in the County rate would be met by a proportioaate rise in the blrough rate. As to the fire alarm question, be ventured the opinion that the easiest way of meeting the situation would be to provide, in addition to the bell, direct telephonic communication from Victoria-square to the lodge at Wilderspool Brewery, in order that the Wilderspool brigade be promptly summoned. ELECTION OF PARISH COUNCILLORS. , -- Keen Competition—A Poll Demanded.

There is keen competition for Perish Council honours at Stockton Heath. At the parish meeting on Monday evening 23 ca.:didates were nominated for twelve seats and a crow,ied meeting dully went through the solemn farce—occanyin4 over an hour—of electing the required number—only to be confronted with a demand for a poll which renders Monday's formality quite inopera- tive, except is t;o far as the nominations are concerned The large attendance wag no doubt accounted for by the expectation of a lively debate on the fire hell ques- tion which has loomed so I trgo of late, but, strange to say, only the briefest reference was made to the re-hanging of the hell and there was no comment OD the recent disastrous fire in Grappenhall Road. Pending the election of councillors, Mr Edwin Bradshaw, clerk of the Parish Council, was voted to the chair.

The nomination papers having been handed in, a show of handi took place, the following being elected: Messrs F Pearson, 99 votes; J Whitley, 92; F Warburton, 90: H.) Westbrook, 90; A Bottomley, 84 ; J McDermid, 77 ; Joseph Jones, 76 ; F Rose, 76 ; J II Clarke, 69 ; .1 W Crossley, 67; Adam Emmett, 66; W Mclntyre, 63. It should be mentioned that Mr W Mclntyre and Mr J Hallows polled an equal number of votes (63), but the Chairman gave his cssting vote in favour of Mr Mclntyre on the ground that he had the lonser period of membership of the Council to his credit. div.head: PALACE AIM HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AIM HIPPODROME.

Schwartz Brothers are the originators of "Tb° Broken Mirror" comedy sketch and do it much better than all imitators. They have had hug°,, audiences absolutely rccking with lsughter this we" at the humour of the idea presented and the Enasterll way it is worked up. With the master on one side and the valet on the other, posing marvellously as the r,Aflection from the broken mirror, there is scope lFr mirth which the brothers employ to the full. TPe ' five Selbins present a novel and spectacular enterta!ly ment in which there is a combination of clever triolc cycling, juggling, daring acrobatics,and roller skating„; The executing of intricate somersaults on skates 9°' cycles is a special feature of the turn and ensures for the troupe round upon round of unstinted approba' tion. The four Durhauis present an acceptabl° musical act, ths playing of the overture to the ..poet and Peasant" on cot.certinas bei,,g very fine. The,' are also excert saxophonists. Abel and Welsh hale adopted the right title .when thpy style therw selves, the most eccentric eccentrics that ever. eccentriqued. They are clever burlesque acrobats, flexible contortionists and exctuciatingly funo; comedians. Miss Edna Latonne is a dashing ori" captivating male impersonator and renders her catC songs in a infectious manner. Her "We all we°' maiching round " number proved highly popular' Tom Purslow is indeed a unique comedian, beine clever mimic and laughter provoker. His come' " duet " caused roars of laughter. Sydn,ey E Brandi, entertains in character monologues, a strong apili to sentiment being made in the story of the tramp, case of burglars t' is a laughable picture shown ou the bioscope.

BRITANNIC ASSURANCE CO. LTD., Established 1866. Chief Offices: BROAD STREET CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. Extracts from the DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending, December 31st, 1912. The Directors have much pleasure in announcing that notwithstanding a substantial increase in the amount distributed by way of claims, the net result of the year's trans- actions has been the addition of .£313,051 to the Accumulated Funds of the Company. The Directors also refer with special pleasure to the results of the Annual Valuation, which enable them to announce an INCREASED BONUS to participating Policy- holders in the ORDINARY BRANCH and an allotment of BONUS TO CLAIMANTS UNDER INDUSTRIAL POLICIES. PREMIUM INCOME: £1,251,669. TOTAL INCOME: 4.,383,614. TOTAL CLAIMS PAID: £8,761,989. ACCUMULATED FUNDS : 13.286 905. ORDINARY BRANCH Premium Income: £237,393.

• ANNUAL VALUATION, The Annual Valuation of the Company's Policy Liabilities has been made by the Consulting Actuary, Mr. T. G. Aukland, F.1.A., F.F.A., The policies in the Ordinary Branch have been valued by a strictly net premium method, whilst in the Industrial Branch the whole of the policies have been valued by the" English Life Table No. 6 (Males)." After making full provision for the policy liabilities a gross surplus of £95,342 is brought out. The amount available for distribution amongst the participating Policyholders in the Ordinary Branch will provide a REVERSIONARY BONUS AT THE INCREASED RATE OF 325. PER CENT FO

THE YEAR to all participating Policyholders in the immediate Profit Class, and make adequate provision for the Policyholders in the Accumulated Profit Class. It is also proposed to allot a CASH BONUS at the rate of ,E 5 PER CENT. UPON SUMS ASSURED UNDER INDUSTRIAL POLICIES OF

which become claims by death or Maturity during the year commencing 10th March,l9l3,and terminating Bth March, 1914, except in cases where auditions have already been made under the terms of the policy. MEMORIAL TO THE LATE MR. HARRY FAIRCLOUGH. A silver challenge cup, with an oak panel, has been subscribed for by the members of the club as a permanent memorial to the late Mr Harry Fairclough, who was captain at the time of his death. The com- petition for the cup will take place during the summer months, and each winner will hove a memento presented to him, and his name will be inscribed on the panel. The winner of the cop will hold it for 12 months, and it, cannot be won outright. New members are being enrolled for the coming ceason, which will commence on April Ist.
